docs.title: What is MiSTer FPGA?
docs.text:
MiSTer is an open-source project that aims to recreate classic computers, video game consoles, and arcade machines using modern hardware. Software and game images run as they would on the original hardware, and you can use peripherals such as mice, keyboards, joysticks, and other game controllers. MiSTer runs on an FPGA board called the DE10-Nano, which connects to your TV or monitor via HDMI. It can be expanded with various add-on boards such as a 7-port USB hub, a 128MB SDRAM module, and either a Digital I/O or an Analog I/O board. The project is under active development, with new cores, features, and bug fixes appearing regularly.

Check the navigation sidebar to the left for documentation on how to use your MiSTer FPGA — new users can start with the Setup guide.

Please join the official MiSTer FPGA Discord Server for help, updates, and a very active community. Follow the official MiSTer FPGA X (formerly Twitter) account for updates, community tweets, and memes. Head to the MiSTer FPGA Forums for classic forum discussions. Check the MiSTer FPGA GitHub Wiki if you can't find the information you need here. Check out My Life In Gaming's MiSTer FPGA 2022 Primer Guide for a comprehensive video review of the MiSTer.

docs.title: Editing These Docs
docs.text: This guide shows how to edit this documentation site. It's similar to editing a wiki page, with a few extra steps. All edits are approved by the administrators of the MkDocs_MiSTer repository on GitHub.

docs.title: How to edit/contribute to pages on this documentation site
docs.text:
First, you will need a GitHub account:

Sign up for GitHub

Next, go to the page you want to edit and click the pen icon in its top right:

Then fork the documentation repository. A repository is where a project's files are stored; a fork is your personal copy of it where you can make changes. Click "Fork this Repository":

Now make your changes in the text editor, following Markdown syntax. The editor's Preview tab shows how your work may appear, but MkDocs-specific tags and formatting (e.g. {target=_blank}, which makes a link open in a new tab) may not display there as they will on the site:

Write a short description of your changes and why you made them, then click "Propose changes" to commit them to your fork:

Next, create a pull request — a request for the repository administrators to accept your changes. Double-check your work first:

The pull request form will appear — your last chance to check your work before asking the administrators to merge your changes into the main repository. The administrators review the pull request and either merge it or close it. Merging updates the site shortly after, so make sure everything is correct:

In this example, user birdybrain submitted a very goofy change, so his pull request was denied and closed. He was quite upset by this and replied disrespectfully — don't be like birdybrain. Be respectful and understanding, and try to work with the administrators:

Once you've edited a page this way, you should now know how to fork a repository, commit changes, and create a pull request on GitHub.

docs.title: Audio Filters
docs.text: The MiSTer has audio filters that make the audio sound less harsh and more balanced. Some old game systems were not designed for raw digital output: they had analog audio filters between the sound hardware and the speakers. These filters are generated from mathematical formulas representing common filters used in real electronics. You can find all of the filters in the Filters_MiSTer GitHub repository.

docs.title: Types of Filters
docs.text:
Arcade LPF - Filters designed to replicate the filtering of common arcade cabinets. Many arcade games' raw audio output is very harsh on the ears; using these filters can help soften the sound. 1st and 2nd refer to the number of filter passes. LPF stands for "low-pass filter", and the kHz value is the cutoff frequency.

Core Specific - Filters for specific cores. Currently there is only one core-specific filter, which replicates the filtering of one model of Super Nintendo.

General LPF - More generalized low-pass filters with a significantly different cutoff frequency compared to the arcade filters.

docs.title: Computer core Internet and console connections
docs.text: Since the May 7, 2018 release, MiSTer supports a serial (UART) connection from FPGA to Linux. Linux runs a PPP or console daemon on this connection, allowing access to the Internet or a Linux shell from FPGA cores.

docs.title: Cores supporting serial connection
docs.text:
• Minimig. Tested on Roadshow TCP/IP, AmiTCP and Miami. Supported speeds are 115200 or 230400 baud — be sure to match the OSD settings with your TCP/IP stack of choice!

    • AmiTCP provides a more complete solution with an ftpd daemon, and many other third-party add-ons are based on it — this package is recommended.
    • Roadshow works very well and is fully compatible with AmiTCP, and offers additional extensions. Follow these instructions for complete setup. It is still a paid, supported product — more information here.
    • Miami was successfully tested. The Miami settings that worked: use a PPP connection via serial.device, set the baud rate to 115200 OR 230400, RTS/CTS to on, and enable 8N1. Set the modem type to null modem. Manually enter an IP suitable for your LAN ending in 254, e.g. 192.168.1.254. Manually add a DNS server, e.g. 8.8.8.8 for Google DNS. Term v4.7 was used to test the console connection. For a more detailed MiamiDX setup guide, see here.

  • ao486. PPP and serial connections are working under DOS, tested with mTCP and various terminal software. PPP is also working under Win3.11/Win95/Win98/NT 4.0. DOS tools are here: dos_ftpd.zip. The DOS FTP server included does not support passive mode, so set your client to use active.

  • PC XT. PPP and serial connections are working under DOS, tested with mTCP/DOS PPP and various terminal software.
  • C64. Serial connection.
  • Tandy Color Computer 3 (CoCo3). Serial connection.
  • Macintosh Plus. Serial and PPP support.
  • AtariST. Serial and PPP support.
  • Apple IIe. Serial connection.

OSD provides an option to switch between PPP and Console on these cores. Both console and PPP use 115200 baud, 8N1 mode, with hardware RTS/CTS flow control for stability.

docs.title: Console connection
docs.text:
Using this connection with a supported terminal application on the FPGA core, you can access the Linux shell to do file management or adjust Linux settings if required.

No special settings are required on the Linux side.

docs.title: PPP connection
docs.text:
With this connection, the core can access the Internet. More importantly, the core can run an FTP daemon to expose its filesystem, so you can use an FTP client on your PC to move files to and from the emulated system.

The PPP daemon uses the /media/fat/linux/ppp_options file (linux\ppp_options from a PC). Most likely you don't need to modify it — a recent update assigns IPs automatically. The core gets a <your_net>.254 IP (for example 192.168.1.254); if you want a different IP or your router already uses .254, modify the ppp_options file. At the bottom of the file, uncomment and modify the last line: 

# You may explicitly define local and remote IPs for PPP link.
# new MiSTer releases don't require it anymore.
# IPs entered here will override automatically assigned IPs.
#192.168.1.1:192.168.1.10

For PPP to work correctly, make sure you see a network icon in the Menu core before starting the other core — otherwise the PPP link won't get IPs. If the core was already started, connect it to PPP and disconnect; the next connection will get the correct IP. You can also switch UART mode in the OSD to renew the IP.

All of the PPP guides below start with the same first step: in the MiSTer System Menu (Win+F12) set the "Uart Connection" to "PPP", Baud to "115200", and save it.

docs.title: MS-DNS configuration
docs.text:
DNS is not acquired automatically by Windows 95/98/NT on a PPP connection and requires manual configuration either in the operating system or in the ppp_options file on your MiSTer's SD card. The latter is the better solution as it allows multiple Windows machines to autoconfigure.

  1. Get a valid DNS server address:
    • Run cat /etc/resolv.conf | awk '/nameserver/ {print $2}' on your MiSTer or other Linux devices on the same network to get the DNS server address(es) it autoconfigured
    • Run ipconfig /all on a modern Windows device on the same network and look for DNS Servers in the output to get the DNS server address(es) it autoconfigured
    • Alternatively, use a public DNS server (8.8.8.8, 8.8.4.4, 9.9.9.9, 1.1.1.1, etc.) at the expense of longer name resolution times
  2. Open ppp_options for editing on your MiSTer SD card:
    • Located at /media/fat/linux/ppp_options when accessed from the MiSTer itself
    • Located at linux/ppp_options when accessed by inserting the SD card into another device
  3. Specify ms-dns entries with the DNS server addresses you got earlier:
    • Find and remove the # at the beginning of the ms-dns line to uncomment it
    • Modify the IP address so it's the valid DNS server address you got in step 1
    • For example, if the DNS server address is 10.0.0.138, ppp_options should look like: 
      # Specify which DNS Servers the incoming Win95 or WinNT Connection should use
# Two Servers can be remotely configured
ms-dns 10.0.0.138
# ms-dns 192.168.1.2

docs.title: PPP connection in MS-DOS on ao486
docs.text:
1. Download the DOS PPPD driver: DOSPPP06.ZIP from HERE.
  2. Grab the latest version of Michael Brutman's mTCP TCP/IP applications for MS-DOS, from the 'Downloads' section HERE
  3. Transfer those zip files over to your ao486's virtual hard drive and unzip them into the directory of your choice (e.g. C:\NETWORK)
  4. In MS-DOS on the core, edit an mTCP config file — either the sample sample.cfg in the SAMPLES directory (you need to add the top MTCPSLIP line to it), or the example below (a simple text file named mtcp.cfg in your installation folder): 
    SET MTCPSLIP=true
mtu 1500
packetint 0x60
hostname ao486_fpga
IPADDR 192.168.1.254 <- Change this to reflect your network. Only the first three octets (e.g. 192.168.1), the last .254 is the default IP assigned to the core !!!
NETMASK 255.255.255.0
GATEWAY 192.168.1.1 <- Change this to reflect your network.
NAMESERVER 8.8.8.8 <- You can change this to reflect your network if you want to.
LEASE_TIME 86400
IRCJR_USER FPGA_User
IRCJR_NICK fpga_user
IRCJR_NAME FPGA_User
  5. Edit your AUTOEXEC.BAT and add the path to your installation folder, as well as the MTCPCFG variable: 
    PATH C:\DOS;C:\NETWORK
SET MTCPCFG=C:\NETWORK\MTCP.CFG
  6. The DOS PPPD driver archive includes the ppp packet driver, which you need to load: 
    epppd com1 115200 local
  7. Enjoy telnet, FTP, IRC, and other Internet applications while you use MS-DOS. Make sure you have ANSI.SYS loaded in CONFIG.SYS if you want to use the telnet client for telnet BBSes. Original discussion HERE.

docs.title: PPP connection in Windows 3.11 on ao486
docs.text:
1. Get the Trumpet Winsock PPP client
    • Download the software. Other newer versions exist, but be warned: only version 3.0 will work.
      • Trumpet Winsock 3.0
  2. License the software — it is still (time-limited) shareware. Once you acquire a license, enter the details in Tcpman under the "Special" menu in "Password registration".
  3. Configure Software
    • Start Tcpman
    • Under File-->PPP Options ensure all checkboxes are unchecked and the text boxes are blank.
    • Under File-->Setup, enter an "IP Address" suitable for your LAN (e.g. 192.168.1.254) and a "DNS Server(s)" (e.g. 192.168.1.1)
      • Under the Driver section select the PPP radio button and click on "Dialer settings..."
    • In the "Dialer settings..."
      • "COMM port" COM1
      • "Baud rate" 115200

docs.title: PPP connection in Windows 95/98 on ao486
docs.text:
1. Get the modem driver from HERE and transfer it to your VHD or a floppy image
    • Click the Windows 95 Start button, point to Settings, and then click Control Panel. Double-click Add New Hardware
    • Select No when Windows offers to search for new hardware. Click Next, then select Modem on the next page.
    • Check "Don't detect my modem", then "Have Disk" on the next page. Navigate to the modem9x.inf location and install it.
  2. Install Dial-Up Networking:
    • Click the Windows 95 Start button, point to Settings, and then click Control Panel. Double-click Add/Remove Programs.
    • Click the Windows Setup tab. Select Communications. Click Details, select Dial-Up Networking and click OK.
    • Click OK to close the Windows Setup dialog box. Dial-up networking should now be under "My Computer".
  3. Create a dial-up connection
    • Open My Computer then Dial-Up Networking. Double-click on Make New Connection.
    • Name it to your liking and be sure to select Generic NULL Modem. Use any phone number — it won't matter. Hit Next, then Finish.
    • Right-click on the newly made connection, then Properties:
      • General tab - make sure the Generic Null Modem is selected and set to COM 1, 115200 baud
      • Server Types tab - select "PPP: Windows 95, Windows NT 3.5, Internet" and uncheck everything except TCP/IP
    • Hit OK, then double-click the dial-up connection to connect. You should now have a working PPP connection under Win95/98.
  4. Important: DNS is not acquired automatically by Windows 95 (or Windows NT) unless you either:
    • Click TCP/IP Settings in the above Server Types tab and configure static name servers (either your router's internal IP address — usually .1 — or a public one like Google's 8.8.8.8)
    • Edit "ms-dns" lines in the ppp_options, see MS-DNS configuration

docs.title: PPP connection in Windows NT 4.0 on ao486
docs.text:
The full guide to installing Windows NT 4.0 and PPP is on the MiSTerFPGA forum:

  1. Set the UART connection to PPP at 115200 baud as described above. Important: plain 115200, not Turbo!
  2. Get the same modem9x.inf driver as in the Windows 95/98 guide above and transfer it to your VHD or a floppy image
  3. Mount Windows NT 4.0 CD-ROM image
  4. Open My Computer and click on Dial-Up Networking. When prompted, navigate to the /i386 folder on the CD-ROM, which contains the "rascfg" files and the rest needed for setup.
  5. During setup, when Remote Access Setup asks you to add a modem, hit Yes, then in the following window, check "Don't detect my modem...". In the next window, click on "Have disk" and point to where modem9x driver is.
  6. From that point on, setup will prompt you to use the Generic null modem — hit OK, hit Continue, check only TCP/IP when prompted, then Continue again. Setup will ask you to restart at some point.
  7. After installing Dial-Up Networking, you will get an Event Error at every boot. It doesn't break PPP, but you can get rid of it by re-running Service Pack 6 (mount the misternt.iso CD-ROM and run sp6ai386) and restarting again when asked.
  8. The New Phonebook Entry Wizard will appear; name your connection and check the "I know all about phonebook..." box to jump to finish. You can use any number (I used 555-1234).
  9. Click on More then Edit entry and modem properties
    • Basic tab - be sure to have "Dial using" set to Generic NULL modem (COM1), speed set to 115200
    • Server tab - uncheck everything except TCP/IP, Dial up server type should be "PPP: WinNT, 98 Plus, Internet"
  10. Important: DNS is not acquired automatically by Windows NT (or Win95) unless you either:
    • Click TCP/IP Settings in the above Server tab and configure static name servers (either your router's internal IP address — usually .1 — or a public one like Google's 8.8.8.8)
    • Edit "ms-dns" lines in the ppp_options, see MS-DNS configuration

docs.title: PPP connection in MS-DOS on PC XT
docs.text:
Follow the MS-DOS on ao486 instructions above, with two differences:

  • The XT core's PPP connection uses the COM 2 serial port instead of COM 1, so load the packet driver with epppd com2 115200 local.
  • In mtcp.cfg, use a hostname appropriate for the core, e.g. hostname PCXT_fpga.

docs.title: Serial (modem) connections
docs.text: The C64, CoCo3, and Apple IIe cores can connect to telnet BBSes through the MiSTer's modem emulation ("Uart Connection" set to "Modem").

docs.title: Serial connection on C64
docs.text:
Note that custom kernels may remove functionality required for this — if in doubt, use the built-in kernel.

The following is an example of connecting to a BBS using Striketerm 2014 and VIC-1011 2400 baud mode:

  1. Start the C64 core.
  2. In the MiSTer C64 Menu (Win+F12), go to "Hardware", set "Expansion" to "RS232", "RS232 Connection" to "Internal", and "RS232 mode" to "VIC-1011", and save it.
  3. In the MiSTer System Menu (Win+F12), set "Uart Connection" to "Modem", Link to "TCP", and Baud to "2400", and save it.
  4. Load Striketerm 2014 from d64, available here.
  5. Keep the defaults in the Main Menu (F1), ensuring you are running at 2400 baud.
  6. Save a BBS to the address book (F5); you can find some here.
  7. Surf the BBS very slowly...

The following is an example of connecting to a BBS using CCGMS Ultimate and UP9600 mode:

  1. Start the C64 core.
  2. In the MiSTer C64 Menu (Win+F12), go to "Hardware", set "Expansion" to "RS232", "RS232 Connection" to "Internal", and "RS232 mode" to "UP9600", and save it.
  3. In the MiSTer System Menu (Win+F12), set "Uart Connection" to "Modem", Link to "TCP", and Baud to "9600", and save it.
  4. Load CCGMS Ultimate from d64, available here
  5. Hit F7 to access the configuration page, then M to change the modem to "UP9600/EZ232", then B to set the baud speed to "9600". Save the config with S.
  6. Access the Phonebook with A from the same configuration page; save some BBS addresses from here.
  7. Enjoy the faster BBS experience.

docs.title: Serial connection on Color Computer 3 (CoCo3)
docs.text:
The following is an example of connecting to a BBS using UltimaTerm 4.0:

  1. Start the CoCo3 core (use Multi-pak Slot 4 Disk or Slot 2 CoCoSDC)
  2. In the MiSTer System Menu Win+F12 set the "Uart Connection" to "Modem", Link to "TCP", Baud to "9600" and save it.
  3. Mount UltimaTerm DSK file, obtainable HERE
  4. Load UltimaTerm by issuing: LOADM"ULTIMATE
  5. Hit Alt+O to open the Options menu, then M for Modem options. Use B to modify the baud rate (Left or Right arrows to change values) to 9600. The rest of the settings should stay at defaults (word length 8, parity none, stop bits 1, duplex full, terminal type ANSI).
  6. Save your changes with Alt+D, then F1.
  7. Hit Alt+A to open Phonebook, add a BBS and dial away.
  8. Alternatively, you can dial directly by issuing an ATDTBBS_Address:port. Full UltimaTerm 4.0 Documentation HERE

docs.title: Serial connection on Apple IIe
docs.text:
Apple IIe has serial support via an emulated Super Serial Card in Slot 2. While some programs can theoretically use up to 19200 baud, the author of this section found it more stable at 1200 and/or 2400 baud.

Terminal programs tested:

  • ACT - Apple Conference Terminal v.3.0.3 HERE

  • Practical Peripherals Communication Program for Apple II v.1.01 HERE

  • Start the Apple IIe core

  • In the MiSTer System Menu (Win+F12), set "Uart Connection" to "Modem", Link to "TCP", and Baud to "1200", and save it.
  • Load either of the terminal programs listed above; both have intuitive menus and 80-column modes.
  • Configure the terminal's baud rate to match the one set earlier (e.g. 1200 baud, word length 8, stop bits 1, parity none, Super Serial Card slot 2).
  • Enter terminal mode and ATDT your favorite BBS

docs.title: Console Connection
docs.text:
The DE10-Nano board has a console port. It lets you log in to Linux without a network connection and provides debug/info output that is sometimes useful for tracking down problems.

Refer to the UART-to-USB (USB Mini-B) connector on the board's right side in the picture below:

docs.title: Connect with Windows
docs.text:
Connect the DE10-Nano board to a PC using the UART-to-USB (USB mini type B) connector next to micro-USB. The PC will recognize it as a virtual COM port. Use any console application to connect to it — I recommend PuTTY.

Verify that COM port settings are correct:

  • Speed (baud rate) - 115200 bits per second
  • Data bits - 8
  • Stop bits - 1
  • Parity - none
  • Flow control - none

Quick video of connecting on Windows:

docs.title: Connect with Linux
docs.text:
1. Make sure you're a member of the dialout group.
  2. Your serial port is likely /dev/ttyUSB0.
  3. Configure it: stty -F /dev/ttyUSB0 115200 cs8 -cstopb -parenb -ixoff -ixon
  4. Watch the output while dumping it to a file: cat /dev/ttyUSB0 | tee mr.log

mr.log now contains a copy of everything shown on screen.

docs.title: U-Boot command prompt
docs.text: Once connected, hold ESC on the PC keyboard and power on or reboot the DE10-Nano (using the reset button) to interrupt U-Boot. You should see a => prompt, where you can edit kernel boot options and more.

docs.title: Using Your CRT With MiSTer
docs.text:
A few methods connect your MiSTer to a classic CRT display; the two main ones are the VGA port on the Analog I/O board and a Direct Video HDMI-to-VGA adapter plugged into the DE10-Nano's HDMI socket.

The vast majority of this content is from the guide written by MikeS11 and ArchiveRL on the MiSTer FPGA GitHub Wiki

docs.title: Boards / Adapters
docs.text:
Both methods produce a nearly identical image, which in most cases should match the original hardware's output 1:1. Their pros and cons:

  • Analog I/O board
    • Pros: extra features (buttons, LEDs, etc.), doesn't need a SoG mod for component output
    • Cons: more expensive, lower color depth in some cores, can't use Dual SDRAM
  • Direct Video
    • Pros: better color depth, much cheaper
    • Cons: no extra features, needs extra modification for component, not all adapters are guaranteed to work

Once you have either an I/O board or a Direct Video adapter, connect it to your TV with a cable and adjust some settings in MiSTer.ini.

docs.title: Cables
docs.text:
• Consumer TVs (15 kHz) with RGB SCART (via I/O board or Direct Video) — besides the I/O board or Direct Video adapter you'll also need a special cable, which you can either make or buy online. It's recommended to get a cable with a 470-ohm resistor on the Composite Sync line (it's best to ask the seller whether it already has one):

    • Some possible sources: MiSTerAddons (US), Retro Access (UK), UltimateMiSTer (PT), Wolfsoft (DE), Antoniovillena (ES).

    • A MiST cable generally works too, but may lack the 470-ohm resistor, and is generally "not guaranteed": Lotharek (PL), Amigastore (EU).

    • Another option is to use a VGA-SCART converter, plus normal SCART/VGA cables. Possible sources: Antoniovillena (SP), Arcadeforge (DE), Retro Upgrades (UK).

    • Note: on a consumer Trinitron, you may also need an extra resistor/potentiometer to fix dull or incorrect colors (forum link).

  • Consumer TVs (15 kHz) with YPbPr component (via I/O board) — a standard VGA-to-component cable should be enough.

  • Consumer TVs (15 kHz) with YPbPr component (via Direct Video) — requires cable modifications to add Sync on Green (SoG). See Direct Video - Setup for YPbPr Signals or this forum thread: Direct Video HDMI to Component CRT 480i TV by thorr.

  • VGA monitors (31 kHz) — a standard VGA cable should be enough.

  • PVM/BVM monitors (via I/O board or Direct Video) — a standard VGA-to-BNC cable (3xRGB + HSync) should be fine.

  • Commodore monitors — a cable for the 1084S monitor is sold by UltimateMiSTer (PT).

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Most of the settings changes are done in your MiSTer.ini file, which is located in the /media/fat/ directory of your SD card. When editing this file, back up your currently working MiSTer.ini, then use a fresh MiSTer.ini from the official repository (right-click this link and choose "Save file as"). All MiSTer.ini settings in this section assume this default file.

docs.title: Analog I/O board
docs.text:
• Consumer TVs (15 kHz) with RGB SCART composite_sync=1

  • Consumer TVs (15 kHz) with component vga_mode=ypbpr You might need to flip the SoG switch on the I/O board

  • VGA monitors (31 kHz) forced_scandoubler=1

docs.title: Direct Video adapter
docs.text:
• Consumer TVs (15 kHz) with RGB SCART direct_video=1 composite_sync=1

  • Consumer TVs (15 kHz) with component direct_video=1 composite_sync=1 vga_mode=ypbpr

  • VGA monitors (31 kHz) direct_video=1 forced_scandoubler=1

  • PVM/BVM monitors direct_video=1 composite_sync=1

docs.title: Connecting to composite or S-Video
docs.text: MiSTer cores now output S-Video / composite (Y/C) natively. The cores generate the two signals on the existing RGB pins: luma (brightness) on the green output and chroma (color) on the red output. An adapter board converts them to the S-Video / composite connectors.

docs.title: Adapter boards
docs.text: MiSTerAddons - Active Y/C Adapter, Ultimate MiSTer - Active Adapter, Antonio Villena - Active Adapter, and UltimateMiSTer - Passive Adapter. There's also an open-source design you can build yourself: GitHub / forum link. The active adapters are recommended for the best quality in both composite and S-Video, but the passive adapter can be a good alternative.

docs.title: Connection requirements
docs.text:
• S-Video:
    • VGA-to-component cable (only required for some monitors, e.g. Commodore 1702)
    • Custom RCA to S-Video connector
  • Composite:
    • VGA-to-component cable plus a 1-male-to-2-female RCA Y-adapter splitter cable. Warning: this method produces severe rainbowing because there is no luma trap.

docs.title: Settings with the Analog I/O board
docs.text:
• Sync-on-green switch: OFF (if you use an active or passive adapter, it generates the sync)
  • INI settings:
    • vga_scaler=0
    • composite_sync=1
    • vga_mode=svideo (cvbs also works but is not recommended)
    • ntsc_mode=0 (0 = normal NTSC, 1 = PAL-60, 2 = PAL-M; no cores currently use these)

docs.title: Settings with a Direct Video adapter
docs.text:
• A sync-on-green circuit is required. Active and passive adapters include one; otherwise see Direct Video - Setup for YPbPr Signals.
  • INI settings: the same INI list as for the Analog I/O board (the board's physical SoG switch doesn't apply — the adapter's circuit covers it), except direct_video=1 instead of vga_scaler=0.

docs.title: Other RGB to composite / S-Video converters
docs.text:
Instead of relying on MiSTer's native Y/C output, you can use an external converter that takes an RGB or component signal and transcodes it to S-Video or composite.

These converters have been reported to work well in S-Video mode, but composite has rainbow artifacts and excessive dot crawl. This is currently unavoidable and expected behavior.

One option is the Axunworks converter. It requires a VGA-to-BNC cable with BNC-to-RCA adapters, and most likely also suffers from artifacts in composite (forum thread). Other options reported to work well are converters from the eBay seller "wakabavideo" and the "Keene SCART to S-Video" brand.

docs.title: Types of CRT displays
docs.text: There are three main categories of CRTs: consumer televisions, computer monitors, and professional video monitors. Some of these categories overlap in compatibility, but the signals intended for one type of CRT are often not ideal on another. Each category has subcategories that aren't important here. Generally speaking, using a CRT with the MiSTer is not a one-size-fits-all experience.

docs.title: Consumer televisions
docs.text:
Typically these are only compatible with a 15 kHz frequency signal (the kind of signal video game consoles used). They were intended to be used with what is known as a "240p" analog signal. From the 1950s up until the late 1980s most consumer televisions only used RF video which is highly susceptible to interference, especially today. Later they began to use composite video (which is still very noisy, but less prone to interference than RF video). Some TVs also supported S-Video (a much sharper signal, more resistant to interference), but it was less common. In many European countries these TVs also supported RGB video by way of SCART connectors (which is about as good as it gets). Finally, near the end of the life of CRT televisions in the late 90s and early 2000s they began to use component video and even HDMI video.

Most used CRT televisions sold today (in the United States) use composite video or component video. In Europe it is more common — though not guaranteed — to find used CRT televisions with RGB SCART support.

docs.title: Computer monitors
docs.text: Computer monitors were usually designed for higher-resolution 31 kHz signals. They often only had a VGA connector, with very few offering other options like DVI. Since these displays were made for higher resolutions, running a 240p signal through them can produce jitter or other undesirable effects, even when scandoubled to 31 kHz. Computer monitors handle retro computer video signals excellently, as that is what they were designed for. There are also multisync monitors capable of natively handling 15 kHz (240p) analog signals. These are less common but are highly sought after by the CRT enthusiast community — if you want one monitor to handle all types of signals, consider acquiring a multisync monitor.

docs.title: Professional video monitors
docs.text:
Professional Video Monitors (PVMs) also go by other names: Broadcast reference monitor, Broadcast video monitor (BVM), Medical Grade Monitor, and more. These displays were designed for professional use, with high-quality components, and were very expensive for their time. PVMs are still made today, but they are now usually very expensive OLED or LCD displays used only in niche business applications. Old PVMs offered a wide variety of connections, sometimes all of the connectors mentioned above, plus specialty connectors such as BNC connectors, which carry the red, green, blue, and sync signals on separate connectors. Some BNC cable configurations also require a fifth, sync-on-green cable.

For retro hardware, a used PVM has these advantages over consumer CRT televisions:

  • Very high-quality designs with more displayed lines (a crisper image), better colors, or superior display technology.
  • They were often designed to be easier to service, and had better shielding against electromagnetic interference.
  • Since around the mid-80s, most of them seem to have supported native RGB input, so in theory the video quality can be far superior.
  • They typically allow very fine control of the image through many dials and buttons on the front.
  • Many support simultaneous output, mirroring the image to another display.
  • A good number of them are also multisync, supporting both 15 kHz and 31 kHz signals, and many are region-agnostic, supporting 50 Hz PAL and 60 Hz NTSC signals.

Unfortunately, PVMs are incredibly expensive today, so if you don't already have one, it may be very difficult to get one now. It is not uncommon to see a mere 9" PVM selling for over $200, and 19" to 24" displays for anywhere from $500 to over $2000, depending on the model's popularity and features.

docs.title: Direct Video
docs.text:
Since autumn 2019, Direct Video has provided analog video output without an I/O board. It offers the same minimal latency as the I/O board's VGA port and even better color depth in some cores. To use it, enable the feature in your MiSTer.ini file and attach a DAC to your HDMI port.

You may use an HDMI-to-VGA converter similar to this one.

NOTE: as of 2021-06-27, it seems very hard to find devices that are compatible with VGA-to-SCART adapters, while devices that work with VGA are still easy to find. More info: Main_MiSTer issue #410

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
Direct Video is compatible with most current cores and will be supported in all future cores coming to MiSTer.

RGBs, RGsB, and YPbPr are supported, although YPbPr has less display compatibility in Direct Video mode than YPbPr from the I/O board.

Note that output resolution and format can vary from core to core. See the analog video configuration table for more information.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
First you need a simple DAC with VGA output. DACs based on the AG6200/AG6201 chip (like the one pictured) are proven to work, fairly inexpensive, and easy to find, and many also output analog audio. The only recommendation here is not to hotplug them while the MiSTer is ON, since you might damage your HDMI port in the process.

Then you need to add the following line to your MiSTer.ini file:

direct_video=1

This enables Direct Video at startup. The HDMI port then outputs the core's raw, unprocessed digital audio/video signal, which your DAC converts. While this mode is enabled, MiSTer won't work with an HD TV or monitor: they need a standard HDMI signal, and the zero-lag Direct Video signal IS NOT standard HDMI.

The analog video signal from your DAC should work with standard CRTs if the loaded core uses standard CRT refresh frequencies (see Core Default Resolutions for an incomplete list; your results may vary). Depending on which kind of analog signal you want, some further configuration is needed, as described below.

docs.title: Setup for RGB signals
docs.text:
For analog RGB output, enable composite sync on the HSync signal in your MiSTer.ini (composite_sync=1), then plug an RGB-compatible VGA-SCART cable into your TV.

For optimal results, Retro Access sells SCART and BNC cables specifically for use with MiSTer.

DISCLAIMER: Many VGA DACs may output a sync signal at 3 volts or more on pin 13 (HSYNC/CSYNC) even when used in Direct Video mode! You will need a 470 ohm resistor on the corresponding SCART sync pin to attenuate this signal to levels that are safe for all video equipment. A variety of professional video equipment can have wide tolerances for higher-voltage sync signals, but other devices — especially external scalers like the OSSC or XRGB Mini Framemeister — can be damaged by repeated exposure to them. Unless you are 100% certain your equipment can tolerate higher voltage signals, it is strongly recommended that you either purchase a cable that has a 470 ohm resistor inline or add one yourself. Retro Access MiSTer SCART cables, for example, come with a resistor inline by default.

docs.title: Setup for YPbPr signals
docs.text:
YPbPr — also known as Component Video — is available in Direct Video mode but has limited compatibility. This is due to limitations of HDMI-to-VGA DACs, which were never designed to produce signals in the YPbPr color space, so their output is slightly out-of-spec. It is possible that your display will accept the Direct Video YPbPr signal with no issue, but it may also appear bright pink due to the way many displays process such signals. For higher YPbPr compatibility you may prefer RGB mode with an external RGB-to-YPbPr transcoder instead, or YPbPr via the I/O board.

To use YPbPr in Direct Video mode, set composite_sync=1 and vga_mode=ypbpr in your MiSTer.ini file.

You'll also need a sync-on-green circuit on your VGA connection. These can be very simple — just a diode (1N4148) and a 330-ohm resistor (any values between 270 and 390 ohms are advised; too high and the sync signal is too weak, too low and it's too strong).

Connection: from HSync -> anode of diode, cathode of diode -> resistor, resistor to Green signal.

docs.title: Doubling frequency
docs.text: This is handy for modern monitors that have a VGA input but typically can't handle 15 kHz signals and require 31 kHz analog video. Set forced_scandoubler=1 in your MiSTer.ini to turn a 15 kHz signal into a 31 kHz one (see which cores output 15 kHz video in Core Default Resolutions).

docs.title: Color Depth
docs.text:
Direct Video produces a 24-bit color signal, superior to the I/O board's 18-bit signal. However, few cores use 24-bit color, so the improved color depth may not make much of an impact depending on the cores you run.

Most cheap DACs, like the ones based on the AG6200 chip, don't produce Full Range RGB. They instead produce Limited Range RGB (16-235) or, much more commonly, a non-spec Limited Range variant (16-255). To compensate, you may want to configure the hdmi_limited option in your MiSTer.ini to adjust the signal being sent to your DAC.

  • Full Range (0-255): hdmi_limited=0.
  • Limited Range (16-235): hdmi_limited=1.
  • Limited Range common DAC variant (16-255): hdmi_limited=2.

docs.title: DIY 2-Player Arcade
docs.text:
by Sorgelig

Assembled an arcade cabinet and looking to connect your joysticks and buttons? You don't need an expensive adapter — all you need is a USB keyboard you can disassemble.

docs.title: 1. Wire the keyboard
docs.text:
Disassemble the keyboard and find the row and column contacts on its board for the following keys: 

        5,         1P coin
        1,         1P start (shift key)
        UP,        1P up
        DOWN,      1P down
        LEFT,      1P left
        RIGHT,     1P right
        LEFTCTRL,  1P button 1
        LEFTALT,   1P button 2
        SPACE,     1P button 3
        LEFTSHIFT, 1P button 4
        Z,         1P button 5
        X,         1P button 6
        C,         1P button 7
        V,         1P button 8

        6,         2P coin
        2,         2P start
        R,         2P up
        F,         2P down
        D,         2P left
        G,         2P right
        A,         2P button 1
        S,         2P button 2
        Q,         2P button 3
        W,         2P button 4
        I,         2P button 5
        K,         2P button 6
        J,         2P button 7
        L,         2P button 8

        9,         Test
        TAB,       Tab (shift + 1P right)
        ENTER,     Enter (shift + 1P left)
        P,         P (pause) (shift + 1P down)
        F1,        Service
        F2,        Test
        F3,        Tilt

You can use a multimeter to find the contacts. Connect your buttons and joystick to these contacts according to the table above. This completes the hardware part.

docs.title: 2. Configure MiSTer
docs.text:
1. Connect the modded keyboard to a USB port, start the Menu core, and go to Define Joystick buttons. Press any button: the screen shows "Keyboard ID: XXXX:YYYY", where XXXX:YYYY is the keyboard's hardware ID. Press ESC to exit this dialog.

  2. Open MiSTer.ini and add the following options, where XXXX and YYYY are the IDs you just saw:

    jamma_vid=XXXX
jamma_pid=YYYY

  3. Save the file and restart the Menu core.

  4. Go to Define Joystick buttons again and assign the buttons using the P1 controls. The screen now shows "Joystick ID: XXXX:YYYY" instead of "Keyboard ID", which means the modded keyboard is recognized as a JAMMA 2-player input device. The P2 buttons are assigned automatically, in the same way as P1.

Your arcade input device is now ready. Unlike normal gamepads/joysticks, it always assigns the P1 and P2 inputs statically, regardless of which player presses a button first.

docs.title: INI Settings
docs.text: The MiSTer.ini configuration file contains global settings, and can also store settings for specific cores. This page describes the global settings, then how to override them for individual cores, and finally some settings that apply only to specific cores.

docs.title: Alternate MiSTer INI files
docs.text:
MiSTer supports up to 4 INI files: MiSTer.ini and 3 alternate INI files, which you create manually (for example, by copying MiSTer.ini). At boot, MiSTer loads MiSTer.ini from the root of the MicroSD card (/media/fat/ when you access the MiSTer remotely or from its terminal).

You can switch to an alternate INI file on the fly in two ways:

  • With a hotkey (see the table below). This is the preferred method, because the screen may become unusable if a setting in the INI file is incompatible with your display.
  • In the OSD: press left to open the Misc Options screen and select the INI file.

The file names matter. With the default names, the hotkeys are:

Filename Hotkey Combination MiSTer.ini Controller: Back + Right MiSTer_alt_1.ini Controller: Back + Left MiSTer_alt_2.ini Controller: Back + Up MiSTer_alt_3.ini Controller: Back + Down

Alternate INI files are useful for hybrid cores that play multiple systems. For example, the Sega Master System core also plays Game Gear games. If you want a vscale_border only for Game Gear games, copy your MiSTer.ini to MiSTer_alt_1.ini and change vscale_border in that copy only; you can then switch the border on for Game Gear games on the fly. Similarly, you can switch your video_mode (screen resolution) or vsync_adjust setting on the fly.

docs.title: Naming alternate INI files
docs.text: Alternate INI files can also have custom names. The name appears on the OSD Information screen (press Left on the gamepad/keyboard, where the IP address and resolution are shown) and in the config section, where you can select the file. The regular MiSTer.ini is called "Main", and a custom file is called whatever follows the underscore: MiSTer_CRT.ini, for example, appears as "CRT" next to "Main".

docs.title: General Video Settings
docs.text:
vscale_mode - Changes how the image is scaled to the screen. 0 fits the whole image to the screen, 1 uses 1:1 integer scaling, 2 scales in 0.5 steps, and 3 scales in 0.25 steps. Modes 4 and 5 are described in Video Scaling.

vscale_border - Sets an overscan border on the screen in pixels (1-399)

hdmi_limited - Changes the color range output over HDMI. 0 = 0-255, 1 = 16-235, and 2 = 16-255. A setting of 2 can be useful if you have problems with some Direct Video adapters. Setting it to 1 can also brighten the image on screens with a dynamic backlight.

hdmi_game_mode - Configures game mode on the HDMI output. It may improve performance on some displays but worsen it on others. 0 - non-game (default), 1 - enabled.

fb_size - Affects the scaling of content drawn to the Linux framebuffer, such as when you run scripts. Best left at 0 for automatic.

video_mode - Sets the resolution for HDMI and VGA_Scaler output. This can be one of the premade values from 0-14 or a custom video mode. See the notes in the .ini for custom video mode syntax. There is also a useful custom video mode tool by morf77 available here which can be used in conjunction with a modeline calculator.

hdr - Configures the use of HDR. 0 - disabled, 1 - enables HDR using HLG (recommended for most users), 2 - enables HDR using the DCI P3 color space (adjust color controls to taste; suggested: video_saturation set to 80).

video_info - Number of seconds to display the video info in the top-left corner of the screen after the resolution or frequency changes.

vsync_adjust - Adjusts the buffer settings for the frames sent to the display. For details, see vsync_adjust. Higher values reduce lag at the cost of compatibility — 0 is the most compatible (and highest-lag) setting, 2 the least.

refresh_min - Forces a minimum refresh rate.

refresh_max - Forces a maximum refresh rate.

docs.title: Analog Video Settings
docs.text:
forced_scandoubler - VGA output will always run in 31 kHz mode (scandoubled) if this setting is turned on, useful for computer CRTs.

vga_mode - Sets the VGA output format: rgb (default), ypbpr, svideo, or cvbs.

ntsc_mode - Only applies when vga_mode is svideo or cvbs. 0 - normal NTSC, 1 - PAL-60, 2 - PAL-M. Note: no cores officially use these settings.

composite_sync - Sends the sync signal on HSync over the VGA output; needed for certain configurations.

vga_scaler - Sends the scaler output to the VGA port (either Analog I/O or Direct Video). This is usually used with computer CRTs and other 31 kHz displays that aren't compatible with 240p TV signals.

menu_pal - Forces the Menu core to run in PAL mode.

direct_video - Changes the HDMI output to an analog signal; only supported by certain Direct Video adapters with AG62xx chipsets. If you have color problems or no image, check composite_sync and vga_mode=ypbpr, and also try setting hdmi_limited to 1. To use vga_mode=ypbpr with component cables, the Direct Video adapter needs a modification that combines HSYNC and Green (see Direct Video).

fb_terminal - Best left at 1. If you have issues running scripts on a CRT or analog display, try switching this to 0 to see if that helps.

vga_sog - Forces sync-on-green via the Analog I/O board (ignores the board's SoG switch).

docs.title: Audio Settings
docs.text:
hdmi_audio_96k - Changes the HDMI audio sampling rate from 48 kHz (default) to 96 kHz. This can help with the audio of systems with unusual sampling rates (like TurboGrafx-16's 32.088 kHz).

dvi_mode - DVI mode over the HDMI connection; it disables audio transmission over HDMI when turned on.

docs.title: Controller Settings
docs.text:
mouse_throttle - Can be used to change the speed of your mouse (1-100). Good for very sensitive mice.

gamepad_defaults - When set to 1, maps default gamepad buttons by position relative to a SNES-style controller layout.

bt_auto_disconnect - Number of minutes of inactivity before Bluetooth disconnects automatically. Default is 0 (off).

bt_reset_before_pair - Resets the Bluetooth adapter before the pairing dialog. If enabled, some input devices may shut down after the reset.

docs.title: Menu Settings
docs.text:
rbf_hide_datecode - Hides the date codes from the core names in the core selection menu.

osd_timeout - The length of time the OSD is displayed when brought up with no inputs pressed. 0 - never time out; the range is 5-3600 seconds.

osd_rotate - Rotate the OSD. Useful when rotating your monitor for certain arcade cores. 0 - no rotation, 1 - rotate right (+90°), and 2 - rotate left (-90°).

docs.title: Debug Settings
docs.text: log_file_entry - Writes the filename under the cursor in the file browser for use by external integrations.

docs.title: Adding Core-specific Settings
docs.text:
It is possible to specify different settings for different cores; for example, you may prefer to use integer scaling just for the Game Boy Advance core so that you don't need any video filters for smooth scrolling. Add a section at the end of the INI file with the core name in brackets and paste your different settings below it, like so:

[GBA]
vscale_mode=1

Or, suppose you wanted to add an option to select 8:7 aspect ratio for the SNES core: 

[SNES]
custom_aspect_ratio_1=8:7

The Menu core can have its own settings too. Create a section named [Menu] to specify settings for it.

You can also make exceptions for all arcade cores with the [arcade] header in the same way, and separate settings for vertically oriented arcade cores with [arcade_vertical] — useful if you want a different default video preset for them, like this example:

[arcade_vertical]
direct_video=0

docs.title: Lag Explained
docs.text:
A common concern among retro enthusiasts is whether a device like MiSTer has lag and whether it creates a less desirable experience than original hardware.

All electronic equipment exhibits some kind of latency, but it only becomes problematic if this latency causes frames to be missed. A frame is typically 16 ms for a system using a 60 frames per second (60 Hz) display.

Lag is only problematic in a few specific cases:

  • Some older games were designed to rely on extremely quick response times (e.g. Punch-Out on NES).
  • If the latency is different between two players, it could introduce an unfair advantage.
  • Lag that isn't constant can be an issue in games that require precise movement. (Most players can adapt to lag that is consistent.)

For a more detailed overview of lag, see https://inputlag.science/.

docs.title: Where lag comes from
docs.text: There are three major categories of lag: input (controllers, mouse, etc.), processing (buffering in the core, execution or delays in code), and display (the video output to your display device).

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
For input, MiSTer primarily uses USB. In this case the overall input lag is the sum of the lag caused by USB polling and the lag from the controller itself (how quickly it processes the signals). The latter is outside the scope of MiSTer and can only be improved by using a better controller. On the MiSTer side, only the lag caused by USB polling can be reduced, and only if the connected USB device supports a lower polling interval. The polling interval is measured in Hz and indicates how often a USB device is polled per second. At 1000 Hz the polling adds at most 1 ms of lag (0.5 ms on average) — a great improvement over the default 125 Hz, which adds up to 8 ms (4 ms on average).

If a game is rendered at 60 frames per second, a single frame takes 1 s / 60 ≈ 16 ms to process. One might think that any polling interval below 16 ms would be perfect; however, USB polling happens independently of the vertical sync. Therefore, even with a 1 ms polling interval, there is a 1/16 chance that the whole frame will be missed and input will be processed on the next frame. The longer the polling interval, the greater the odds of a missed frame. With a polling interval of 8 ms, the odds of input missing a frame are 50%. Native polling rates and input response vary across consoles and even games.

docs.title: Processing
docs.text: Processing is where FPGA emulation has a key advantage. Software emulators repeatedly execute and then wait for the next screen refresh, whereas FPGA cores run in real time, as the original hardware did. In most circumstances, cores therefore have no CPU bottlenecks that slow them down arbitrarily, and need no large extra buffers to hold data.

docs.title: Display
docs.text:
MiSTer’s two primary display outputs are analog and HDMI.

The analog output is driven as the original system would have, with no buffering, so its latency is effectively identical to a real console's — from this point of view, the analog output has no lag of its own.

HDMI output must be scaled up to a higher resolution, which requires additional processing. How much latency the scaler adds depends on the vsync_adjust setting: from about 4–30 lines up to roughly 2 frames (see Video lag below).

Your television or monitor may add further latency, but this varies by device, so no definite number can be given here.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
If lag is critical to you, it's best to play on a CRT using a recommended and widely tested USB controller. Some users have tested and ranked USB controllers by performance; see their results. Another thorough list of tested controllers is MiSTerAddons and Lemonici's MiSTer Input Latency Chart.

Even over HDMI, however, MiSTer can provide a better experience than many other devices.

docs.title: Video lag
docs.text:
The vsync_adjust option in MiSTer.ini (at the root of the SD card) configures the HDMI upscaler, trading compatibility against latency:

  • vsync_adjust=2 is the best option if your TV is compatible with it. It uses the core's original refresh rate and pixel clock, giving sub-frame latency. According to Grabulosaure, who made the scaler, the actual latency is around 4 to 30 lines with vscale_mode=1, and slightly more in other modes (video).
  • vsync_adjust=1 is the second-best option, with 1 frame of latency. It uses a framebuffer, but keeps the system's original vsync and varies the pixel clock per core.
  • vsync_adjust=0 is the weakest option for latency, but the most compatible: up to 1-2 frames of latency and slightly less smooth scrolling. It always outputs 60 Hz with an NTSC-standard pixel clock, so it is more compatible with modern displays. However, you will notice occasional jitter, because the core's refresh rate doesn't match the display's.

docs.title: Input lag
docs.text:
USB controllers usually report a polling interval, which the host (the MiSTer Linux kernel) respects when polling their inputs. Most USB devices can actually perform better when polled more often, without any side effects.

To set a higher USB polling rate, go to the linux folder on your SD card and rename u-boot.txt_example to u-boot.txt. The file contains the following options; change them only if you run into problems: 

v=loglevel=4 usbhid.jspoll=1 xpad.cpoll=1
loglevel: 4 is the default value. You can set this to 9 to get debugging messages with the dmesg command via SSH. See below for how to check the jspoll/cpoll values applied to your controller.

usbhid.jspoll: specifies the interval for USB HID controllers, usually DirectInput.

xpad.cpoll: specifies the interval for USB XInput controllers. XInput is the controller standard of Microsoft's Xbox consoles and PC, and most popular controllers use it. Its values work the same way as usbhid.jspoll's.

Both parameters take the same values:

  • 0 — the default; the value requested by the controller is used (even without a u-boot.txt).
  • 1 — recommended; 1000/1 = 1000 Hz polling. If you encounter issues, try higher integer values: the higher the interval, the higher the possible lag. Don't go above 8 (1000/8 = 125 Hz).

To check the applied value, run systool -m usbhid -A jspoll or systool -m xpad -A cpoll from the Linux shell.

docs.title: What is the fastest controller I can get?
docs.text:
Almost any standard USB controller works well with MiSTer, but based on user feedback and input lag testing, these are a few excellent choices:

  • 8BitDo M30 2.4G connected in wired mode
  • Sony DS4 in wired mode
  • Hori Fighting Commander (later revisions), either the PS4 or Xbox One variant — pick your favorite
  • DIY USB adapter using open source firmware available here

Bluetooth-connected devices generally work fine, but expect the highest input latency from them.

Keep in mind that even "high latency" controllers should add at most 16 ms (1/60th of a second, one frame) of lag, or rarely, depending on the controller, 32 ms, and not constantly. That is not a lot, so if you don't notice lag, you can safely use any decent USB controller. Variable lag (for instance, response varying between 1 and 3 frames) is more noticeable than consistent lag. Very few controllers add more than 1 frame of lag.

There is no single definitive fastest controller, but quite a few are near the top. For a definitive, community-sourced list, see MiSTerAddons and Lemonici's MiSTer Input Latency Chart: the controllers were tested on MiSTer with a separate device connected to the DE10-Nano's headers, for objective results.

docs.title: MGL Files
docs.text:
MGL files are shortcuts that load a game directly from the MiSTer Menu core. They can be placed in the root of the SD card to appear at the top of the menu, or in a menu folder — a regular folder prefixed with an underscore (_) that shows in the menu. You can create your own menu folders.

Not all cores support MGL files, though all the most popular cores do. Console support is good, but computer cores generally don't work well with them, unless they have some mechanism to auto-boot a loaded game.

docs.title: MGL Format
docs.text:
MGLs are simple XML files with the file extension .mgl. Whatever name you give to an MGL file (excluding the extension) is what will be shown for its entry in the menu. E.g. My Favorite Game.mgl will display in the menu as My Favorite Game.

Example MGL files:

<mistergamedescription>
    <rbf>_console/snes</rbf>
    <file delay="2" type="f" index="0" path="puzzles/dummy.sfc"/>
</mistergamedescription>

<mistergamedescription>
    <rbf>_console/psx</rbf>
    <file delay="1" type="s" index="1" path="dummy.chd"/>
</mistergamedescription>

<mistergamedescription>
    <rbf>_Computer/ao486</rbf>
    <file delay="1" type="s" index="2" path="dummy.vhd"/>
    <file delay="1" type="s" index="4" path="cds/dummy.iso"/>
</mistergamedescription>

<mistergamedescription>
    <rbf>_Console/SMS</rbf>
    <setname>GameGear</setname>
    <file delay="1" type="f" index="2" path="some/other.zip/path/dummy.gg"/>
</mistergamedescription>

<mistergamedescription>
    <rbf>_Console/Gameboy</rbf>
    <setname same_dir="1">GBC</setname>
</mistergamedescription>
  • rbf: Relative path to the core's RBF file from the SD root, excluding its file extension and timestamp.
  • setname: Sets a core's name to this value, changing its games folder and config file.
    • setname same_dir="1": Sets a core's name to this value, changing its config file while keeping the core's original games folder
  • file: The file to be loaded into the core and its launch arguments.
    • delay: Number of seconds to wait before load/mount.
    • type: Either f to load a file into memory or s to mount a file.
    • index: The slot the file is loaded into in the core.
    • path: Path to the game file relative to the core's games folder.
  • reset: Triggers a reset on the core. You probably don't need this.
    • delay: Number of seconds to wait before reset.
    • hold: Number of seconds to hold the reset (optional; about 100 ms if omitted).

The rbf tag must be present.

The file tag is optional. It can be used more than once in an MGL. Useful for cores that have multiple file slots.

The setname tag is optional, and the change it makes is only temporary. It is useful for cores that play multiple systems, or that you often switch between different configurations. With same_dir="1", you can load games from the core's normal games folder while using a custom configuration.

The type and index attributes depend on what values were configured by the core's developer. See below for how to check those.

If a core pops up the OSD menu after loading the game or the game doesn't load, try increasing the delay value.

docs.title: MGL Arguments
docs.text:
Some MGL arguments for common cores:

System RBF Delay Index Type Atari 2600/7800 _Console/Atari7800 1 1 f Atari 5200 _Console/Atari5200 1 1 s Atari Lynx _Console/AtariLynx 1 1 f Commodore 64 _Computer/C64 1 1 f Famicom Disk System _Console/NES 2 1 f Game Boy (Color) _Console/Gameboy 2 1 f Game Boy Advance _Console/GBA 2 1 f Game Gear _Console/SMS 1 2 f Genesis _Console/Genesis 1 1 f Master System _Console/SMS 1 1 f Sega CD _Console/MegaCD 1 0 s Neo Geo _Console/NeoGeo 1 1 f NES _Console/NES 2 1 f PlayStation _Console/PSX 1 1 s Sega 32X _Console/S32X 1 1 f SNES _Console/SNES 2 0 f TurboGrafx-16 _Console/TurboGrafx16 1 0 f TurboGrafx-16 CD _Console/TurboGrafx16 1 0 s

A more comprehensive list of MGL arguments documented by Wizzo can be found here.

docs.title: Finding MGL Arguments
docs.text:
If the core you're looking for isn't in these lists, either test the combinations yourself or check the core's source on GitHub to find the values directly.

For example, the index numbers and file types supported by the TurboGrafx-16 core can be found in TurboGrafx16.sv on GitHub.

Find the section starting with parameter CONF_STR and look for the file type you're launching — in this case "S0,CUECHD,Insert CD;". The S0 means type s with index 0.

See the Core Configuration String page for detailed information on this format.

docs.title: Arcade Cores
docs.text:
Arcade cores cannot be launched using MGL files. If you want to make a shortcut to an arcade core elsewhere in the menu, you'll instead have to symlink (symbolic link) it there.

For example, either through SSH or the console (press F9 from the menu): 

# ln -s /media/fat/_Arcade/dummy.mra /media/fat
# ln -s /media/fat/_Arcade/cores /media/fat

This creates a shortcut to an arcade core in the root of the MiSTer menu. It can also be done with menu subfolders.

Note the second line, which symlinks the cores folder. You have to do this once for each folder you want to symlink MRA files into.

docs.title: MIDI Features
docs.text: There are multiple options for using MIDI on the MiSTer.

docs.title: The mt32-pi Project
docs.text: Dale Whinham (aka d0pefish) created mt32-pi, an open-source MIDI synthesizer for the Raspberry Pi. For current instructions, see the MiSTer FPGA section of the mt32-pi wiki. There are also two add-on boards designed by Sorgelig for using mt32-pi with the MiSTer.

docs.title: Computer cores with MIDI support
docs.text: When an ALSA-compatible USB MIDI device is attached, the Minimig and ao486 cores get two extra 'UART Connection' menu options, 'USBMIDI' and 'USBMIDI-38K', in addition to 'None', 'PPP', and 'Console'.

docs.title: Minimig
docs.text:
Use 'USBMIDI' with the Amiga (Minimig) core. It sets the UART connection speed to 31250 baud, the standard MIDI speed.

Many Amiga applications and most games don't need any additional MIDI drivers. Some "newer" applications may require the CAMD driver (Aminet).

docs.title: ao486
docs.text:
Use 'USBMIDI-38K' with the ao486 core. It sets the UART connection speed to 38400 baud, because DOS PC UARTs couldn't run at the standard MIDI speed of 31250 baud.

Some sequencer applications and Microsoft Windows may support MIDI on the serial port, but DOS games typically require an MPU-401 interface, which ao486 unfortunately lacks. Instead of a hardware MPU-401, the SoftMPU TSR can be used with a good degree of success.

docs.title: SoftMPU
docs.text:
SoftMPU requires the QEMM memory manager (QEMM 8.03 was used for testing). QEMM's "stealth" option seems to be incompatible with ao486, so it is advisable to skip that part of the optimize process. After adding SoftMPU to AUTOEXEC.BAT, it's a good idea to run QEMM's optimize again to free up as much of the lower 640 KB of conventional RAM as possible.

Although less common, some DOS games and applications require MPU-401 interrupts. Enabling them can break compatibility with other software that doesn't use interrupts.

Starting SoftMPU without MPU-401 interrupts:

SOFTMPU.EXE /MPU:330 /OUTPUT:COM1

Starting SoftMPU with MPU-401 interrupts:

SOFTMPU.EXE /SB:220 /IRQ:5 /MPU:330 /OUTPUT:COM1

The Rev.0 Roland MT-32 used in testing needed the 'DELAYSYSEX' switch to prevent buffer overflow in certain games, but it made Sierra games send SysEx commands excessively slowly. This is unnecessary for General MIDI modules and newer-revision MT-32s.

SOFTMPU.EXE /MPU:330 /DELAYSYSEX /OUTPUT:COM1

docs.title: MidiLink
docs.text:
The MidiLink daemon (midilink) currently supports the following switches/options:

TESTSER  - this option sends a test message to the serial port once 
           the daemon is started.  

TESTMIDI - this option sends a middle 'c' note to the MIDI device 
           once the daemon is started. 

QUIET    - this option suppresses MIDI debug output.  

38400    - this option sets the serial speed to 38400 baud 
           (default is 31250 baud) - used with ao486 core.

docs.title: MIDI adapters reported to work
docs.text:
• Creative EMU XMIDI (Known to mangle SYSEX messages)
  • Roland UM-ONE
  • M-Audio Midisport Uno

docs.title: Multi-Button Mapping
docs.text:
When you override the gamepad settings inside a core, you can also map button combinations (e.g. A+B) to a single button, if your gamepad has enough physical buttons. For this, after you define a gamepad, MiSTer asks whether you want to set up "alternate mappings".

The alternate mapping is active at the same time as the main mapping. It lets you:

  • map two physical buttons to the same core button (e.g. an alternate button for Start), or
  • map one physical button to a two-button combination in the core (e.g. physical X to the core's A+B).

docs.title: Bind core button to two physical buttons
docs.text:
The simplest use is mapping an extra physical button. Only this additional button needs to be defined in the alternate map, as follows:

Map D-Pad A B main define Btn 1 Btn 2 alt skip skip Btn 3

With this setup, physical buttons 2 and 3 are both mapped to the core's B button.

This also works with gamepad directions. For example, for games that use Up as a jump input, you can map a third physical button to Up.

docs.title: Bind physical button to core button combo
docs.text:
A more advanced setup uses both mappings in parallel, making one physical button press two core buttons at the same time:

Map D-Pad A B main define Btn 1 Btn 3 alt skip Btn 3 Btn 2

With this setup, Button 1 is A, Button 2 is B, and Button 3 is A+B.

This is particularly useful for the Neo Geo core, where some fighting games use A+B and C+D as strong hits. Unfortunately, Neo Geo games aren't consistent with each other, so no single mapping works for all of them. The examples below show mappings for several games.

docs.title: Example: Neo Geo Breakers / Breakers' Revenge
docs.text:
Assume a six-button arcade controller (for Street Fighter 2) with 3 punch buttons on top and 3 kick buttons below, and map the buttons so Breakers / Breakers' Revenge gets the same layout.

The game uses these attack buttons:

  • A: Weak Punch
  • B: Weak Kick
  • C: Strong Punch
  • D: Strong Kick

In addition, most characters have an extra "command" move mapped to:

  • Weak Punch + Strong Punch
  • Weak Kick + Strong Kick

To match the Street Fighter 2 layout, assign this across six buttons:

- Weak Strong Weak+Strong Punch A C A + C Kick B D B + D

This translates to the following buttons:

- Weak Strong Weak+Strong Punch Btn 1 Btn 2 Btn 3 Kick Btn 4 Btn 5 Btn 6

To get this layout, use the following assignments in the main and alternate maps:

map d-pad A B C D main define Btn 1 Btn 4 Btn 3 Btn 6 alt skip Btn 3 Btn 6 Btn 2 Btn 5

(In the alternate map, the d-pad and all other buttons can be skipped.)

docs.title: Example: Neo Geo King of Fighters / Fatal Fury Special
docs.text:
Both of these games use the same attack layout as Breakers, but their button combinations differ:

- Weak Strong Combo Punch A C A + B Kick B D C + D

The mapping is similar, with some buttons rearranged:

map d-pad A B C D main define Btn 1 Btn 3 Btn 2 Btn 6 alt skip Btn 3 Btn 4 Btn 6 Btn 5

docs.title: Example: Neo Geo Samurai Shodown
docs.text:
This game has yet another layout, changing the order of base attacks:

- Weak Medium Strong Slash A B A + B Kick C D C + D

Map it as follows:

map d-pad A B C D main define Btn 1 Btn 3 Btn 4 Btn 6 alt skip Btn 3 Btn 2 Btn 6 Btn 5

docs.title: Counterexample: The Last Blade 1 and 2
docs.text:
Similar to the above, but the button combo differs:

- Weak Medium Special Slash A B B + C Kick C D C + D

In this case, it is not possible to map C three times — so you must choose whether to map B+C or C+D.

docs.title: Option 1: Map B+C to button 3
docs.text:
map d-pad A B C D main define Btn 1 Btn 2 Btn 3 Btn 5 alt skip skip Btn 3 Btn 4 skip

(Btn 6 remains unassigned)

docs.title: Option 2: Map C+D to button 6
docs.text:
map d-pad A B C D main define Btn 1 Btn 2 Btn 6 Btn 5 alt skip skip skip Btn 4 Btn 6

(Btn 3 remains unassigned)
