docs.title: Advanced Networking
docs.text: The MiSTer has several advanced networking features.

docs.title: Network access
docs.text:
The MiSTer board can be accessed through the on-board Ethernet port. The system has FTP, SSH, and SFTP services running.

User name: root Password: 1

If you connect to your MiSTer over the network frequently, consider Setting up a hostname for your MiSTer so you don't have to look up or remember your MiSTer's IP address.

docs.title: FTP/SFTP
docs.text:
FTP lets you upload files to or download files from your MiSTer over the network, without removing the SD card. SFTP is a similar file transfer protocol that runs over SSH; note that not all FTP clients support it.

You can use any FTP or SFTP client, as long as transfers are in binary mode, not ASCII. ASCII transfers will corrupt the data.

Once connected to the MiSTer, your SD card's contents will be at /media/fat.

If you don't have a compatible FTP client already, then try FileZilla. It is a solid choice for all modern operating systems (Linux, MacOS and Windows). Older versions of FileZilla such as 2.1.9a are compatible with Windows 95/NT3.5+ and can be used inside the ao486 core with a PPP connection.

Another good FTP client for modern Windows operating systems is WinSCP.

Once one of these clients is installed, run the program and open the Site Manager dialog.

FTP Client Site Manager Location FileZilla File -> Site Manager WinSCP Tabs -> Sites -> Site Manager

Set Protocol to either FTP or SFTP and fill out the Host, User and Password fields. For example: if the MiSTer's IP address is 192.168.2.8 and you want to log in as root, then Host is 192.168.2.8, User is root, and Password is the user password.

Optionally set the Default Remote Directory to /media/fat so the client opens the SD card directly after connecting. Likewise, you can set the Default Local Directory to your local MiSTer folder.

FTP Client Remote Directory Location FileZilla Site Manager -> Advanced -> Default Remote Directory: WinSCP Site Manager -> Advanced -> Directories -> Remote Directory:

Click Connect or Login — you should now be able to upload and download files.

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
Secure Shell (SSH) is a standardized network protocol for remotely operating computers over a network; it gives you a remote text terminal to your MiSTer.

On Linux and macOS, open a terminal and run ssh <user>@<MiSTer IP> — for example ssh root@192.168.2.8 to log in as root.

If your Windows machine doesn't have ssh in Command Prompt, you can download and run PuTTY instead. Using the same example as above type root@192.168.2.8 into the Host Name text field. Ensure Port is set to 22 and Connection type is set to SSH then click Open.

Enter the password when prompted; you can then run commands as if at the MiSTer console.

docs.title: Share Mounting
docs.text:
The MiSTer can mount a network share from another computer or server as if it were local storage. CIFS and NFS shares are supported. If you want to use them, download the following helper scripts to /media/fat/Scripts; each *_umount.sh script unmounts the share again.

Share type Mount script Unmount script CIFS cifs_mount.sh cifs_umount.sh NFS nfs_mount.sh nfs_umount.sh

cifs_mount.sh mounts the share at /media/fat/cifs, and MiSTer gives the folders mounted there preference. nfs_mount.sh mounts the share so that its folders take priority over identically named folders in /media/fat on the MicroSD card, which you will then no longer see. See Core Paths for how this priority order works.

docs.title: CIFS Share Troubleshooting
docs.text:
There is a known problem with certain cores (at least ao486 and NeoGeo) and certain CIFS share configurations, caused by some open bugs in Samba.

If certain cores don't start when loading games from a CIFS share, but work fine from SD or USB, check whether Kernel Oplocks are enabled on the share. If they are, do one of the following:

  • Disable them.
  • Enable them globally on your Samba server.
  • Move your MiSTer files to a separate share used only by the MiSTer, without Kernel Oplocks.

Choose whichever suits your use case best. Many NAS devices enable Kernel Oplocks by default for good reason: they should prevent bad file synchronization, corruption, and data loss when a share is used through different protocols (e.g. CIFS and NFS) or by software running on the NAS, such as a torrent client.

docs.title: RetroNAS
docs.text: RetroNAS, a project by Dan Mons, makes it easy to set up a network attached storage (NAS) device focused solely on compatibility with retro gaming devices. MiSTer is one of its primary focuses, and it works quite well. All you need is a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 and an external storage drive. Remember: a NAS is not a backup! You could lose data if a NAS is the only place you keep important data. The project has a simple installation guide, MiSTer-specific instructions, and YouTube video guides for installation and MiSTer FPGA-specific configuration.

docs.title: Tailscale Networking
docs.text:
Adding your MiSTer to a Tailnet has a lot of benefits: keeping access to a NAS with your games while traveling, remotely administering a less-technical friend's MiSTer, and remote SSH/SFTP for running scripts and installing cores, to name a few.

If you do not already have a Tailnet, follow the instructions here to get started. Make sure you add at least one computer/NAS/phone to the Tailnet once it's created.

To install Tailscale on your MiSTer, you can either use this easier scripted install method or follow the manual steps below.

Go to the Tailscale Package Repository and download the ARMv7 binary package (it will look something like arm: tailscale_x.xx.x_arm.tgz).

Extract the archive on your computer and SFTP the files (tailscaled and tailscale) to your MiSTer. The examples below use /media/fat/linux/tailscale/, but any directory under /media/fat/ works — adjust the paths accordingly.

SSH into your MiSTer and change to the directory where you put the extracted Tailscale files. Create a directory to house the Tailscale state on boot with mkdir .state. Now start the Tailscale Daemon with the following command: 

# /media/fat/linux/tailscale/tailscaled --tun=userspace-networking --statedir=/media/fat/linux/tailscale/.state/
--tun=userspace-networking is added because the MiSTer Linux kernel is not compiled with TUN support, so running it in userspace allows the daemon to start. --statedir=/media/fat/linux/tailscale/.state/ prevents the daemon from erroring on a cold boot, when the OS root directory is mounted read-only.

Once the daemon starts, run the following command to join your MiSTer to your tailnet: 

# /media/fat/linux/tailscale/tailscale up --accept-routes
--accept-routes is only needed if you have a machine on your Tailnet set up as a subnet router.

When that command finishes, paste the URL at the bottom of its output into your browser to join the device to your Tailnet.

Once the MiSTer is joined to the Tailnet, create a tailstart.sh file in the tailscale directory with the following contents: 

#/bin/sh

/media/fat/linux/tailscale/tailscaled --tun=userspace-networking --statedir=/media/fat/linux/tailscale/.state/ > /dev/null 2>&1 &
/media/fat/linux/tailscale/tailscale up --accept-routes > /dev/null 2>&1 &

Once the file is created, run: 

# chmod +x tailstart.sh
To have Tailscale start at boot, edit the user-startup.sh file in /media/fat/linux/ and add the following line to the bottom: 
/media/fat/linux/tailscale/tailstart.sh

Now your MiSTer will connect to your Tailnet after every reboot.

docs.title: Network settings and configuration
docs.text: By default, MiSTer uses dhcpcd (not to be confused with dhcpd) to acquire a local network IP address from a DHCP server. It is a powerful DHCP client with too many configuration options (dhcpcd.conf) to cover here, so this section covers only the most likely reasons to modify its behavior on a MiSTer. For full documentation read dhcpcd.conf (5).

docs.title: MAC address configuration
docs.text:
A MAC address (Media Access Control address) is a network address assigned to the hardware of every network interface. It lets network switches learn where to route traffic — like an IP address, but statically assigned to hardware and only relevant within your local network.

Much like IP addresses, MAC addresses have to be unique for the network to function properly, but unlike IP addresses, they cannot be dynamically assigned by a DHCP server — MAC addresses are static by design.

Some installers like Mr Fusion randomize the MiSTer's MAC address during setup, but others use the same MAC address every time. As a result, it is common for two or more MiSTers to have the exact same MAC address on their onboard Ethernet port.

If two MiSTers with the same MAC address are on the same network at the same time, the network switches may start sending packets to the wrong MiSTer and cause connections to fail. Fortunately, if this is the case, it's possible to override the default MAC address.

docs.title: Log in to the Linux terminal on the MiSTer
docs.text: From the MiSTer's startup menu, press F9 to get a Linux terminal, then log in as root (see Network Access for the default credentials).

docs.title: Change MAC address
docs.text:
Open u-boot.txt for editing by running nano /media/fat/linux/u-boot.txt. The file should contain a line similar to this: 

ethaddr=EA:C8:21:56:E3:43

Edit the MAC address so that no MiSTers on your network share the same address. MAC addresses are made up of six sets of two characters that range between 00-FF and are separated by :. When changing the MAC address, avoid these addresses that have special meaning:

  • Multicast (any address where the first set ends in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, B, D or F):
    • ❌ EB:C8:21:56:E3:43
    • ✔️ EC:C8:21:56:E3:43
  • Broadcast (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF)
  • All zeros (00:00:00:00:00:00)

Once done, save with Ctrl+O and exit with Ctrl+X, then run reboot to restart the MiSTer with the new MAC address applied.

docs.title: Hostname configuration
docs.text: dhcpcd can be configured so that MiSTer offers its preferred name to your DHCP server, but it's disabled by default. Enabling it lets you connect to your MiSTer by name instead of looking up its IP address.

docs.title: Log in to the Linux terminal on the MiSTer
docs.text:
Log in to the MiSTer's Linux terminal as described above.

Alternatively, you can log in remotely with SSH. This is recommended if possible as you will be able to copy and paste the commands instead of typing them out by hand.

docs.title: Check your local network has a top-level domain assigned
docs.text:
Before enabling this feature, you should be sure that your network router supports top-level domains (TLDs) in the local network.

To do this, run dhcpcd -U | less and look for at least one domain_name entry that looks like this: 

domain_name=lan
Remember the value after the = for later and press Q to return to the terminal. If you find more than one domain_name value, remember them all. If you have no domain_name value in the results then your network router is not offering a top level domain and there's no point in proceeding.

Alternatively, run this command to find and filter domain_name values for you: 

dhcpcd -U 2>/dev/null | grep domain_name= | cut -c13-
It produces output like: 
lan

docs.title: Enable sending preferred name to DHCP server
docs.text:
Open the dhcpcd configuration file for editing by running nano /etc/dhcpcd.conf.

Press Down until you find this text: 

# Request a hostname from the network
#option host_name
Uncomment the option by removing the # in front of it so it looks like this: 
# Request a hostname from the network
option host_name
Once done, save with Ctrl+O and exit with Ctrl+X.

docs.title: Set the MiSTer's preferred name
docs.text:
To set the name itself, run nano /etc/hostname. You should see a word in the file (likely MiSTer). Change it to whatever you want your MiSTer's name to be. You can choose any name, but for best compatibility with other network devices follow these constraints:

  • Only use alphanumeric characters (A–Z; no kanji or Cyrillic)
    • The name is case-insensitive; mix uppercase and lowercase as you like
  • Avoid symbols (!, ?, #, % etc.) and especially periods (.)
  • Avoid starting the name with a number (0 to 9)
  • Avoid using spaces and multiple words
  • Try to choose a name that is no more than 15 characters total

Once done, save with Ctrl+O and exit with Ctrl+X.

Run hostname to confirm the MiSTer's name has changed, then run reboot to restart the MiSTer with the new network settings applied.

docs.title: Test the name change
docs.text:
Assume you set your MiSTer's name to timemachine and your top-level domain is .home. Replace these with the domain you found earlier and the name you actually set.

From another computer on the network, run ping timemachine.home. If you see replies, you can now use timemachine.home to reach your MiSTer on your local network. The MiSTer should now be accessible from at least one of the top-level domains you found earlier.

docs.title: Static IP Address configuration
docs.text: Before configuring a static IP address, consider whether it's really necessary. A static IP can conflict with another network device assigned the same address, and an address outside the network's subnet range will leave your MiSTer unable to connect to anything. If in doubt, try Hostname configuration first.

docs.title: Log in to the Linux terminal on the MiSTer
docs.text:
Log in to the MiSTer's Linux terminal as described above.

You can do this over SSH, but it is not recommended: once the IP address changes, you may lose network access (and therefore your SSH connection) to the MiSTer.

docs.title: Find the network interface name
docs.text:
A DE10-Nano MiSTer always has at least two network interfaces:

Interface Name Description lo Linux virtual network loopback device (not interesting) eth0 The DE10-Nano's built-in Gigabit Ethernet

These two interface names should be consistent across all MiSTers. However, if you want to set a static IP address on a USB network card, you will first need to know the name Linux has given to the interface. Run ip link. The output looks similar to this: 

1: lo: <LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 65536 qdisc noqueue state UNKNOWN mode DEFAULT group default qlen 1000
    link/loopback 00:00:00:00:00:00 brd 00:00:00:00:00:00
2: eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc mq state UP mode DEFAULT group default qlen 1000
    link/ether 01:02:03:04:05:06 brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
If necessary, run ip addr instead to see the IP address currently assigned to each interface (if any): 
1: lo: <LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 65536 qdisc noqueue state UNKNOWN group default qlen 1000
    link/loopback 00:00:00:00:00:00 brd 00:00:00:00:00:00
    inet 127.0.0.1/8 scope host lo
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
2: eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc mq state UP group default qlen 1000
    link/ether 01:02:03:04:05:06 brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
    inet 10.0.0.221/24 brd 10.0.0.255 scope global dynamic noprefixroute eth0
       valid_lft 40368sec preferred_lft 34968sec
There will be an additional entry for each USB Wi-Fi and/or Ethernet adapter MiSTer has recognized. Take note of the interface name you want to change (they are case-sensitive) before proceeding.

docs.title: Assign a static IP address to an interface
docs.text:
Assume you want the network interface named eth0 to be assigned a static IP address of 192.168.0.128. Replace these values with the network interface name you got in the previous step and the IP address you want to set it to.

Open the dhcpcd configuration file by running nano /etc/dhcpcd.conf. Press Down until you're at the bottom of the file, then type: 

interface eth0
static ip_address=192.168.0.128/24
These lines are order-sensitive, so be sure to add them at the very bottom of the file. Any line below an interface line will apply to that interface until the next interface line. Any line above the first interface line will apply to all network interfaces.

You can optionally specify any combination of options for an interface, here are some useful ones:

Option Description static routers= Manually specify routers/gateways to the Internet static domain_name_servers= Manually specify DNS servers to resolve names ntp_servers= Manually specify NTP servers to get time from

With these options specified, an interface configuration looks like: 

interface eth0
static ip_address=192.168.0.128/24
static routers=192.168.0.1
static domain_name_servers=8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1
ntp_servers=192.168.0.1 0.pool.ntp.org 1.pool.ntp.org 2.pool.ntp.org

Once done, save with Ctrl+O and exit with Ctrl+X. Run reboot to restart the MiSTer with the new network settings applied.

docs.title: Re-enabling DHCP
docs.text:
If your static IP configuration isn't working, or you want to revert to automatic DHCP, open /etc/dhcpcd.conf again and put a # at the beginning of each line you want to revert. Commenting lines out is as good as removing them, but lets you restore them later if you change your mind.

To revert all of your configuration, comment out every line you added like so: 

#interface eth0
#static ip_address=192.168.0.128/24
#static routers=192.168.0.1
#static domain_name_servers=8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1
#ntp_servers=192.168.0.1 0.pool.ntp.org 1.pool.ntp.org 2.pool.ntp.org
Just like before: save the file and reboot to apply the new settings.

docs.title: RTC Board
docs.text:
Some cores (ao486, Minimig) use a clock, so MiSTer provides them with the real time. When an Internet connection is active, MiSTer can get the time from the Internet; the RTC board provides it offline.

This simple board provides the real time without an Internet connection. It supports two types of battery holders and several types of RTC ICs, and plugs into the LTC connector.

docs.title: Assembly notes
docs.text:
• If a through-hole battery holder is used, cut all its plastic pins and make sure the holder sits fully on the board, without gaps. Otherwise it may touch the I/O board and cause a short circuit.
  • For a through-hole holder, also cut the pins as short as possible, so they don't protrude under the board and cause a short circuit.
  • The board has a hole on the side opposite the connector. Put a plastic (or other non-conductive) screw in it as a leg, to stop the board from bending and touching the main board.
  • The SMD holder (left picture) is preferable, because it is slimmer.

docs.title: Usage notes
docs.text:
To save the real time to the RTC, connect the MiSTer to the Internet and let it run for about 15 minutes — or update it from the console (see the commands below).

By default the time zone is UTC (GMT). To get your local time zone, do the following:

  • Connect to MiSTer by FTP/SFTP.
  • Navigate to the /usr/share/zoneinfo/posix folder and find the file named after your place or time zone.
  • Copy that file to your computer under the name timezone.
  • Copy it back to the MiSTer into the /media/fat/linux folder, keeping the name timezone.

From the console you can also force the hardware clock to update and read the time from it:

  • Store datetime to RTC: hwclock -wu
  • Read RTC: hwclock -u

docs.title: Video Modes
docs.text: The video_mode INI setting supports several ways to specify the video mode.

docs.title: Automatic Detection
docs.text: If no video_mode setting is specified, MiSTer will attempt to determine the correct video mode using EDID information from the display device. This will only work for devices connected to the HDMI port. If a valid video mode cannot be determined, the default 720p mode is used.

docs.title: Video Mode Presets (video_mode)
docs.text:
MiSTer has 15 built-in video mode presets (0–14) covering common display modes for televisions and monitors. For example: 

; Number 8 - 1920x1080 - 60 Hz - 16:9 - FHD 1080p
video_mode=8

Number Resolution Refresh (Hz) Aspect Ratio Name 0 1280x720 60 16:9 HD 720p 1 1024x768 60 4:3 XGA 2 720x480 60 3:2 3 720x576 50 5:4 4 1280x1024 60 5:4 SXGA 5 800x600 60 4:3 SVGA 6 640x480 60 4:3 VGA 7 1280x720 50 16:9 HD 720p PAL 8 1920x1080 60 16:9 FHD 1080p 9 1920x1080 50 16:9 FHD 1080p PAL 10 1366x768 60 16:9 WXGA 11 1024x600 60 128:75 WSVGA 12 1920x1440 60 4:3 13 2048x1536 60 4:3 iPad Retina 14 2560x1440 60 16:9 1440p

docs.title: Custom Video Modes
docs.text:
A custom mode can be set by specifying the width, height, and refresh rate like so: 

; 1920x1200 at 75Hz
video_mode=1920,1200,75
The maximum width is 4096, the maximum height is 2048, and the refresh rate can be any whole integer. The DE10-Nano may not be able to output the mode you select, or your display may not accept it. The maximum recommended video frequency is 210 MHz, which limits the maximum resolution to 2048x1536. Pixel repetition can push resolution further, but it also has limits.

The VESA Coordinated Video Timings standard is used to calculate the timing information for the requested video mode. By default the reduced blanking version of the standard is used. This is compatible with most flat panel displays but may not be as well supported on older displays and CRT monitors. You can use regular CVT timings by adding the cvt flag to the end of the video mode: 

; 1600x1200 on a CRT monitor
video_mode=1600,1200,60,cvt
Regular CVT timing requires a slightly higher clock speed for a given resolution, so some higher-resolution modes aren't achievable with it. An online video timing calculator can help you understand the differences between the two methods.

docs.title: Manual Modelines
docs.text:
Video mode timing can be fully specified with a modeline consisting of nine values that define the horizontal timing, vertical timing, and pixel clock. 

video_mode=hact,hfp,hs,hbp,vact,vfp,vs,vbp,fpix
hact and vact define the active (visible) size of the video mode in horizontal and vertical pixels, respectively. hfp, hs, and hbp define the duration of the horizontal front porch, sync, and back porch in pixels. vfp, vs, and vbp define the same properties for the vertical timing. Finally, fpix is the pixel clock frequency in kHz (pixel clocks are usually specified in MHz, so multiply the MHz value by 1000).

MiSTer modelines are similar to XFree86 modelines, but the information is expressed slightly differently. You can convert an XFree86 modeline to a MiSTer one with morf77's custom video mode tool, used together with a modeline calculator.

docs.title: Additional Flags
docs.text:
Additional flags can be appended to custom modes and modelines:

  • +hsync / -hsync - set the horizontal sync polarity
  • +vsync / -vsync - set the vertical sync polarity
  • pr - use HDMI pixel repetition (custom modelines only)
  • cvt - use normal CVT timing (custom mode only)
  • cvtrb - use reduced blanking CVT timing (custom mode only)

docs.title: HDMI Pixel Repetition (pr)
docs.text:
HDMI pixel repetition enables MiSTer to output a higher resolution video signal without using additional resources or requiring higher clock speeds. It does this by instructing the ADV7513 HDMI transmitter to duplicate each pixel that it sends to the display. This doesn't increase the fidelity of the final image — in most cases it reduces it — but it enables a wider selection of video modes.

MiSTer is limited to a maximum horizontal resolution of 2048 pixels and a maximum pixel clock of 210 MHz. This is enough for 2048x1536 (209 MHz, iPad resolution), the maximum native resolution supported, and also for 1920x1440 (184 MHz), a non-standard 4:3 resolution that some displays accept. The more commonly supported 2560x1440 mode is out of reach: it exceeds the limits in both horizontal resolution and pixel clock (240 MHz).

Pixel repetition makes a mode like 2560x1440 possible by lowering the horizontal resolution to 1280 pixels, which lowers the pixel clock to 120 MHz. The 1280x1440 image produced by the MiSTer scaler is stretched horizontally by the ADV7513, so the display receives the full 2560x1440.

Supporting the non-uniform scaling of the core's output requires an updated framework, and pixel repetition only works with cores that have been updated. Older cores output 1920x1080 when a mode requiring pixel repetition is requested.

docs.title: Video Scaling
docs.text: MiSTer has a built-in scaler that converts the cores' low-resolution video to a higher resolution, optionally using filters to improve the picture on modern displays. This page explains how to configure the scaling options.

docs.title: Video Scale Mode (vscale_mode)
docs.text:
The MiSTer.ini file at the root of your MicroSD card controls how the core's original video is scaled to your display. A few lines into that file you'll see:

vscale_mode=0          ; 0 - scale to fit the screen height.
                       ; 1 - use integer scale only.
                       ; 2 - use 0.5 steps of scale.
                       ; 3 - use 0.25 steps of scale.
                       ; 4 - integer resolution scaling, use core aspect ratio
                       ; 5 - integer resolution scaling, maintain display aspect ratio

Here's what each does:

docs.title: vscale_mode=0 (Fit Vertically to the Display Height)
docs.text: This is the default setting when you first turn on your MiSTer. If the game resolution is 256x224, fitting it vertically into a 1920x1080p display means dividing 1080 by 224 — which doesn't come out even (1080 / 224 ≈ 4.82). Some pixels may therefore not be scaled evenly. Some people don't mind this since it fills the screen entirely from top to bottom. You may see some shimmering pixels — if you do, use the interpolation video preset or one of the adaptive scanline filters to alleviate it.

docs.title: vscale_mode=1 (Integer Scaling)
docs.text: This setting makes the final scaled resolution multiplier of the core's video output a whole number (e.g. 2x, 3x, 4x, 5x, 6x, etc.). If your video_mode is set to 1920x1080p, the previous example of 256x224 is scaled 4 times as large (4 * 224 = 896) and the remainder is left as a black border — but your pixels are correctly scaled so there should be no shimmering (unless your display is causing it). Some people prefer this for the crispest pixels and a much lower chance of undesirable video artifacts; others don't like that it doesn't fill the screen the way 0 does.

docs.title: vscale_mode=2 and 3 (Fractional Integer Scaling)
docs.text: This setting is similar to vscale_mode=1, but instead of whole-number increments (e.g. 2x, 3x, 4x, etc.), it scales in increments of 0.5 (e.g. 2x, 2.5x, 3x, 3.5x, 4x) or 0.25 (e.g. 2x, 2.25x, 2.5x, 2.75x, 3x). On some monitors this can greatly reduce shimmering (though not all) while using sharper filtering (or none at all). Test vscale_mode=2 and 3 per core to see what looks best.

docs.title: vscale_mode=4 and 5 (Dynamically Scaled Video Mode)
docs.text: These modes, recently added by wickerwaka, dynamically change your video_mode to keep integer scaling while still filling the screen. They are ideal on a 2560x1440p or 4K display, where you can fill the screen vertically with very close to zero shimmering and video artifacts. If you don't want to learn how they work, just set one and test it.

docs.title: vscale_mode=4 (Integer resolution scaling using the core's aspect ratio)
docs.text:
If you have video_mode=13 set in your MiSTer.ini file, then you're telling the MiSTer to set your display to 2048x1536p at a 60 Hz refresh rate.

Take the 256x224 example, displayed at a 4:3 aspect ratio: you need a resolution that fits all of 256x224 integer-scaled at that ratio (like vscale_mode=1 explained above). 2048x1536 is the maximum in either direction. 1536 is almost but not quite 7×224, so MiSTer uses 6 as the multiplier, giving a vertical resolution of 1344. The horizontal resolution has to keep the 4:3 ratio, so 256 scales by the equivalent amount — 1792 — I personally use an aspect-ratio calculator to check.

That looks like a lot of work, but vscale_mode=4 does all of the math for you.

You may have mixed results with vscale_mode=4 — for instance, the PSX core changing resolutions prompts a full resync, which some people find jarring.

docs.title: vscale_mode=5 (Integer resolution scaling maintaining the display's aspect ratio)
docs.text: This works like vscale_mode=4, but it disregards the core's aspect ratio and only calculates the integer-scaled resolution that fits your screen's aspect ratio. Say you have a 1920x1200 display (16:10 aspect ratio) and are using video_mode=1920,1200,60 — the 16:10 aspect ratio will not be changed. This could be useful if you have a specific display you want to fill horizontally with some cores, or a 31 kHz computer monitor that supports higher resolutions where you want to fit console cores into its 4:3 aspect ratio.

docs.title: Addon Boards
docs.text:
Artwork by Hewhoisred

MiSTer has various add-on boards that are somewhat optional: the 128 MB SDRAM board, for example, is needed to run all of the cores, and the Analog I/O board lets you easily connect your MiSTer to a classic CRT television or monitor. You can buy these boards from various online sellers, or assemble one yourself by ordering the PCB from a PCB manufacturer, buying the components, and soldering it.

docs.title: 128MB SDRAM Addon Board
docs.text:
Several cores need the 128 MB SDRAM board to load games at all. A 32 MB SDRAM board is a cheaper alternative, but some games on Neo Geo, Game Boy Advance, and a few other cores may not work with the smaller module.

When plugging in the SDRAM board, make sure to support the DE10-Nano from beneath with your thumbs. Forcing in the SDRAM board without support can bend the DE10-Nano board and permanently damage it.

Removing the SDRAM board can be tricky with some GPIO connectors, and sometimes simply pulling won't work. Pulling with force often bends the GPIO header. For very tight connectors, wiggle the SDRAM board back and forth to ease it out slowly, bit by bit.

docs.title: USB Hub Addon Board
docs.text:
The USB Hub add-on board provides an OTG USB hub with one power-only USB port in the back and six USB 2.0 ports on the other three sides. It connects to the DE10-Nano in one of two ways: a slim external board plugs into the internal headers, or a bridge joins the two MicroUSB ports.

The hub needs its own power, so you may need a power splitter to supply both the DE10-Nano and the hub. If you use a Digital I/O board, a DC-to-DC jumper cable plus a single cable to the Digital I/O board's barrel jack powers the whole stack.

docs.title: Digital I/O Addon Board
docs.text:
Get this board if you want a few more options, like the features below. It is typically cheaper than the Analog I/O board, and it leaves the second SDRAM slot free for future cores that may need it.

  • 3 buttons: Reset, On-Screen Display (OSD), and User (for various user interactions without a keyboard)
  • 3 status LEDs: Power, Disk, and User
  • Secondary MicroSD card slot that may be required by some older computer cores — it isn't typical MicroSD storage; think of it as a little floppy drive
  • Mini-TOSLINK optical digital audio port
  • Full-size TOSLINK optical digital audio port
  • User IO port — it looks like a USB 3.0 port but it is not! It's actually for direct serial communication with peripherals and adapters like SNAC adapters and MT32-Pi
  • Fan power header and fan mounting holes for better cooling
  • Doesn't use the 2nd set of 2x20 headers on the DE10-Nano, so it is compatible with Dual SDRAM configurations

docs.title: Analog I/O Addon Board
docs.text:
Get this board instead of the Digital I/O board if you want simultaneous video output to a CRT and an HDMI display. Otherwise, the cheaper Digital I/O board should be sufficient.

It has the same 3 buttons, 3 status LEDs, secondary MicroSD slot, User IO port, fan power header, and fan mounting holes as the Digital I/O board (see above), plus:

  • Power On/Off switch
  • Barrel jack that can power the DE10-Nano
  • VGA port for analog video output — see Advanced - CRT for connectivity options
  • Simultaneous analog video and HDMI video output
  • Sync-on-green override/auto switch
  • 3.5 mm analog audio port doubling as a Mini-TOSLINK optical digital audio port
  • 3.5 mm audio-in port for ADC-in (e.g. tape input for some computer cores)
  • Uses the 2nd set of 2x20 headers on the DE10-Nano, so it is not compatible with Dual SDRAM configurations

docs.title: MT32-Pi Lite MiSTer Addon Board
docs.text: MT32-Pi is a baremetal emulator of the Roland MT-32 synth module. This add-on board is Sorgelig's version of the new MT32-Pi design, which uses a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. It plugs into the side of the MiSTer, into the User IO port of the Digital I/O or Analog I/O board. Get it if you want upgraded MIDI sound in cores and games that support it, such as the ao486 and X68000 cores. YouTuber MiSTer Walrus FPGA has a video showing how the MT32-Pi sounds.

docs.title: MT32-Pi Raspberry Pi HAT Addon Board
docs.text: This is a Raspberry Pi HAT add-on board for the MT32-Pi. It is intended for the Raspberry Pi 3A+ due to its square shape, but the 3B and 4 also work. You will also need a short USB 3.0 Type-A male-to-male cable if you choose this option.

docs.title: Real Time Clock Addon Board
docs.text: You need this board if you want your MiSTer to have a real-time clock, which various cores use. For how the board works and how to use it, see Advanced - RTC Board.

docs.title: ADC Analog Audio Input Addon Board
docs.text: The ADC add-on board lets certain computer cores load data from computer tape audio over an analog audio input, either from recordings or from an actual retro tape player.

docs.title: Bluetooth
docs.text: The MiSTer supports Bluetooth adapters and Bluetooth-connected controllers.

docs.title: Compatible adapters
docs.text:
Generally speaking, most Bluetooth 4.0 adapters use one of two similar chips, the CSR8510 or the BCM20702, and both are compatible. Bluetooth 5.0 adapters are a little different, but many of them work as well. Known compatible adapters include:

  • ASUS USB-BT500 (5.0)
  • Edimax BT-8500 (5.0)
  • MiSTerAddons.com's Bluetooth 4.2 / WiFi AC600 Combo Adapter
  • MiSTerFPGA.co.uk's CSR8510 Bluetooth 4.0 Adapter
  • MiSTerKits.com's CSR8510 Bluetooth 4.0 Adapter
  • ZEXMTE Long Range USB Bluetooth (5.0)

Many more adapters work, and most adapters seem to work fine. However, some hardware revisions may change compatibility even for the models listed here, so your results may vary.

docs.title: How to pair your Bluetooth controller or keyboard
docs.text:
1. Open the pairing prompt: press F11 on a keyboard connected to the MiSTer, or, if you have a Digital I/O or Analog I/O board, press and hold its OSD button.
  2. Put your controller into pairing mode and wait. The MiSTer should find it and connect within moments.
  3. You may need to define the controller's inputs, even if you have used the controller over a cable before, because the MiSTer sees it as a different controller over Bluetooth.

docs.title: Bluetooth connection to MiSTer unstable?
docs.text: If your Bluetooth connection is unstable (for example, the controller randomly disconnects), try a USB extension cable or pigtail adapter to move the Bluetooth adapter away from the USB hub. For some users, the USB hub can add interference and disrupt certain adapters, such as the ASUS USB-BT500 in some cases. The root cause is not currently known.

docs.title: Cases
docs.text: There are many MiSTer FPGA cases to choose from: DIY project-box builds, retro-fitted old computer or console injection molded cases, 3D-printed designs, and manufactured aluminum heatsink cases. And remember, you can be creative and have fun with your case design of choice.

docs.title: Get some ideas
docs.text: If you want to make your own case, the "Show us your MiSTer" thread on the official MiSTer FPGA forums is a great source of ideas, with both store-bought and custom-built MiSTers on display.

  • RnSKSkunkwerks laser-cut Star Wars inspired plates

docs.title: CD-based ROMs
docs.text: MiSTer loads CD-based games from CUE/BIN and CHD images. This page explains how to store them, and whether USB CD drives are supported.

docs.title: Will MiSTer ever support USB CD drives?
docs.text:
The short answer is no. The long answer is that:

  1. There is too much hardware variation in CD drives and their drivers for support to be worth it.
  2. Everything added to the MiSTer's Linux image and Main binary must be very carefully considered, because the goal is to keep them lightweight.

Drive support is also not a priority, as properly dumped CD-ROM images are bit-perfect where it counts (excluding randomized subchannel data and garbage-data fill-in).

docs.title: CUE/BIN folders and CHD files
docs.text:
Every CD-based core currently supports CUE/BIN. Place each CUE/BIN game in its own folder, separate from your other CUE/BIN games.

CHD is a compressed CD image format that almost every CD-based core also supports. CHD files don't need separate folders.

docs.title: Multi-disc games
docs.text:
For multi-disc games (e.g. on PlayStation / PSX), place each disc's files in the same subfolder:

./Valkyrie Profile (USA)/Valkyrie Profile (USA) (Disc 1).chd
./Valkyrie Profile (USA)/Valkyrie Profile (USA) (Disc 2).chd

The MiSTer then names the save file after the subfolder (Valkyrie Profile (USA).sav), so all discs share one save. You can also switch discs by loading the other disc image, without resetting the core.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text: Answers to frequently asked questions about MiSTer. If something is missing, feel free to contribute by editing this page on GitHub with the Edit (pen) icon in the top right.

docs.title: Is MiSTer hard to set up? Is it really only for technical people who like to tinker?
docs.text: No and no, although people who enjoy tinkering can get a lot more out of their MiSTer if they wish. The minimum setup only requires attaching an SDRAM board to a DE10-Nano and preparing an SD card. See the Setup Guide for details.

docs.title: How does the accuracy of MiSTer cores compare to other FPGA options?
docs.text: Most MiSTer cores are as accurate as, if not more accurate than, those of any other major FPGA product available today. Most people would not be able to tell these cores apart from the original hardware.

docs.title: Does MiSTer have lag?
docs.text: It depends on your setup, but it ranges from imperceptibly low to around one frame. Zero latency is possible with certain equipment and tweaks; see Input Latency for a detailed explanation.

docs.title: When will MiSTer support cartridges or USB CD drives?
docs.text: Never, officially. The project aims to give the original hardware experience without needing the original hardware. Supporting cartridges is physically impractical given the number of GPIO pins available from the FPGA. USB CD drives all have different drivers, latency, and buffering, and they would add unpredictable latency compared with the current method of loading CD games. See also CD-based games.

docs.title: Why doesn't MiSTer have a fancy GUI with cover art and metadata?
docs.text:
For several reasons:

  1. MiSTer's menu is designed to take up very little space on the FPGA and as few resources as possible on the ARM processor.
  2. The DE10-Nano has no graphics processor, so a fancy GUI would be rendered slowly in software by the CPU, unless it were rendered on the FPGA.
  3. The menu has to fit and remain usable on a wide variety of very low-resolution analog displays.

docs.title: Will any MiSTer core ever get save states?
docs.text:
The Game Boy, GBA, Lynx, WonderSwan, NES, and PSX cores support savestates.

Before savestates can be added, a core must either be written from scratch to support them or be significantly reworked to support pausing. Adding savestates to an FPGA-based emulator is not as simple as adding them to a software emulator. There are no specific plans to add them to other cores at this time, but it may happen one day.

docs.title: I heard the DE10-Nano board uses subsidized components. Is MiSTer doomed if that stops?
docs.text: No. The DE10-Nano is manufactured at a very large scale for students and is widely available. When it reaches end of life, the open-source cores and infrastructure will be ported to another widely available board.

docs.title: I see a defect that some other people aren't seeing. Should I get a different DE10-Nano?
docs.text: No. Report the defect and wait for a fix. There is no magically better DE10-Nano.

docs.title: I found some other Cyclone-based dev board on sale and it has built-in WiFi. Can I use it for MiSTer?
docs.text: Generally, no. Someone may always take the time to port things to another board, but different pins and memory mean the cores won't simply work on it, and unless the board is a significant upgrade it would never get official support. Supporting another platform takes a lot of work, so there are no plans to support multiple unofficial hardware platforms.

docs.title: Does MiSTer need an I/O board?
docs.text: No. The I/O board is optional, but it offers features that may be important to some users, such as 3.5 mm and optical audio, CRT output, and tape audio input.

docs.title: Do I need an I/O board to get analog video output to my CRT?
docs.text: No. You can use an HDMI-to-VGA adapter instead; see Direct Video.

docs.title: Which cores require SDRAM?
docs.text: See the Console Cores and Computer Cores lists, which are kept up to date. Many Arcade cores require SDRAM as well.

docs.title: Why do some cores require an SDRAM add-on board when other cores do not?
docs.text: Usually because the core needs reliable read and write timing to work properly without bugs. The original NES, for instance, accesses the ROM directly, so its timings are much tighter and SDRAM is required. The DE10-Nano's built-in DDR3 memory has variable latency for random reads and writes, which makes it unsuitable for systems that need reliable timing.

docs.title: Do I need the official USB Hub Add-On Board?
docs.text: No, but you will probably want at least an inexpensive OTG hub, such as the MakerSpot Micro USB OTG Hub, or a regular hub with an adapter. Use a powered hub if you have many devices.

docs.title: Do I need to have a USB keyboard with me to use MiSTer?
docs.text: Yes, it's a good idea to always have a USB keyboard available. A cheap, compact wireless keyboard reduces clutter.

docs.title: What power supply is compatible with MiSTer?
docs.text:
The DE10-Nano needs a 5 V power supply rated for at least 2 A, with a center-positive coaxial "barrel" plug of 5.5 mm outer diameter, 2.1 mm inner diameter, and 11.0 mm length.

If you use a USB Hub add-on board with a lot of power-hungry peripherals (WiFi, Bluetooth, multiple controllers, a mechanical hard drive), consider a similar 5 V supply with more current (4–5 A). Typically this is only needed if you have a mechanical hard drive, make heavy use of the charging port, or power an MT32-Pi from the User IO port, because these draw a lot of current.

docs.title: Does my MiSTer need cooling?
docs.text: A heatsink (passive cooling) is recommended. 22 mm × 22 mm is the ideal size, but 20 mm × 20 mm is more than enough and more common. Active cooling with a fan helps but is not strictly required. Some faster and more complex cores, such as ao486, SNES, N64, and PSX, may generate a lot of heat.

docs.title: The DE10-Nano is rated for up to 100°C operation and it doesn't get nearly that hot. Do I really need a fan or heatsink?
docs.text: A number of complex cores (like ao486) benefit from a cooler chip, because heat can affect the tight timings they require. A heatsink is recommended to avoid any possible glitches, and a fan on top of it is even better. You won't damage your DE10-Nano if you use neither.

docs.title: My fan is very loud, is there anything I can do about that?
docs.text:
Probably. Many I/O boards, though not all, have a jumper near the fan connector that switches the fan's voltage from 5 V to 3 V. It is most likely either next to the fan power connector (you may have to remove the mezzanine board to reach it) or on the underside of the board.

Jumper on the top side of the board:

Jumper on the underside of the board:

Moving the jumper to the other position should slow the fan down and make it quieter.

docs.title: My MiSTer needs a case. What should I do?
docs.text: Either make one yourself or buy one from an online vendor. For DIY, 3D-print files are available online (e.g. on Thingiverse). See Cases for designs and ideas.

docs.title: What kind of screws do I use with the DE10-Nano's 14 mm-long brass standoffs?
docs.text: M3 screws; 8 mm is a good length.

docs.title: I've seen "Update Framework" or "Update Sys" in the news. What does that mean?
docs.text: The "framework" (or "sys") contains the elements that all cores share, such as I/O and video scaling. The message means that the framework part of that core was updated.

docs.title: Can I customize the update/downloader script to ignore certain things?
docs.text: Yes. Add filters to /media/fat/downloader.ini as described in this guide.

docs.title: Can I use the downloader script to download more cores than it currently does?
docs.text: Yes. The downloader script supports custom databases; see this guide.

docs.title: What are unstable cores? How do I install one?
docs.text:
Unstable cores are built automatically from the latest commits to a core's repository, so they include the developers' most recent changes and are updated whenever new code is pushed. They may contain bugs or unfinished features, but they eventually mature into a stable release. The update scripts intentionally don't install them, but there are good reasons to install one, such as testing a bug fix or a new feature. Not every core has automated unstable builds.

Unstable builds are uploaded to the MiSTer-unstable-nightlies GitHub organization, which hosts forks of the core repositories. Download them from the Releases tab of the core's repository. Ignore the releases folder in the repository's file tree: it contains the stable upstream builds. To install a build, copy its .rbf file to the appropriate folder on your MiSTer's MicroSD card. You may want to use a dedicated /_Unstable/ folder to keep these builds separate from stable cores.

docs.title: Why doesn't this core from another repo work? Why is MiSTer so hard to use?
docs.text: MiSTer repositories are self-contained, and the official updater script only fetches cores from the active official MiSTer repositories. Cores from other repositories are not fully integrated, so your results may vary. Some of their developers have their own Discord servers or forums where you can ask for support.

docs.title: How do I make MiSTer boot into the NES core and a specific game?
docs.text:
Combine two options, autobooting a core and starting the core with a given ROM:

  • In MiSTer.ini, set bootcore=NES_20201102.rbf (or the core version you have), and comment out ;bootcore_timeout.
  • In your NES games folder (e.g. /media/fat/games/NES/), copy the FDS BIOS as boot0.rom and the .nes ROM you want to boot as boot1.rom.

For more options, see the NES core documentation.

docs.title: Can I use original console controllers?
docs.text: Yes. Many USB adapters for original console controllers are available; see the USB controller recommendations below. They can also be connected directly to the I/O board's User port (SNAC), as described below.

docs.title: Any USB controller recommendations?
docs.text:
Almost any USB controller works with MiSTer, and Bluetooth or 2.4 GHz USB adapters work for wireless. Controllers that many users seem to like and that have low input latency:

  • Sony DualSense (PS5 Controller) - Very low lag, fast pairing, and a touchpad that can be used as mouse input in cores with mouse support (for example, for SNES lightgun games or as a spinner).
  • 8BitDo M30 Bluetooth and 8BitDo M30 2.4G - These have fewer buttons than PlayStation-style controllers and no analog sticks, so they may limit you if they are your only controllers.
  • 8BitDo SN30 Pro 2 - Versatile connectivity and a comfortable design, similar in shape to the PlayStation DualShock, with an SNES look and button layout.
  • 8BitDo Arcade Stick - Low lag both wired and wireless, with somewhat low lag variation; the pushbuttons and joystick can be replaced (DIY).
  • iBuffalo SNES Controller - A little overpriced now, but one of the lowest-lag controllers tested.

There are many, many more. MiSTerAddons' input latency tests can help you decide, and see the USB overclock instructions for the fastest response.

Excellent USB adapters for original console controllers:

  • UltimateMiSTer.com's DaemonBite adapters (Portugal) - Support multiple kinds of controllers, using an RP2040 chip and the GP2040 firmware.
  • MiSTerAddons.com's Reflex Adapt (USA) - One main device that supports multiple controller types through separate adapter cables.
  • Timville Triple Controller DaemonBite (USA) - A spinoff of MickGuyver's DaemonBite adapters that supports original NES, Genesis, and SNES controllers. You can also build it yourself with these instructions. A 3D-printed housing is available for purchase, or you can print it yourself from these 3D files.
  • 2600-daptor D9

docs.title: Can I increase the polling rate of my USB controller to improve input latency?
docs.text: Yes. See Input Latency.

docs.title: How do I add a second controller to MiSTer?
docs.text: With no core loaded, plug in the controller and set it up in the Menu core, then define it in the OSD of each core as needed. This is only necessary if the controller is a different make/model (a different VendorID/ProductID) from the controllers you have already defined; a second DualShock 4, for example, shouldn't need its inputs defined again. For the same reason, different devices that share a VendorID/ProductID may need to be reconfigured whenever you switch between them, and there is currently no way around this. This includes 8BitDo and Mayflash adapters used with multiple controllers, because the ID belongs to the adapter.

docs.title: What are the methods for connecting controllers to the serial port of the I/O add-on board?
docs.text:
SNAC (Serial Native Accessory Converter) connects original controllers directly to supported cores (SNES, Genesis, NES, and TG16). SNAC adapters are sold online by various sellers:

  • MiSTerFPGA.co.uk's SNAC adapters (best used with their SNAC extension cable)
  • UltimateMiSTer.com's SNAC Adapters (best used with their SNAC extension cable)
  • MiSTerAddons.com's SNAC V1, SNAC V2, and SNAC V3, all of which use external controller adapters made for them and sold separately.

For details on SNAC, see this page.

docs.title: What about light guns?
docs.text:
Original light guns such as the NES Zapper are too timing-sensitive to work over USB, but they work fine in supported cores through the I/O board (SNAC, see above).

MiSTer also supports several USB light guns, such as the GunCon 2, GunCon 3, Gun4IR, and Sinden:

  • GunCon 2 requires a CRT and a way to tap into the sync signal.
  • GunCon 3 and Gun4IR work on all displays.
  • Sinden requires a modern display and dedicated files for MiSTer.
  • Reflex Adapt supports an overclocked GunCon 1, which performs better than the GunCon 2 when 1 ms (1000 Hz) polling is enabled.

Each core requires its own calibration. Calibrate your gun from the distance you plan to play at, and use a white screen for best results.

Never let the calibration value go below 0: saving a calibration with a negative value will likely make the core crash. To fix this, delete the core's light gun calibration file from the "config" folder on your MiSTer's MicroSD card.

docs.title: How do I set up MiSTer for 1080p, shimmer-free gameplay?
docs.text: Run the updater script, then use one of the video presets and filters it installs, in the Video Processing menu of the secondary OSD. See Video Configuration for details.

docs.title: How do I get the scanline filters on my MiSTer to look good?
docs.text:
For the best results, without shimmering artifacts during motion, use integer scaling: set vscale_mode=1 in MiSTer.ini, or use the core's own integer scaling options (and 5x, if supported). Not all cores have OSD options for integer scaling.

"Integer scaling" means the source resolution (e.g. 240p) is scaled to the target resolution (e.g. 1080p) by a whole-number factor only (1, 2, 3, 4...). With the MiSTer set to 1080p in MiSTer.ini and a core that natively outputs 240p, integer scaling enlarges the image 4x (4 × 240 = 960). The remaining 120 lines are left as black borders at the top and bottom of the screen.

You can use other settings if you want the scaler to fill the screen, but scanlines won't be "perfect" unless the source resolution divides evenly into the target resolution (e.g. 240p into 1200p at 5x).

docs.title: I have a 4K or other higher-than-1080p display, does MiSTer support that resolution? I'd like to enjoy better video scaling.
docs.text: MiSTer can't quite reach 4K. To change the resolution, edit MiSTer.ini on your SD card: for example, video_mode=12 for 1920x1440p or video_mode=13 for 2048x1536p (the hardware maximum). video_mode=14 gives 2560x1440p using your display's pixel repetition feature, but your display's upscaling may then cause some tearing or resizing artifacts. Whether these higher resolutions work may depend on your display and signal chain.

docs.title: Other cores work but I get a black screen for this one. What do I do?
docs.text: Try setting vsync_adjust to 0 (this was the default setting), because your display may not support all refresh rates.

docs.title: My CD games don't work! Help!
docs.text: Unzip them; CD games must not be zipped. Use ISO/WAV/BIN/IMG + CUE files or CHD. See CD-based games for how to store them.

docs.title: How do I handle multidisc games? The core keeps resetting when I change to another disc!
docs.text: Put all discs of the game in the same subfolder; the core then shouldn't reset when you mount the next disc. See Multi-disc games for an example.

docs.title: What version of the CD card BIOS do I need for TurboGrafx-16 CD/PC Engine CD?
docs.text: Use the Japanese version 3.0, commonly found as Super CD-ROM System (Japan) (v3.0).pce.

docs.title: How do I change the wallpaper/background on the Menu core when I turn on my MiSTer?
docs.text:
By default, the Menu core background shows simulated TV static. Press F1 in the Menu core to cycle through color bars, plain black, and a wallpaper.

The wallpaper option looks for menu.jpg or menu.png in the root of your MicroSD card (/media/fat/ when the MiSTer is running). If neither file exists, it picks a random .png or .jpg from the ./wallpapers folder each time the Menu core loads. The image's EXIF rotation metadata affects its orientation; if the image appears rotated, change this value with an online EXIF editor.

docs.title: Can you take screenshots on the MiSTer?
docs.text:
Yes. Press Win+Print Screen for an upscaled screenshot, or Shift+Win+Print Screen for the raw output of the core (which may be distorted or have an odd aspect ratio). Screenshots are stored in ./screenshots, in a folder named after the core.

These screenshots are simple and don't include any video processing effects. To capture the fully processed image you see on a modern display, you need a capture card that supports the desired resolution. A card often used in the community is the Magewell USB HDMI Gen 1 or Gen 2, which can be found used on eBay for a fraction of the retail price.

Example: raw screenshot from the NES core

Example: upscaled screenshot from the Neo Geo core

docs.title: Why use FPGA when other proven solutions exist, such as Raspberry Pi?
docs.text:
The following was originally written by Sorgelig, founder of MiSTer FPGA

There are debates about how to refer to the process of simulating real hardware using FPGA. Some people insist it's not emulation but rather true hardware replication, while any simulation using a traditional CPU should be referred to as emulation. I have my own opinion here. :) From my point of view, if the FPGA code is based on the circuitry of real hardware (along with the usual tweaks for FPGA compatibility), then it should be called replication. Anything else is emulation, since it uses different kinds of approximation to meet the same objectives. Currently, it's hard to find a core that can truly be called a replica – most cores are based on more-or-less functional recreations rather than true circuit recreation. The most widely used CPU cores – the Z80 (T80) and MC68000 (TG68K) – are pure functional emulations, not replications. So it's okay to call FPGA cores emulators, unless they are proven to be replicas.

To go back to the original question, then, why FPGA, if it's also just emulation? Well, FPGA emulation is fundamentally different than emulation on a CPU. Traditional emulators on CPUs execute code sequentially. This is a tricky method of emulation because real hardware has many chips and all of them work in parallel. The CPU, video chip/logic, audio chip, memory arbiter – all of them are working at the same time. So a traditional emulator has to take care of all these parts and try to emulate the whole orchestra at the same time by quickly "running" from one chip to another. This requires a lot of CPU power to emulate even an old and slow retro computer. Sometimes even a modern CPU working at 100 times the speed of the retro computer is not enough, so the emulator has to use approximation, skip emulation of some less important parts, or assume some standard work of the emulated system without extraordinary usage. Let's take a well-known emulator, UAE, emulating an Amiga. On a Raspberry Pi 3, you can run some Amiga CPU benchmarks and get crazy numbers like 100 times the original 68000 processor. So you may assume you have an emulated Amiga that is 100 times faster than the real one. No, you don't. If you run different kinds of demos or games, you will see the video stutter sometimes. For example, if you play the well-known "State of the Art" demo by Spaceballs, you will notice video stuttering at some points, while a real Amiga 600 with 1x CPU speed plays the whole demo very smoothly. This is how traditional emulators on Raspberry Pi work.

FPGA emulation works very differently from traditional emulation on CPU. An FPGA is a large array of simple triggers and other logic – just like any other chip/CPU. The only difference is that specific chips/CPUs have these triggers and logic permanently connected, while FPGA allows you to connect them however you want. A special HDL (hardware description language) describes how to connect all these triggers/logic cells. Everything in FPGA works in parallel like in the original chips/devices. Thus, FPGA is pretty close to the original hardware. FPGA doesn't need high frequencies to emulate retro computers; it works at much lower frequencies than traditional emulators require. Since everything in FPGA works in parallel, it is no problem to handle any possible usage of the emulated system. Developers using FPGA usually concentrate on the specific part to make it work correctly – and it will work as it should in any possible scenario. In the same reference demo, "State of the Art," using FPGA emulation, you can see smooth video through the whole playback, as on the original hardware.

You may want to ask, "So why not make all emulators on FPGA then?" The answer is: FPGA programming is not so trivial. Every bit in FPGA works in parallel, so the developer needs to think in parallel as well :). What is trivial on CPU is not trivial on FPGA – although some parts that are trivial on FPGA cost a lot in CPU code.

docs.title: Hotkeys
docs.text: This page lists the MiSTer hotkeys. Hotkeys save time, and some actions can only be done with a keyboard or gamepad hotkey. Some hotkeys work only in the Main Menu core, some work inside cores during gameplay, and some work everywhere.

docs.title: In any core, with OSD closed
docs.text: Hotkey Description F12 Open the Menu/On-Screen Display Alt+F12 Open core select menu Win+Print Screen Take a screenshot (upscaled) Shift+Win+Print Screen Take a screenshot (raw output) Left Ctrl+Left Alt+Right Alt Press the "User" button — usually resets the current core; same as the I/O board button Left Shift+Left Ctrl+Left Alt+Right Alt Full reboot/reset; same as the I/O add-on board's Reset button Controller: Button + Menu hotkey Turn on/off turbo/autofire for the pressed button Controller: Direction + Menu hotkey Set rate of turbo/autofire in milliseconds (ms)

docs.title: With the OSD open, in any core
docs.text: Hotkey Description F12 Close OSD F11 Pair Bluetooth controller Hold I/O board OSD Button Alternate method to Pair Bluetooth controller Left Go to information screen (shows currently selected INI file and volume) Right System screen (change core, set filters, gamma, etc.) Controller: Back + R/L/U/D Select Alternate INI file if defined (Default/Alt1/Alt2/Alt3) Controller: Select Expands submenus in the OSD when highlighted Controller: Shoulder Buttons Cycles through the OSD options in a core in either direction

docs.title: In the Main Menu core only
docs.text: Hotkey Description F1 Switch background type (static, wallpaper, color bars, black) F2 Hide / Show core dates F9 Open Linux terminal / command line interface, use F12 to go back to menu Controller: LB + X / Y Test the rumble motors on your controller

docs.title: Some computer cores
docs.text:
Some computer cores make use of the Windows key (Win) on your keyboard.

Hotkey Description Win+F12 Open the OSD

docs.title: Light gun cores
docs.text:
Some console cores make use of USB/BT light guns, such as the Guncon2, Guncon3, Gun4IR, Sinden, etc.

Read this guide for more information.

More calibration info here.

Hotkey Description OSD Open + F10 Enters light gun calibration. For best results, use a white/bright image

docs.title: Cores that support savestates
docs.text:
Very few cores support savestates (NES, PSX, GameBoy, GBA, WonderSwan, AtariLynx). There are four savestate slots available. In those cores, a standard savestate button can be assigned on your controller (called SaveStateBtn here):

Hotkey Description Alt+F1 - F4 Save the state in slots 1-4 respectively F1 - F4 Restore the state from slots 1-4 respectively Controller: SaveStateBtn + Left/Right Switch the savestate slot Controller: SaveStateBtn + Start + Down Save to the selected slot Controller: SaveStateBtn + Start + Up Restore from the selected slot

docs.title: Controllers
docs.text: MiSTer supports a wide variety of input devices. It also offers options for configuring them and several quality-of-life features that work in most (sometimes all) cores. This page covers special configurations for devices such as spinners, gamepads, joysticks, and keyboards.

docs.title: What devices are supported?
docs.text:
Generally, any normal USB HID-compatible input device should work: keyboards, arcade spinners, USB adapters for original controllers (such as the Raphnet and DaemonBite retro adapters), and even modern console controllers like the PS5 DualSense. If you have an Analog I/O or Digital I/O board, supported cores can also use original controllers through SNAC, including lightguns that normally only work with the original system.

USB and Bluetooth gaming controllers get these standard features:

  • Autofire
  • Mouse emulation from your joystick
  • Up to 6 players

docs.title: Default Joystick Player Assignment Method
docs.text:
• After a core starts, press a button on any connected controller to make it the Player 1 gamepad/joystick.
  • Press a button on a second controller to make it the Player 2 joystick (if the core supports it).
  • Continue the same way for Player 3, Player 4, etc.
  • If you assigned the players in the wrong order, open the OSD's secondary menu (press Right after opening the OSD) and select "Reset player assignment" to start over.
  • Resetting the core also resets the player assignments.

If a controller doesn't seem to work, you may need to reboot the MiSTer into the Menu core and define the controller's inputs, if you haven't already. Also, if two attached controllers report the same Vendor ID and Product ID to Linux, you may not be able to use both at the same time; this depends on how the controller is made.

docs.title: Advanced Joystick Player Assignment Method
docs.text:
You can also assign joystick players manually, based on which device is which. This is useful, for example, in an arcade cabinet with two USB encoder joysticks, where the right one should always be Player 2. Each controller can be identified in one of three ways:

  1. Wireless Bluetooth devices: by their Bluetooth MAC address.
  2. Wired devices: typically by their VendorID and ProductID.
  3. Multiple devices that share the same VendorID and ProductID: by their USB port location.

The easiest way to find this information is to enable debug in MiSTer.ini, then open a console connection or SSH into your MiSTer as root and run killall MiSTer; /media/fat/MiSTer. The debug output shows the information whenever you plug in or unplug a USB device. Enter it in your MiSTer.ini as described in the section starting with Permanently assign specific controller to specific player in the default MiSTer.ini.

docs.title: Maximum number of players
docs.text: The MiSTer framework supports up to six players on separate USB or Bluetooth controllers. Individual cores may support fewer: for instance, as of January 2026, the Saturn core supports up to 2 USB/Bluetooth controllers. If a core supports SNAC, you may be able to add more players through it.

docs.title: Autofire
docs.text:
Any defined button supports autofire. To turn it on, press and hold the button, then quickly press and release the button defined as BUTTON OSD (joystick) or KBD TOGGLE (keyboard). Repeat this to step up to the next autofire rate. To turn autofire off, keep stepping through the rates until the message says autofire is disabled for that button. Each button can have its own autofire rate.

By default, MiSTer offers autofire rates of 10, 15, and 30 Hz. To set custom rates, add or edit the autofire_rates line in MiSTer.ini. Custom rates are rounded down to the nearest rate that repeats cleanly at 60 Hz. You may find that some games work better with certain rates, and that some rates (particularly 30 Hz) are too fast for certain games to process.

autofire_rates=7.5,10,15,20,30

Advanced users may set a custom autofire rate as a pattern of button presses and releases. Prefix the pattern with 0b, then use 0 for each frame the button should be released and 1 for each frame it should be held.

autofire_rates=0b000011111

This line would configure a single autofire rate in which the button is held for five frames, released for four frames, and the cycle then repeats. You can freely mix numeric and pattern-based rates in your autofire_rates line. MiSTer will ignore any rates it is unable to properly process.

docs.title: (Advanced) Built-in Custom Rates
docs.text:
Shooting games often favor very particular autofire rates. For convenience, one such rate is built in and can be selected with a keyword instead of a calculated pattern: put the keyword in the autofire_rates= line where you would put a custom rate or pattern. More may be added in the future as the community recommends them, or as the maintainer of the autofire feature gets better at shooting games.

Value Target Game Resulting Rate GUNFRONTIER Gun Frontier 6.67 Hz

docs.title: Autofire and the joystick/D-pad
docs.text: By default, autofire does not apply to the D-pad/joystick. To allow autofire on directional inputs, add autofire_on_directions=1 to your MiSTer.ini.

docs.title: Mouse emulation
docs.text:
Your joystick can emulate a mouse if you defined the "Mouse Emu" button when you set up your inputs in the Menu core. Hold Mouse Emu and Alt+M; the buttons you defined as Mouse Left/Right/Middle Btn then act as mouse buttons, and the left analog stick (if defined) moves the pointer. To keep mouse emulation on permanently, press BUTTON OSD while holding Mouse Emu. In permanent mode, Mouse Emu becomes a sniper button that makes pointer movements smaller.

Only the buttons defined for mouse emulation switch to mouse functions; the other buttons keep working as regular joystick buttons. A gamepad with many buttons can therefore act as a mouse and a joystick at the same time, which is useful for some games, such as Walker on the Amiga.

docs.title: Serial Native Accessory Converter (SNAC)
docs.text: SNAC adapters let you connect original controllers and peripherals to MiSTer cores. Cores that support SNAC are specially built to expose serial connections on specific pins of the DE10-Nano. As a result, when you pull the trigger of an NES Zapper aimed at your CRT, the signal arrives almost instantly, as it would on original hardware. This matters for devices like lightguns, which need zero lag to work.

docs.title: Using a Lightgun
docs.text: Besides original lightguns over SNAC, MiSTer supports several USB/Bluetooth lightguns, such as the GUN4IR, GunCon 2, GunCon 3, and Wiimote. They can be used with various cores, for example as a Zapper in the NES core or a GunCon 1 in the PSX core. For more on GunCon 2 support, see the GunCon2-MiSTer repository.

docs.title: Lightgun Calibration
docs.text:
The lightgun must be calibrated in each core:

  • With the OSD open, press F10 to show the calibration screen, then follow the prompts to shoot each edge of the image.
  • It is recommended to load a game and calibrate to the edges of the game image, rather than to the edges of the whole (widescreen) TV.

docs.title: Lightgun Joy1/Joy2 assignment
docs.text:
• This setting must match the player number your lightgun is assigned to in the core. See Default Joystick Player Assignment Method.
  • On some systems, such as the NES, SNES, and Genesis, the lightgun connected to the player 2 port. Many games for these systems also work with the lightgun as player 1 (Joy1), but some require a normal controller as player 1 and the lightgun as player 2 (Joy2).

docs.title: Using A Mouse
docs.text:
MiSTer supports mice, mainly for the computer cores whose original systems had them.

A mouse can also act as an emulated lightgun. A Wiimote with a powered sensor bar works on the same principle: once paired with the MiSTer, it is used as a mouse.

A mouse can also act as a paddle-style controller.

docs.title: Are gaming keyboards worth it?
docs.text: No. High-performance, expensive keyboards and mice give no benefit on MiSTer, major or minor. They often expose many extra functions and virtual devices that clutter the input subsystem, which may add input lag, make the device completely unresponsive, or stop other devices such as gamepads from working. If you have problems with a gaming keyboard, try a simpler keyboard. The general advice is not to buy a specialty gaming keyboard just for MiSTer — it may end up being a waste of money.

docs.title: What about rumble support?
docs.text: Rumble (controller vibration) has recently been added to the Game Boy, Game Boy Advance, and PlayStation cores. For the PlayStation core, make sure your controller's rumble is supported: in the Menu core, hold "L" and press "X" or "Y" (SNES-style layout) to test each of the two motors. Rumble only works reliably with controllers in X-Input mode.

docs.title: What about PlayStation 3-5, Xbox 360 and Xbox One, Switch, and third party Bluetooth gamepads?
docs.text:
The ideal wireless solution for these gamepads is a third-party USB dongle, such as the 8BitDo retro receiver (specifically the 8BitDo Wireless Bluetooth Adapter), or a name-brand Bluetooth 4.x/5.0 adapter.

The 8BitDo receiver supports Bluetooth PlayStation, Xbox, Wii, Switch, and 8BitDo gamepads without using the MiSTer's Bluetooth setup menu. Its main appeal is ease of use and quick pairing. Its drawbacks, compared to Bluetooth 5.0 adapters (including TP-Link and Asus models):

  • It may add lag, and may have limited range and line-of-sight issues.
  • Each receiver pairs with only one controller at a time, so multiplayer needs one receiver per controller. Regular Bluetooth pairing has no such limit.
  • The receiver sits between your gamepad and the USB host as a compatibility layer and always presents itself as the same controller, whatever gamepad you connect. Some gamepad features, such as the PS5 controller's mute button and touchpad, are therefore unavailable. A Bluetooth 5.0 adapter pairs the gamepad directly with the MiSTer, so it is less likely to have such limitations, although some features still won't work until the development team adds framework and Linux support for them.

Grey and orange (brick-decorated) 8BitDo USB adapters are functionally the same on the latest firmware. Depending on the controller model, gamepads can switch between input modes with hotkeys; some models, such as the 8BitDo SN30 Pro 2, have a switch on the back instead. 8BitDo's website doesn't document these hotkeys, but the firmware update log does:

  • X-Input mode: Hold SELECT+UP for 3 seconds.
  • PSC (PlayStation Classic) mode: Hold SELECT+DOWN for 3 seconds. This is useful for gamepads with few buttons (12 in total, with the D-pad counting as 4) that still need to open the MiSTer OSD. In this mode, L+R+START opens the OSD inside cores; this combination is hard-coded in MiSTer specifically for 8BitDo adapters, so don't assign an OSD button when configuring buttons in the Menu core. You may also lose autofire and mouse functionality in this mode.

Other 8BitDo adapters, such as the 8BitDo Retro Receivers for SNES, NES, and Genesis consoles, are always in X-Input mode when connected via Micro USB.

docs.title: JammaSD support
docs.text: MiSTer supports the JammaSD by detecting whether a pressed button belongs to Player 1 or Player 2. Configure Player 1 as a joypad in the Menu core (and remap it in cores if needed); Player 2's inputs are then defined automatically, as if it were a second identical joypad. A second JammaSD can be plugged in for Players 3 and 4. JammaSD support uses a VID/PID that should be the same on all devices; if yours differs, set it in MiSTer.ini with the jamma_vid/jamma_pid/jamma2_vid/jamma2_pid options.

docs.title: Keyboards
docs.text: MiSTer supports keyboard remapping, which is useful for reduced-size or localized keyboards. Key remapping is system-wide, so every core uses the same key mapping. There is no macro key functionality — single keys are remapped to other single keys. Some multimedia keys generate several key codes and cannot be remapped. Each keyboard model's key map is stored in /media/fat/config/kbd_[VID]_[PID].map. To reset all keys to their defaults, delete the map file with the matching VendorID and ProductID in the filename. Key remapping is available through the Menu core only.

docs.title: Joystick emulation
docs.text: Keyboards can be switched to joystick emulation. Define the keys used for joystick emulation the same way you did for joysticks. Autofire is also supported the same way as for joysticks (Menu+button). The button defined for "KBD TOGGLE" provides a quick switch between keyboard and joystick use for defined keys.

docs.title: Mouse emulation
docs.text: Keyboards can be switched to mouse emulation. Define mouse emulation buttons in the Menu core the same way as for joysticks, in the Define Gamepad menu option.

docs.title: Emulation switch
docs.text:
To switch between emulation modes, press Num Lock or Scroll Lock until the desired mode is selected.

The switching sequence is Mouse >> Joy1 >> Joy2 >> None

The LEDs on your keyboard will display the emulation modes:

  • Mouse emulation: NumLock LED + ScrLock LED
  • Joystick 1 emulation: NumLock LED.
  • Joystick 2 emulation: ScrLock LED.

docs.title: Common functional keys/combos used in cores
docs.text:
• F12 - open/close OSD menu/submenu
  • Alt+F12 - quick core selection (like in Menu core).
  • Left Ctrl+Left Alt+Right Alt - presses the "USER" button, which usually triggers reset in the emulated system.
  • Left Shift+Left Ctrl+Left Alt+Right Alt - MiSTer reset (load Menu core).

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Some systems provide write support, which requires additional attention when you reset/shut down the MiSTer. MiSTer tries not to keep pending writes and flushes to disk as soon as possible. Still, the safer way to reset from a core that was probably writing to disk recently is Left Shift+Left Ctrl+Left Alt+Right Alt — this flushes all caches to disk before restart. Cores without write support can be restarted with the hard reset button or powered down without concern.
  • The Left Ctrl+Left Alt+Right Alt sequence can be replaced by other well-known combos through the INI file.
