docs.title: Game Saves
docs.text: Many MiSTer cores let you save your game, either by simulating the original hardware's save features or with savestates. Most cores don't have savestates, but a steadily increasing number do.

docs.title: Normal game saves
docs.text:
MiSTer writes your in-game saves to the MicroSD card only when you open the On-Screen Display (OSD). To save:

  1. Save inside the game.
  2. Open the OSD and select "Save Backup RAM".
  3. In most cores, open the OSD again. You should see a "Saving..." pop-up; if you don't, your save probably wasn't written.

While a save is being written with the OSD open, the yellow LED on the Digital I/O or Analog I/O board lights up, and it turns off when the save is complete.

Having to open the OSD takes some getting used to, but it is necessary. MicroSD cards survive only a limited number of writes before they begin to fail, and because these cores run in the FPGA, some of them may otherwise write to the card constantly, several times a second, without a signal telling them when to back up the save to a file.

docs.title: Autosave option
docs.text:
Because of the MicroSD card's limited write endurance, almost no core autosaves by default: autosave could generate too many writes and make the card fail sooner. MiSTer's Autosave option only writes when you open the OSD, so it doesn't cause constant writes, and turning it on is still recommended in every core that offers it:

  1. Open the OSD and turn on the Autosave option, if available.
  2. Press Right on your controller (or keyboard) to open the secondary OSD menu, and select "Save Settings".

"Save Settings" saves the setting for that core only; other cores keep their own settings.

docs.title: Save file conversion
docs.text: The save files of most MiSTer cores are compatible with many popular emulators. Where they differ, Euan Forrester's MiSTer Save File Converter converts them. It also converts many other emulator save formats, and converts MiSTer saves back into emulator-compatible files.

docs.title: Back up your saves
docs.text: Back up your saves from the MicroSD card regularly: when MicroSD storage fails, it usually fails suddenly and completely. Various tools can do this, such as FreeFileSync, which can run a scheduled batch job that backs up specific MiSTer folders. See the FreeFileSync documentation for details.

docs.title: The MiSTer FPGA's correct DIP switch configuration on the DE10-Nano
docs.text: If your keyboard or other low-level hardware doesn't work, one or more of the DIP switches on your DE10-Nano may be misconfigured.

docs.title: Upper DIP Switches
docs.text: Make sure the DIP switches are configured as shown:

docs.title: Lower DIP Switches
docs.text:
If your I/O board is based on the 9.2 I/O board and AV mezzanine board, you don't need to set any of the lower switches: the framework detects the configuration of these boards automatically. Settings for earlier boards are below.

I/O boards before 9.2

If you have a Digital I/O board and a 2nd SDRAM module, turn the first large DIP switch in the 2nd picture above On (up) and the rest Off (down): Credit for 2nd and 3rd pictures goes to Nat from MiSTerFPGA.co.uk

Board SW0 SW1 SW2 SW3 Analog I/O Off Off Off Off Digital I/O Off Off Off On

docs.title: My gamepad doesn't work
docs.text: If your gamepad doesn't work in the menu, make sure you have defined its inputs. If it works in the menu but not in a core, define the gamepad in that core's secondary OSD menu. If it works in neither, check that your DIP switches are correct as shown above.

docs.title: My keyboard doesn't work right
docs.text: If you have a fancy gaming keyboard with lots of macros and RGB lights, the stock power supply may not provide enough power. You may want to consider a power supply with more amps to fix this, such as the Mean Well GST18A05-P1J; this DigiKey search result gives an idea of what is required. Generally, you need a 5 V supply rated above the stock 2 A, with a center-positive 2.1 mm x 5.5 mm x 11.0 mm barrel plug. Mean Well and Triad are often recommended, but they are not the only option if your retailer doesn't carry them.

docs.title: The lights on my MiSTer light up, but I don't get video out of the HDMI port
docs.text:
If your MiSTer seems to boot but there is no video from the HDMI port:

  1. Check that the cable is good and firmly connected at both the MiSTer and the display.
  2. Try another cable, just in case.
  3. Remove the SD card and insert it again. If the MiSTer can't read the card, or the card is empty, it fails to boot completely.

To check whether the MiSTer has booted, try connecting to it via SSH or FTP. If you can connect, it has booted.

docs.title: Fixing missing certs
docs.text:
If wget fails, you may be missing security certificate files. The default system ships without any, so wget can only download over HTTPS with --no-check-certificate. To install the certificates:

  1. Open the Linux terminal with F9; log in as root with password 1.
  2. cd /etc/ssl/certs
  3. cp cacert.pem cacert.pem.bak (back up the existing cert)
  4. wget --no-check-certificate https://curl.se/ca/cacert.pem -O cacert.pem

If the download succeeded, wget now works normally.

docs.title: WiFi shows two IP addresses and no internet connection
docs.text:
If the MiSTer has no Internet connection (for example, you can't update it) and ip addr shows two IP addresses on wlan0, the two addresses may be the cause. Some WiFi adapters seem to do this even on regular Linux computers, and the underlying cause can't be fixed. In many cases there is no Internet access if one of the two addresses is an "APIPA" address (169.254.x.x). To clear the problem temporarily, run:

ip addr flush wlan0

The problem may come back when your DHCP lease expires and new addresses are assigned. On most home networks, the DHCP server is the router/modem.

docs.title: Fixing a corrupted Linux image on the MiSTer
docs.text:
Sometimes MicroSD cards corrupt data over time; this is normal. Rarely, it corrupts the MiSTer's Linux files. If you notice low-level problems such as the following (the list is not exhaustive):

  • HDMI video output not working anymore
  • USB controllers and even keyboards not working
  • Internet no longer working
  • Sound not working over HDMI
  • WiFi not working

then it is best to try re-downloading the Linux files and overwriting the old ones:

  1. Remove the MicroSD card from your MiSTer and insert it into your PC.
  2. Download the latest sd-installer release archive (usually the .7z file at the bottom of the list) from https://github.com/MiSTer-devel/SD-Installer-Win64_MiSTer and unzip it on your PC.
  3. Copy the contents of the archive's linux folder over the linux folder on the MicroSD card, overwriting the existing files.

This is essentially what the update script's "Linux Update" does, and it should restore everything to the normal defaults. If you use WiFi, you may need to repeat the WiFi setup.

docs.title: Video Configuration
docs.text:
MiSTer offers several basic video customization features:

  • Adjustable resolution (video_mode)
  • Framebuffer options (vsync_adjust) that reduce input latency and video stutter
  • Video filters, including scanlines
  • Shadowmasks
  • Gamma correction
  • 5x overscan mode, which pushes a 1200p image into 1080p for square pixels and nearly the original overscan of a CRT, depending on the game's resolution

docs.title: Video Presets
docs.text: Video Presets let you load a pre-made configuration that looks good and works in most situations, which makes them a good starting point. Open the OSD, press right, go to Video Processing → Load Preset, and pick one that looks good to you:

docs.title: MiSTer.ini video settings
docs.text:
The MiSTer.ini file contains many video settings; this page covers only a few of them. CRT-specific settings are covered in Advanced - CRT.

You can edit MiSTer.ini with any text editor (Windows Notepad, Visual Studio Code, Notepad++, etc.), or run the ini-settings.sh script in the scripts folder, which offers a simple interface for changing options.

docs.title: video_mode
docs.text:
The video_mode option sets the output resolution. The available presets are listed in comments above it:

; 0 - 1280x720@60
; 1 - 1024x768@60
; 2 - 720x480@60
; 3 - 720x576@50
; 4 - 1280x1024@60
; 5 - 800x600@60
; 6 - 640x480@60
; 7 - 1280x720@50
; 8 - 1920x1080@60
; 9 - 1920x1080@50
;10 - 1366x768@60
;11 - 1024x600@60
;12 - 1920x1440@60
;13 - 2048x1536@60
;14 - 2560x1440@60 (Pixel Repetition)

For example, video_mode=0 sets 1280x720@60. Most people will probably want 1920x1080@60, so my advice would be video_mode=8. The ini-settings.sh script also shows which value selects which resolution.

For a detailed explanation of video modes, see Advanced - Video Modes (thanks to Wickerwaka).

docs.title: vsync_adjust
docs.text:
Most modern displays work fine at 60 Hz, but some games run at a "non-standard" refresh rate, such as 60.6 Hz for arcade Donkey Kong. To handle this, MiSTer uses a framebuffer: the game keeps running at 60.6 Hz while frames are sent to the display at 60 Hz. Because the game produces frames slightly faster than they are sent, the framebuffer occasionally has to adjust, which causes a small stutter. Using a framebuffer adds a minimal amount of lag. vsync_adjust controls this behavior:

vsync_adjust=0
Outputs at your monitor's refresh rate (e.g. 60 Hz), with about 1-2 frames of lag. Video can be a little jittery, because the core still runs at its native rate, which isn't exactly 60 Hz. 
vsync_adjust=1
Outputs at exactly the game's frame rate (e.g. 60.6 Hz), with 1 frame of lag. Video is very smooth, but this mode is less compatible with modern televisions. 
vsync_adjust=2
Draws video to the screen as fast as possible and can achieve consistent sub-frame lag (not counting your controller's and display's own lag). Video is very smooth. However, this is the least compatible mode, and it may result in unplayable behavior on some televisions with certain cores. Because of the way this mode works, the refresh rate of the scaled output also differs from that of the core's original video output.

As a rule of thumb, start at vsync_adjust=2 for the smoothest video and lowest lag. If a core you want to play doesn't work, reduce it to 1 or 0. Your results may vary depending on your display and the core.

docs.title: Variable Refresh Rate (VRR)
docs.text:
MiSTer supports Variable Refresh Rate (VRR). VRR reduces sync loss on your display when the core outputs a non-standard refresh rate and you use a low-lag vsync_adjust setting (1 or 2).

VRR requires a recent build of the Main MiSTer binary (a new release is currently pending; early builds are posted in the #unstable-nightlies channel of the MiSTer FPGA Discord). You also need either an updated MiSTer.ini or the following lines added to your existing one:

; Variable Refresh Rate control
; 0 - Do not enable VRR (send no VRR control frames)
; 1 - Auto Detect VRR from display EDID. 
; 2 - Force Enable Freesync
; 3 - Force Enable Vesa HDMI Forum VRR
vrr_mode=0
; Freesync min/max framerate parameter defaults to the min/max capability reported by the display
; Freesync minimum framerate. 
vrr_min_framerate=0
; Freesync maximum framerate
vrr_max_framerate=0
; VESA VRR base framerate. Normally set to the current video mode's output framerate
vrr_vesa_framerate=0

VRR is off by default, for broad compatibility and to keep the MiSTer easy to use. Set vrr_mode=1 to auto-detect what your display supports; results vary, and some displays can't sync with this setting. If auto-detection fails, force VRR on with 2 (FreeSync) or 3 (VESA HDMI Forum VRR). Some displays label FreeSync as "AMD FreeSync", but it is an open standard and not exclusive to AMD products. Some displays also label VESA VRR as "G-Sync", even though it isn't necessarily the same as NVIDIA's proprietary G-Sync standard.

Results with VRR vary. Before changing this setting, make sure you can easily edit MiSTer.ini, because the setting may leave you without display output until you revert it. The refresh rate reported by the MiSTer may also differ from the one reported by your TV. This is expected: TVs measure refresh rate with proprietary methods whose accuracy can't be verified without expensive test equipment.

Enabling VRR might give measurably smoother video: Ace reported that the repeated and skipped frames he saw on his display disappeared. Multiple testers also observed better sync stability with some non-standard refresh rates. There is no guarantee your display will behave the same way.

docs.title: Core exceptions
docs.text:
You can override settings for specific cores. For example, my monitor doesn't play nice with the low-lag setting on the Genesis core, so in my MiSTer.ini I added this section to the end of the file:

[Genesis]
vsync_adjust=0

Whatever vsync_adjust is set to in the main section, the Genesis core will now always use vsync_adjust=0, the most compatible mode. A wildcard applies one exception to multiple cores:

[dkong*]
vsync_adjust=1

This rule applies to every core whose name starts with dkong. You can also make an exception for all arcade cores:

[arcade]
vsync_adjust=1

For the internal core names to use in exceptions, see Developer Reference - Core Names.

NOTE — Exceptions for individual arcade games use the <setname> value from the MRA file, not the internal core name. For example, Arkanoid (Japan).mra contains:

<setname>arkanoidj</setname>

so the exception for this game is [arkanoidj]. For a list of setnames, see Developer Reference - MRA Setnames.

docs.title: Video processing tutorial
docs.text: This tutorial walks through the main video processing options.

docs.title: Filters and scanlines
docs.text:
MiSTer can apply upscaling filters and scanlines to enhance the video output or make it look like a retro CRT. With the video output set to 1920x1080p, the NES core running Duck Tales should look something like this by default:

To improve this, open "Video Processing" in the secondary OSD menu (press F12 or the menu button you assigned, then press right):

On this screen, Video Filter: defaults to NearNeighbour, a nearest-neighbour filter. Scaling 240p video to 1080p requires enlarging each pixel, but 240 doesn't divide evenly into 1080 (1080 / 240 = 4.5), so some pixels can't be perfectly square. Nearest neighbour helps fool your eyes into seeing the pixels as squarer than they are.

Select Video Filter: to choose a filter file; the label changes to Horz filter:. For normally oriented (non-rotated) games, the horizontal filter is the upscaling filter that softens or sharpens the image.

Select <none> below it to browse the filter files. For now, select Interpolation (Medium).txt, which gives softer edges while keeping the illusion of square pixels.

The pixels are now a bit smoother:

Interpolation also makes scrolling look smoother than sharper filters such as the default nearest neighbour.

For scanlines like those of a CRT (and of the scanline option in some emulators), set Vert Filter: the same way. It filters horizontal lines from top to bottom, i.e. vertically. Under Vert Filter's From File option, select Scanlines - Brighter.txt. The options should now look like this:

docs.title: 5x Vertical Crop (1080p only)
docs.text:
Note: this feature only works if the output resolution in MiSTer.ini is a 1080p mode.

With the scanline filter on, you might notice that some scanlines look darker than others. This is because 240p (this game's resolution) doesn't divide evenly into 1080p, but it does divide evenly into 1200 (5 × 240 = 1200). To make the scanlines even, stretch the image vertically so all pixels are perfectly square: in the regular core menu, select Video & Audio → Vertical Crop and change Disabled to (216p)5X. Not all cores have this option; the NES core does.

A few lines at the top and bottom are cut off. This is fine: original CRTs cut off about the same amount, and most games keep no information at the top and bottom edges. The Scanlines - Brighter.txt scanlines are now evenly spaced, and the image should look a lot better.

This video demonstrates 5x mode:

docs.title: Shadowmasks
docs.text: Shadowmasks are another layer of options. They modify the red, green, and blue color channels to create effects such as the grille or mask of an old CRT screen or the pixel layout of old LCD handhelds. There are many shadowmasks; this tutorial uses Squished VGA Bright v2.txt, in the author's opinion one of the most versatile color shadowmasks. It attempts to resemble consumer computer monitors and some TVs, which had red, green, and blue phosphors in a particular pattern. With this shadowmask added, the same game looks like this:

docs.title: Gamma curves
docs.text:
On an old CRT, gamma is the relationship between voltage and brightness. Picture a graph with voltage on the x-axis and brightness (more precisely, luminance) on the y-axis. On a modern TV this is ideally a straight line. On an old CRT it is a curve: at medium voltage, brightness is a lot lower than you'd expect.

Image Source

MiSTer outputs the linear curve, so gamma filters can restore a curve similar to the one you were used to on an old television. This is especially helpful after adding a "brighter" scanline and a shadowmask (which imitates a CRT's phosphors). Gamma is a matter of personal preference, so try it and judge for yourself.

This example applies a very mild gamma curve, gamma_113.txt from the Pure_Gamma folder, which is allegedly close to a typical consumer CRT's gamma curve.

This video demonstrates the gamma controls:

docs.title: WiFi
docs.text: WiFi is optional and simple to set up on the MiSTer. You'll need a compatible dongle, the wifi.sh script (provided with the Mr. Fusion image), and a keyboard attached to your MiSTer to type in your WiFi password.

docs.title: Suggested WiFi Adapters
docs.text:
Neither the DE10-Nano nor the MiSTer add-on boards have built-in WiFi, so you need a compatible USB WiFi adapter. Not all models are compatible, so try to stick with decent name brands. Many users have found that most small ASUS, TP-Link, CanaKit, and Edimax USB adapters work out of the box. Adapters reported to work:

  • ASUS USB AC53 nano rev A1
  • TP-Link AC1300 Archer T3U or Nano AC600 Archer T2U
  • CanaKit Raspberry Pi WiFi dongle
  • Edimax EW-7612UAn v2 or EW-7811UN or EW-7822ULC
  • Netgear A6100 or A6150
  • D-link AC1300 MU-MIMO Wi-Fi Nano USB Adapter DWA-181

Your results may vary, because newer hardware revisions of these adapters may not be supported. Advanced users can compile their own drivers.

docs.title: Set up WiFi with a script
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the scripts menu in the on-screen display (OSD).
  2. Select the "wifi" script and run it.
  3. Select your WiFi network's SSID (the name of your WiFi).
  4. Type your WiFi password and press Enter.
  5. It should connect and ask you to press any key to continue.

A small WiFi icon at the top of the main menu shows that you are connected. The setting should be saved, and the MiSTer will reconnect automatically whenever the adapter is plugged in and within range of your network.

docs.title: Manual WiFi setup
docs.text:
If the script doesn't work, you can try to set up WiFi manually. This method is slightly more advanced, so feel free to ask the community for help before trying it:

  1. Edit the file /media/fat/linux/_wpa_supplicant.conf with a text editor that supports Unix/Linux line endings.
  2. Replace put_your_SSID_here with your WiFi network's SSID, and put_your_password_here with your WiFi password.
  3. Change the country code to the one that matches your country.
  4. Rename _wpa_supplicant.conf to wpa_supplicant.conf.
  5. Reboot the MiSTer.

After the reboot, the WiFi icon should appear at the top of the Main Menu's OSD. Be patient: the MiSTer is not very fast at connecting to WiFi — it's a simple device with simple capabilities — so this may take quite a while.

docs.title: Core Paths
docs.text: Each core looks for its games in a folder named after the core. This page lists where that folder can be, and which location is used if it exists in more than one.

docs.title: Standard Core Paths
docs.text: They are of the form /media/fat/games/<CORE>, where <CORE> is the internal core name of the given system. Check each core's README to determine the appropriate full path.

docs.title: Standard USB Core Paths
docs.text: They are of the form /media/usb<0..5>/games/<CORE>, where <0..5> indicates the number of USB drives mounted by the operating system.

docs.title: Standard CIFS Core Paths
docs.text: They are of the form /media/fat/cifs/games/<CORE>.

docs.title: Other Paths
docs.text: Other valid paths exist for backwards compatibility and to ease testing. You should use the standard paths instead whenever possible.

docs.title: Path Priority
docs.text:
There is a priority order of core paths. When you plug in a USB drive containing a /games/PSX folder (mounted as /media/usb<0..5>/games/PSX), the MiSTer PSX core looks there instead of the local /media/fat/games/PSX on the MicroSD. Here is the priority list from Main_MiSTer's file_io.cpp, from highest to lowest priority:

  1. /media/usb<0..5>
  2. /media/usb<0..5>/games
  3. /media/network
  4. /media/network/games
  5. /media/fat/cifs
  6. /media/fat/cifs/games
  7. /media/fat
  8. /media/fat/games

If the core's folder isn't found in any of these locations, the core should create it automatically.

docs.title: What Is a Core
docs.text:
In MiSTer terminology, a "core" is the system the FPGA is currently configured to simulate. By default, the FPGA is configured as the "Menu" core on power-on. Then, if you open the OSD, go to _Console, and select NES, the FPGA is reconfigured as the "NES" core.

Hardware Description Language (HDL) developers use the term "core" for things programmed onto the FPGA. For instance, the MiSTer FPGA framework uses Intel's "Altera PLL Core" — a portable chunk of logic that lets developers configure the chip's clock speeds. There are HDMI cores, Ethernet cores, serial data cores, and so on.

However, for MiSTer, a core refers to the system being emulated: the PSX (PlayStation) core, the Minimig (Amiga) core, the SNES core, and many more.

docs.title: What happens when I load a core?
docs.text:
Imagine every time you load a core you are connecting a different console, computer, or arcade system to your television. Select the Genesis core in the menu and load it, and you have essentially plugged a Genesis into your television — without wrestling with cables. What actually happens is that the .rbf file reprograms the FPGA chip: the digital logic for the NES is replaced with the digital logic for the Genesis (both combined with the MiSTer FPGA core components).

You may worry that all this rewriting could shorten the FPGA's lifespan. It isn't something to worry about: SRAM-based FPGAs like this one are considered to have an unlimited number of writes, and many millions of rewrites to the same area are normal.

docs.title: Core updates and issues
docs.text:
Cores on MiSTer are the result of the collaboration between many people over many years and across multiple prior open-source projects. Most console and computer cores have now been compared to original hardware to a high level of precision (e.g. audio capture comparison), with the few remaining issues documented on their respective GitHub repository pages. Check the relevant core's page before submitting an issue.

For a list of core repositories, see the MiSTer FPGA GitHub Organization. Each core's page leads to its release folder, its Issues page, and its README, which ideally lists all of the core's features and limitations in detail.

There are other unofficial MiSTer FPGA cores out there, but they aren't listed here — they may not work correctly, and the list is always changing.

docs.title: Cheats
docs.text: Some MiSTer cores can apply cheats in-game. The cheats use a specific format and are downloaded automatically from gamehacking.org when you run the downloader script. The cheat files follow specific rules, described below.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Cheats should be stored in cheats/system/rom_filename.zip, where system is the core name (NES, SNES, Genesis, etc.).

For example:

cheats/NES/Taboo (USA).zip for the NES ROM Taboo (USA).nes

The filename of the zip must match the ROM name exactly. Cheats will be loaded automatically when you load a ROM, and can be enabled and disabled from the menu in supported cores.

If the .zip cheat file does not match the ROM name, the cheat engine checks the ROM's CRC32 and selects the .zip cheat file with a matching CRC32. ROM name matching has priority over CRC32 checking.

Individual cheats are in .gg format and should be stored in zip files.

docs.title: How to use cheats with CD-ROM images
docs.text:
Because CD-ROM images are large, MiSTer intentionally doesn't check their CRC32 hash. To use cheats with a CD image, place the cheat zip in the same folder as your CUE/BIN or CHD file. Cheats are typically matched to the CD image by filename: the cheat zip's filename must match that of the CUE/BIN, CHD, or ISO. The PlayStation core uniquely also supports a second method, which loads cheats based on the game's internal Game ID (e.g. SCUS-94163); see Using cheats on the MiSTer PSX core. If the cheats don't load, check the following:

  1. The cheat zip file is in the same subfolder as the desired CUE/BIN, CHD, or ISO.
  2. The filename of the zip file is identical to the filename of the CUE/BIN, CHD, or ISO.
  3. (for the PSX core only) The Game ID of the desired game matches the target Game ID of the zip file.

If cheats for the CD game do not work when everything else looks correct, your version of the game may be different from the one the cheats were made for.

docs.title: Making your own codes
docs.text:
All types of cheat codes for 16-bit systems and earlier can be decoded into four pieces of information: an address, a compare value, a replace value, and usually a flag saying whether the compare value is used. A .gg file stores these in binary as four 32-bit integers in little-endian byte order.

For example, if the address is 0xFF1CA0, the compare value is 0xB5, and the replace value is 0xFF, the file would look like this:

01 00 00 00 A0 1C FF 00 B5 00 00 00 FF 00 00 00

The first four bytes are little-endian 0x00000001 for "compare enabled", the second four are the little-endian address, the third set is the compare value, and the fourth is the replace value. Note that not all codes use a compare value.

For cheats with multiple codes, add another 16 bytes at the end of the file in the same format as the first.

You can decode Game Genie codes into these values with tools like this:

https://gamehacking.org/system/nes

docs.title: RTC Support
docs.text: MiSTer has Real-Time Clock support in many of its cores. If you have an Internet connection or the RTC board installed, these cores will show the correct date and time or utilise it.

docs.title: Cores with RTC support (and how to test each)
docs.text:
• ao486 (PC) (DATE on MS-DOS prompt)
  • Archie (Acorn Archimedes) (Apps > Alarm)
  • GBA (checked with Pokémon Sapphire, wall clock in first room)
  • Game Boy (GB and GBC) (Pokémon Gold: set clock, go one room right, set day of week, save, restart; clock is in the menu screen)
  • MSX ("MSX3") (DATE on MSX-DOS prompt)
  • BBCMicro (BBC Micro Master 128K) (PRINT TIME$ in BBC Master mode)
  • Menu (on top of the panels)
  • Minimig (Amiga) (Utilities > Clock)
  • NeoGeo (DIP Settings: ON > BOOK KEEPING > CABINET/COIN, check date of log entries)
  • PC8801mk2SR (PC-88) (PRINT DATE$ shows year 85 but the correct month and day; PRINT TIME$ shows the correct time)
  • QL (Sinclair QL) (PRINT DATE$)
  • SNES (Daikaijuu Monogatari II, Tengai Makyou Zero; after setting the clock, reload the core so that the clock takes the real time)
  • TSConf (top of Wild Commander screen, also MaxiClock plugin)
  • X68000 (DATE on HUMAN68K prompt)
  • Zet98 (PC-98) (DATE on MS-DOS prompt)
  • ZXNext (ZX Spectrum Next) (main menu in Next mode)

docs.title: Genesis
docs.text:
Note: This core is being deprecated in favor of the new hardware-accurate MegaDrive core by Nukeykt, developed from analysis of decapped chips. The turbo and sprite limit features are currently unavailable in the MegaDrive core.

The Genesis core is a port of the fpgagen core to MiSTer, with significant enhancements and additions. The audio filtering options have been adjusted according to real hardware using MDFourier.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Composite Blending effect (e.g. Sonic Waterfall transparency)
  • CPU Turbo option (e.g. Road Rash gameplay speed)
  • Increased sprite limit
  • Audio filtering options for Model 1, Model 2, Minimal, and No Filter
  • Switch between YM2612 (Model 1) or YM3438 (Model 2/3) FM synth
  • Multitap: 4-way, Team Player, J-Cart
  • SVP chip (Virtua Racing for Genesis supported)
  • Auto-region header detection using the new style and the old style combined
  • Corrected aspect ratio option for 320x224 game resolutions (e.g. Castlevania Moon)

docs.title: Region detection
docs.text:
There are two methods of region detection.

  1. Header: Detects a character in the ROM header to determine the game's intended console region (Japanese, European, or American). This is the default and preferred method, as it works with the entire commercial lineup. Multi-region games (which have multiple region codes in the header, e.g. JUE) use the region priority setting described below.

  2. File extension: Changes the region according to the ROM's filename extension.

    • BIN = Japanese
    • GEN = America
    • MD = Europe

The region priority list controls which region a multi-region game (with multiple region codes in its header) loads as, in order of preference. For example, US>JP>EU tries US first, falls back to JP if no US code is present, then EU. The first available region in the list is the one used on load.

docs.title: YM2612/YM3438 and Genesis Model 1/2 audio filtering
MegaCD
docs.text: The MegaCD core is a MiSTer project original developed by srg320 (Sergey Dvodnenko) that aims to simulate the Sega CD / Mega CD add-on for the Sega Genesis. It uses the same fpgagen logic and many of the improvements made to it in the MiSTer Genesis core, plus a significant amount of additional logic to handle the CD add-on hardware.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Almost all features from the Genesis core
  • CUE/BIN support
  • CHD support
  • Automatic region detection
  • Multiple BIOS capability
  • Pier Solar support
  • MSU-MD support

docs.title: Sega CD Mode 1 Audio - MSU-MD and Pier Solar Support
docs.text:
To use MSU-MD or to play the Sega CD version of Pier Solar on the MiSTer core, the following conditions need to be met:

  • The MegaDrive/Genesis cartridge ROM and the CUE/BIN (or CHD) image of the full game must be placed in the same folder.
  • The MegaDrive/Genesis cartridge ROM must be renamed to cart.rom to load it into SDRAM when the CUE/CHD is loaded.
  • In the case of MSU-MD, the ROM must be patched with the correct MSU-MD patch so it can tell the core what tracks to play and when.

If you meet all of these conditions and the game still doesn't work, then there are a few likely explanations:

  1. Your ROM patch is actually an MD+ patch. MD+ is not currently supported.
  2. Your ROM is not patched at all.
  3. You didn't rename the cartridge's ROM to cart.rom.
  4. Your CUE file is incorrect.

If a set of MSU-MD ROMs you downloaded doesn't work, apply the patch to a fresh ROM yourself and see whether that works.

docs.title: NES
docs.text:
The Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) MiSTer core is packed with features:

  • Automatic Famicom Disk System (FDS) disk swapping
  • Custom palette loading
  • Overscan and screen-edge masking
  • An extra sprites hack
  • SNAC support, so you can use an original Zapper lightgun on a CRT over analog video output

docs.title: Extra Sprites mode
docs.text: The NES could only show a limited number of sprites on screen at once. Some games displayed more sprites than this, making the sprites flicker so that all of them stayed on screen. The NES core can partly remove this limit, which reduces flicker when many sprites are on screen, in games like Rygar. This doesn't work with every game that flickers: some flicker was added intentionally by the original developers for other reasons.

docs.title: Palettes
docs.text: The NES core has built-in palettes and can also load custom palettes. The NES has no native color palette, because it didn't output colors as red, green, and blue values like other consoles. Emulators therefore need palettes that approximate the original viewing experience as closely as possible. Since that experience sometimes varied depending on the TV, several palettes are available. This also makes fun and ridiculous palettes possible, such as RetroSho's Virtual Boy palette. For more on NES palettes, watch this YouTube video by NesHacker (and read the pinned comment, as a few details were technically inaccurate).

docs.title: Famicom Disk System BIOS boot
docs.text: Download the blank FDS boot2.rom and place it in ./games/NES/. When you start the core (assuming the FDS BIOS is already there as boot0.rom), it boots to the FDS BIOS as if a blank disk were inserted.

docs.title: Famicom Disk System Blank Disk Boot Example Video
PSX
docs.text:
The Sony PlayStation (PSX) MiSTer core is the most feature-filled and heavily developed core so far:

  • Multiple controller options
  • Automatic BIOS region swapping
  • Both memory card slots with manual file loading
  • Speed-increasing modes
  • In-game texture modification

Writing a PSX FPGA implementation is a huge task, and this core by Robert Peip (FPGAzumSpass) is still under active development. This page highlights some of its features.

docs.title: Controller Support
docs.text:
The MiSTer PSX core supports a very large list of control options that original hardware had available to it.

  • DualShock (later controller with analog sticks and rumble/vibration capability)
  • Digital Pad (original PSX controller without analog sticks)
  • Analog Pad mode (dual analog sticks mode enabled)
  • GunCon
  • NeGcon (can also be used as a steering wheel via the "Wheel-NegCon" option in the OSD)
  • Racing Wheels (some analog racing wheels work if you switch to "Wheel-Analog" in the OSD)
  • Mouse
  • Justifier
  • SNAC (requires a special adapter to use real PSX controller accessories; memory cards and even the PocketStation can technically be used in this mode)
  • Analog Joystick
  • Pop'n Music Controller

docs.title: DualShock Support
docs.text:
DualShock controller mode is a catch-all solution. Ideally, it identifies what the game requires and ought to put itself into the right mode (Digital or Analog) for that game. However, some games don't register controller inputs when the controller is in the wrong mode. If this happens, switch to the other mode manually and see whether the problem goes away.

As on the original DualShock controller, you can switch between digital and analog modes with a button press (or several buttons, depending on your controller):

  • On a DualShock 4 or DualSense (PS5) controller, press the center touchpad once. Each press switches between Analog and Digital.
  • On other controllers, press L3+R3+Up/Down or L1+L2+R1+R2+Up/Down, depending on the "DS mode" setting in the OSD.

docs.title: Manual Memory Card Loading
docs.text: You can load PlayStation memory card files (.mcd or .sav) manually in the OSD. By default, the core automatically fills slot 1 with a blank memory card file, so it is probably best to load your file into slot 2. Alternatively, turn off the Automount Memory Card 1 option in the OSD to stop slot 1 from being filled automatically. If you have a SNAC adapter with a memory card slot connected, the core also supports real PlayStation memory cards over SNAC.

docs.title: Libcrypt Support
docs.text: Some games use a copy-protection scheme called "Libcrypt" and don't work unless it is circumvented. To circumvent it, place an .sbi file with the same name next to the game's .cue file; it is loaded automatically when the CD image is mounted. The whole collection of .sbi files can be downloaded from redump.info.

docs.title: Fixed blanks
docs.text:
The original PlayStation gave software developers a wide variety of resolutions, and some games shake the screen by moving the image outside the screen bounds. Both can cause sync loss and unstable scaling when the resolution changes. The Fixed Horizontal Blanks (HBlank) and Fixed Vertical Blanks (VBlank) options stabilize the video output. If you have sync problems, or resolution changes don't look right, try these options.

  • Fixed HBlank also makes everything fit within the original 4:3 aspect ratio of the PSX video output, so turn it on in nearly all situations if you want the original resolution.
  • Vertical Crop becomes available when Fixed VBlank is on. It is similar to the 5x scaling in other cores; because many PSX games use either 224p or 216p, it has two settings.
  • Horizontal Crop is made for some PAL games; see what works best for you.

Examples:

  • Metal Gear Solid benefits from Fixed HBlank: without Fixed VBlank turned on, the screen shaking in some scenes would make a modern display lose sync.
  • Final Fantasy VII benefits from Fixed VBlank. Fixed HBlank alone gives the proper 4:3 aspect ratio, but the resolution visibly "jumps" when the game switches from the world map to a battle. With Fixed VBlank and Vertical Crop -> On (224/270), this transition no longer causes a jarring change in resolution or screen position:

There are more games like these; test to see what works best.

docs.title: Black Transitions
docs.text: Some resolution and screen transitions are so quick that the framebuffer isn't fully cleared in DDR3. This option prevents ghost images of previous frames from appearing over scaled video (HDMI or vga_scaler).

docs.title: Deinterlacing Methods
docs.text: The MiSTer PSX core supports two methods of deinterlacing the occasional interlaced video on the PlayStation. Weave is the default and often preferred, giving you the most stable image. Bob is very jittery, but may look better on real CRTs in some situations.

docs.title: Sync 480i for HDMI
docs.text: This option syncs the 480i output when playing on an HDMI display. It will improve the speed at which the resolution changes from 480i to 240p for many displays.

docs.title: Rotate
docs.text: If you need to rotate the screen 180°, go to the Audio and Video options in the OSD and toggle "Rotate" on or off.

docs.title: Dithering On/Off Toggle
docs.text: Dithering can be turned on or off. In some games this can cause undesirable color banding; in others it can clean up the checkerboard look without much loss. Find out what works best for each game.

docs.title: Render 24-bit
docs.text: Enables 24-bit rendering, which may make the graphics of some games look much smoother without needing dithering to avoid color banding. Try it out.

docs.title: Dither 24-bit for VGA
docs.text: MiSTer's Analog I/O board was not originally designed with 24-bit RGB color in mind, so only 18-bit video comes out over it. This option will dither 24-bit video sources from the PSX (most situations are not 24-bit, usually just FMV sequences from some games) so the lack of those 6 bits is not apparent over analog video. This has no effect on HDMI video and shouldn't be used if you are using a direct video adapter, which has full 24-bit RGB support.

docs.title: Widescreen Hack
docs.text: The MiSTer PSX core has a widescreen hack mode. Many games are almost entirely 3D, with very little 2D, so the visible landscape can potentially be widened without stretching the 3D models. Some games work well with this, others don't — your results may vary. Multiple aspect ratios are available — 3:2, 5:3, and 16:9 (what most modern displays use) — to leave options open for various displays and games. Example using R4 - Ridge Racer Type 4:

docs.title: Texture Filter
docs.text: The PlayStation didn't have any built-in texture filtering like some other consoles did (Nintendo 64 is a popular example). This means many of the textures had rough edges. In some cases this is fine, but in some games it can be very displeasing. This option in the MiSTer PSX core lets you smooth out the textures on 3D objects. A good example is Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2, shown in the video below:

docs.title: SPU RAM select
docs.text:
The MiSTer PSX core is the first released core which supports the optional Dual SDRAM modules. This was necessary early in development, as a single SDRAM module didn't have enough bandwidth to hold the test ROMs and small games alongside the other components that needed to be in SDRAM at the same time. Dual SDRAM has not been required for the PSX core for a long time; the official release is a single-SDRAM build compatible with the Analog I/O board.

Toggling this option while a game is running will most likely crash the game. If you have a Dual SDRAM build of the core and you enable this option, you will likely have to reset the game to get it to work.

The only known difference in the Dual SDRAM build of the MiSTer PSX core is imperceptible: the audio samples are measurably more accurate by a tiny fraction of a millisecond — the human ear can't tell that 1 or 2 out of 44,100 samples per second were dropped.

This option to use Dual SDRAM for the SPU is disabled by default in the regular releases of the core. To get a build with Dual SDRAM support, either compile the core yourself from the "PSX_DualSDRAM.qpf" Quartus project file using Quartus 17.0.2, or get the latest test build from the MiSTer FPGA Discord in the #test-builds channel.

docs.title: Miscellaneous Options
docs.text: This section covers the core's speedhacks, which can improve the performance of PlayStation games at the potential cost of some compatibility, and its information overlays.

docs.title: Fastboot
docs.text: Fast boot bypasses the BIOS boot logo and screen when starting a game. This can make it a lot quicker to get into the game; however, a small number of games may exhibit bugs or other compatibility issues. If you notice bugs in a game, turn off Fastboot first before submitting a bug report.

docs.title: Unsafe Options
docs.text:
The core offers various options to improve gameplay for some games, but those options cannot be considered stable across all games. If you use one or more of these options, the core will warn you every time you start a game.

Note: Please do not report bugs with these options turned on — first confirm whether the issue persists without them.

  • 480i to 480p hack: Renders some games at full 480p resolution, so that 480i 3D games look less jittery and have no horizontal interlacing lines interrupting the image. Only works for some full-3D 480i titles, and may look buggy in some games.
  • Turbo: Increases CPU, DMA, memory, and GTE performance by ~10% (Low), ~20% (Medium), or 50% (High). Cheats cannot be used while Turbo is on and are disabled automatically.
  • Pause when CD slow: CD data must be returned in a fixed time frame, otherwise the core will pause until the data has arrived. Disabling this removes these pauses but risks the game hanging when CD data arrives late.
  • PAL 60Hz Hack: Runs PAL games at 60 Hz. PAL games will often run faster with this hack on. Screen height is limited to 256 lines in this mode, so some games might be cropped.
  • CD Fast Seek: The CD seeks the next sector in the minimum possible time. Decreases game loading times, but some games depend on the long loading times and will crash.
  • CD Speed: Runs the CD drive at a fixed higher speed to decrease loading times, but some games depend on the long loading times and will crash. The CD automatically slows to original speed for FMVs or CD audio playback and speeds back up in loading areas. The higher speed rates are more unstable and require proper storage; BIN/CUE files perform better than CHD here.
  • Limit Max CD Speed: Holds back any new CD data until the game has processed the last data. Mostly useful to prevent CD data overrun when using higher speed modes, leading to overall faster loading times due to fewer read retries.
  • RAM: 8 MB option from development consoles. Only use for homebrew that requires it, otherwise there is a high chance of crashing games.
  • GPU Slowdown: Slows down GPU fill rate.

docs.title: Overlays
docs.text:
Three information overlays are available, disabled by default:

  • FPS Overlay - Frames per second.
  • Error Overlay - Error messages (see Error Messages below).
  • CD Slow Overlay - Displays an indicator that the CD access time is slower than expected. If you use a spinning hard disk or a NAS for ROM storage, the core will pause and wait for data if there is an unexpected delay. This indicator shows when this occurs.

docs.title: Using cheats on the MiSTer PSX core
docs.text: PSX cheats are detected differently from other MiSTer cores. On other cores, the cheat file carries a CRC32 hash in its filename, checked against the CRC32 of the loaded ROM. PSX (and other CD-based cores with cheat support) works differently: CD images are too large for a CRC32 check, so the internal Game ID is scanned instead and the cheats file with the same Game ID is loaded. For example, when Final Fantasy VII Disc 1 is loaded, MiSTer detects Game ID SCUS-94163 and loads SCUS-94163.zip from ./cheats/PSX/. Note that when the Data Cache enhancement is enabled in the OSD, cheats are disabled and will not function. This is by design.

docs.title: Core variants
docs.text:
There is an internal variant of this core referred to as PSX2XCPU (sometimes abbreviated to just PSX turbo core, or 2X).

It is not officially distributed and needs to be installed manually. We document it here strictly for reference.

This variant introduces a 2x CPU speed-up, from approximately 33 MHz to 66 MHz. Unlike other unofficial/experimental dual-SDRAM variants, it only uses one 128 MB SDRAM board. Very few games benefit from using it in comparison to the official version, as generally the Turbo option in the official core is sufficient.

In the 2X variant with Turbo on, the CPU can run at up to 3–4 times its original speed, which can be too fast: for example, the risk of games hanging is much higher.

The variant is currently a branch in the core repo.

Please do not report issues in these experimental builds.

docs.title: Error Messages
docs.text:
If there is a problem recognized by the MiSTer PSX core, an error overlay is displayed, showing which error has occurred. You can hide these messages with the "Error Overlay" OSD option, which is on by default.

List of error codes:

  • E2 - CPU exception (only relevant if the game shows issues)
  • E3 through E6 - GPU hangs (e.g. corrupt display list)
  • E7 - CPU2VRAM with mask-AND enabled
  • E8 - DMA chopping enabled
  • E9 - GPU FIFO overflow
  • EA - SPU timeout
  • EB - DMA and CPU interlock error
  • EC - DMA FIFO overflow
  • ED - CPU Data/Bus request timeout — will also appear if the BIOS is not found or is corrupt, or if no SDRAM module is installed
  • EE - Dotclock used as timer report (only relevant if the game shows issues)
  • EF - BusWidth for SPU was set to 8 Bit (but should be 16-bit)

docs.title: Saturn
docs.text: The Sega Saturn MiSTer core, originally developed by srg320 (Sergey Dvodnenko), is a suitable modern replacement for the original hardware for the vast majority of the Sega Saturn library.

docs.title: Controller/Accessories Support
docs.text:
• USB/Bluetooth:

    • Supported (maximum 2 controllers):

      • Control Pad (the default controller)
      • Mouse
      • Light guns

    • Not supported:

      • Full 3D Control Pad support 1
      • Twin-Stick
      • MIDI
      • Keyboard + FDD Operator
      • Video Card
      • NetLink
      • Floppy Disk Drive
      • Keyboard
      • Multitap

  • SNAC:

    • Supported:

      • Control Pad
      • 3D Pad
      • Virtua Gun (aka Stunner)
      • Twin-Stick (with Cyber Troopers Virtual-On)
      • Shuttle Mouse

    • Not currently supported:

      • Saturn MIDI Interface Box
      • Multitap (via SNAC) 2

docs.title: Media support
docs.text:
• Multi-disc support
  • BIN/CUE and CHD support (see CD support)
  • Multiple region support and automatic region detection

docs.title: Single BIOS
docs.text: Place a BIOS file named boot.rom in the games/Saturn folder, and the core loads it automatically at startup. For the best experience, use a region-free BIOS if you have one.

docs.title: Multiple BIOS
docs.text:
To use multiple BIOSes and/or control which one is used per game (automatically when opening the core), place files named cd_bios.rom in either:

  • the same folder as the game
  • a parent folder of the game (e.g. a folder for Japanese releases containing the Japanese Saturn BIOS, with the games in subfolders)

docs.title: OSD options
docs.text:
The core's OSD menu also allows:

  • manual loading of BIOS (when named with a *.bin extension)
  • setting automatic region detection

docs.title: Options
docs.text: This page documents a key option; see the core's OSD for the others.

docs.title: "Fast timings"
docs.text:
After loading the core, the OSD menu Hardware -> Timings offers these settings:

  • Normal (default)
  • Fast (commonly referred to as "fast timings")

While Fast is available, it can break some titles (e.g. freezes and graphical glitches) and is best not used as the default3. It exists to address issues in the Normal mode of the released core.

docs.title: Dual SDRAM vs Single SDRAM builds
docs.text:
MiSTer systems are expected to have a single 128 MB SDRAM module, and official core releases target at most one module.

As part of their development workflow, developers can start with two SDRAM modules on their development hardware for convenience (at the expense of losing some analog functionality). This provides extra bandwidth before the core is optimized for the official single-SDRAM releases that end users run.

During development, before a core reaches that stage, or when it reaches the limits of the hardware, Dual SDRAM variants of cores may be distributed unofficially in the community. Some enthusiasts also build dual-SDRAM stacks while using experimental builds.

For the Saturn core, Dual SDRAM builds are still made and discussed because the official single-SDRAM build has a few outstanding, but generally minor, issues. Some of these can currently be mitigated with the fast timings option, but not all. The Dual SDRAM releases are not official, and using the single-SDRAM builds is still encouraged.

More info here from the developer.

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text:
Limitations are documented per feature throughout this page.

The remaining GitHub issues cover these more thoroughly4.

docs.title: Source code
docs.text:
Available here.

  1. Analog triggers (to replicate the 3D Control Pad) are not currently supported. If set to the 3D Control Pad, the core simply does not feed input to the triggers (e.g. to map digital input to analog signals, or to use the 3D Control Pad's digital compatibility mode, which would be equivalent to the already supported Control Pad mode). ↩

  2. Support for multitap is not currently included in the core as of January 2026, although it was implemented previously and may be re-added at some point ↩

  3. See these comments: 1, 2 ↩

  4. Some issues may be out of date and no longer apply (and/or require more testing before closing) ↩

docs.title: SNES
docs.text: The Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES) MiSTer core has many features, such as CPU and Super FX turbo modes, lightgun and mouse support, and a configurable WRAM initialization value. It also supports nearly every enhancement chip ever released. This very powerful core was primarily developed by srg320, who didn't even have the original hardware at the time.

docs.title: Enhancement chip support
docs.text:
Here are the currently supported SNES enhancement chips, with example games that used them:

  • Super FX / GSU-1 (Star Fox, Star Fox 2, Stunt Race FX)
  • Super FX 2 / GSU-2 (Super Mario World 2: Yoshi's Island, Doom)
  • CX4 (only used in Mega Man X 2 and Mega Man X 3)
  • DSP-1 (Super Mario Kart and Pilotwings)
  • DSP-2 (only used in Dungeon Master)
  • DSP-3 (only used in SD Gundam GX)
  • DSP-4 (only used in Top Gear 3000)
  • OBC-1 (only used in Metal Combat: Falcon's Revenge)
  • S-DD1 (only used in Star Ocean and Street Fighter Alpha 2)
  • SA-1 (Kirby series, Super Mario RPG)
  • SPC7110 (Far East of Eden Zero, Momotarou Dentetsu Happy)
  • ST1010 (F1 ROC II: Race of Champions)
  • S-RTC (Daikaijuu Monogatari II)

Currently the only enhancement chips not supported are MX15001TFC (Nintendo Power Flash Cartridges), ST011 (Hayazashi Nidan Morita Shougi), and ST018 (Hayazashi Nidan Morita Shougi 2). This is mostly because the core is already near the limit of what the DE10-Nano's Cyclone V can fit.

docs.title: Satellaview Support
docs.text: The core also supports the Satellaview: place the BSX/BS-X ROM in the ./games/SNES/ folder and rename it to bsx_bios.rom. The core used to require patched ROMs, but now every original Satellaview ROM runs without patches, except those that required an Internet connection, extra peripherals, or similar.

docs.title: Super FX Turbo
docs.text: The Super FX Turbo option overclocks the Super FX chip so that games run a little faster. Combined with the Turbo CPU option, games like Star Fox get a higher framerate. However, the game then runs faster than intended, so your results may vary. Such hacks may also make bugs more likely, so please do not report bugs that occur while using Turbo options.

docs.title: TurboGrafx-16
docs.text: The MiSTer TurboGrafx16 core is an extremely accurate TurboGrafx-16 / PC-Engine implementation. Originally based on Gregory "Torlus" Estrade's FPGAPCE, it has been pushed even further to a high degree of accuracy by MiSTer devs and PC-Engine experts. It supports the SuperGrafx, CD-ROM, and Arcade Card.

docs.title: Controller Options
docs.text:
The OSD lets you change which original controller your controller simulates. For example, Pachio-Kun was played with a pachinko-style controller that had an angled slider for aiming the pachinko balls; you can use a mouse for this movement instead.

The Turbo Tap controller is also supported. This is separate from MiSTer's built-in turbo feature: the Turbo Tap had a specific turbo frequency that suits some games better, and enabling this option makes the buttons use turbo at that controller's original rate.

Another option switches to the rarely used PC-Engine 6-button controller. The "HORI Fighting Commander PC" and a few other controllers had this I–VI button layout, each with turbo tap functionality. Only a select few games supported it:

  • Advanced Variable Geo
  • Art of Fighting
  • Asuka 120% Maxima Burning Fest
  • Fatal Fury 2
  • Fatal Fury Special
  • Flash Hiders
  • Flash Hiders Taikenban (Demo)
  • Kabuki Klash
  • World Heroes II
  • Ys IV - Dawn of Ys

docs.title: Arcade card
docs.text: A few TurboGrafx16 games required the Arcade Card add-on. To run them, set the "Arcade Card" option in the "Hardware" sub-menu to "Enabled"; they should then work.

docs.title: Color palette options
docs.text: The original TurboGrafx-16's composite video encoder altered the colors from their raw RGB values — so the colors you saw on a CRT back then differ from what emulators and even RGB-modded original hardware show today. Kitrinx and Artemio Urbina developed a mathematically derived, color-corrected palette that represents the composite video output instead. Since games were likely developed with these composite colors in mind, it's kept as the default. For more vibrant colors, switch to Raw RGB via the Audio & Video → Colors option. A video demonstrating the difference:

docs.title: Overscan and border color
docs.text: The original TurboGrafx-16 had a border that was mostly hidden by the CRT's bezel. The MiSTer core leaves this overscan area hidden for a cleaner look on modern displays. To restore it — and optionally use the original system's color instead of black — change the Overscan and Border Color options.

docs.title: Extra sprites per line
docs.text: The original TurboGrafx-16 hardware had a hard limit on sprites per line — games exceeding it made sprites flicker and disappear. The MiSTer core isn't bound by this limit. The default matches the hardware, but you can set this option to "Extra" in the OSD's Audio & Video sub-menu and see whether it makes the game more pleasant. Example video:

docs.title: Audio boost options
docs.text: Some games had inconsistent audio levels compared to each other, and even between their own channels. The MiSTer TurboGrafx16 core lets you boost CD Audio, ADPCM, and all audio by varying degrees — useful when vocals are quieter than the music, sound effects feel too quiet, or a whole game is much quieter than the others.

docs.title: Analog Simulation
docs.text:
Article by MiSTer core developer Jegor van Opdorp (SupraDeus/jopdorp)

Many old computers have analog parts — for example, audio boards with partly analog synthesis, and desktop computers with tape input.

There is currently no convenient way to directly simulate electronic circuits — e.g. from their SPICE netlists — in real time on MiSTer. To implement these circuits in FPGA, you need to simulate the circuit's behavior yourself.

The Arcade-Battlezone core is an example of a core with analog sound synthesis.

docs.title: A way to approach the problem
docs.text:
1. Find YouTube videos of people playing the actual game to get an idea of the sounds it has.
  2. Play the game in an emulator, paying extra attention to sounds that differ between the emulator and the video of the actual machine.

  3. Identify the digital and analog parts of the schematic.

    • The digital parts run at the system clock speed, or sometimes at a separate clock source closer to the audible frequency spectrum. In Arcade Battlezone, for example, a 12 kHz input feeds a digital noise circuit whose output goes into an analog integrator circuit, producing the explosion sound (its implementation is listed at "inverting amplifier" below). The analog parts output at the audio sample rate, i.e. 48 kHz.

  4. Implement all the digital parts. Common digital components in sound systems include:

    • linear feedback shift register: An implementation of a similar circuit in Arcade BattleZone can be found here.

    • flip-flops, like the JK flip-flop, implemented here.

  5. Identify analog circuits with isolated behavior, i.e. 1 input, 1 output. These can be individually implemented and tested.

  6. Identify common, easily recognizable and implementable parts, such as:

    • low pass filters This can be implemented using an IIR low-pass filter; find the parameters with this spreadsheet.

    Some IIR filter implementations:

    • Blockade Low Pass Filter
    • Blockade Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) 1st Order Filter

    A simpler type:

    • Blockade Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) Filter

    • high pass filters

    • inverting amplifiers

    This is essentially a sign inversion of the sample, followed by a (fixed sign) multiplication.

    • non inverting amplifiers

    This is just a (fixed sign) multiplication of the sample.

    • differential amplifiers

    • inverting integrators

    or

    This is essentially a sign inversion of the sample, followed by a multiplication, with the result being stored in a reg.

    The multiplication is run repeatedly each audio clock cycle, resulting in a "release/decay" type amplifier envelope.

    An example of an implementation of this can be found here

    • other common opamp circuits
    • additive mixers

    An additive mixer just adds up or averages two signals. If the resistance is higher for one signal than the other, this will result in a volume difference between them.

  7. For the parts that need more attention, note them and try to guess their function. Differentiators and integrators combined with 555 timers and noise inputs can be tricky.

  8. Implement the mixers
  9. Implement the filters
  10. Implement the difficult parts of the circuit:
    1. Implement the circuit in a simulator.
    2. Figure out what input goes into the circuit when the game gets played.
    3. Run the simulation with the correct input and save the output as a .wav file.
    4. Analyze the output by viewing it in a wave editor like Audacity and listening to it.
    5. Is the input always the same (not noise), and does the circuit always respond the same way (not generating noise)? If so:
    6. Sample the output of the simulation.
    7. Convert the sample into an array literal and trigger it as needed — in this case the sample is usually just triggered by a pulse.
    8. If the analog circuit has noise as input or has variable inputs such as a number-controlled frequency or speed, you will need to:
    9. Make a mathematical model of the analog circuit.
    10. Implement the model in an easy-to-use programming language such as Python.
    11. Compare the output of the mathematical model with the output of the circuit simulation using the same inputs. They have to be close — not numerically identical, but indistinguishable to the ear.
    12. Rework your mathematical model to eliminate real-time division, in two steps:
      1. algebraically
      2. by precalculating any remaining divisions into lookup tables
    13. You can also create other kinds of lookup tables, for example a sine wave.
    14. Implement the mathematical model in HDL.
    15. Verify the outputs of the HDL with a testbench.
    16. Hook up the chip to the rest of your core!

docs.title: sys - arcade_video
docs.text: arcade_video is used mostly in arcade cores. It provides helpers to optionally enable the scandoubler (based on ini settings), handle rotation on HDMI, and optionally handle gamma and different color widths.

docs.title: Instantiating arcade_video
docs.text:
Set up the module with these parameters:

  • WIDTH - the width of one scanline
  • DW - pixel width in bits. Most arcades don't use a full 24 bits
    • 6 : 2R 2G 2B
    • 8 : 3R 3G 2B
    • 9 : 3R 3G 3B
    • 12 : 4R 4G 4B
    • 24 : 8R 8G 8B
  • GAMMA - allow gamma controls

clk_video needs to be 4x ce_pix and above 40 MHz.

    input         clk_video,
    input         ce_pix,

The fx input is driven by status[5:3], using a config string such as "O35,Scandoubler Fx,None,HQ2x,CRT 25%,CRT 50%,CRT 75%;",

docs.title: Rotating vertical games
docs.text:
Optionally add screen_rotate and pass whether the game needs to rotate counterclockwise (ccw) or clockwise (cw).

screen_rotate uses DDRAM for the rotation framebuffer. If your core needs DDRAM for something else, see MCR3 for an example that shares DDRAM between an audio file and screen_rotate; use its ddram module to share DDRAM between screen_rotate and your own hardware, instead of giving screen_rotate exclusive use of it.

screen_rotate screen_rotate
(
          .*,
          .rotate_ccw(ccw)
);

module arcade_video #(parameter WIDTH=320, DW=8, GAMMA=1)
(
    input         clk_video,
    input         ce_pix,

    input[DW-1:0] RGB_in,
    input         HBlank,
    input         VBlank,
    input         HSync,
    input         VSync,

    output        CLK_VIDEO,
    output        CE_PIXEL,
    output  [7:0] VGA_R,
    output  [7:0] VGA_G,
    output  [7:0] VGA_B,
    output        VGA_HS,
    output        VGA_VS,
    output        VGA_DE,
    output  [1:0] VGA_SL,

    input   [2:0] fx,
    input         forced_scandoubler,
    inout  [21:0] gamma_bus
);

docs.title: Core Configuration String
docs.text:
MiSTer provides an on-screen display (OSD) that can be toggled on and off by pressing F12 on your keyboard (or OSD button). For each core that is loaded, this menu can be configured to add specific options for that core.

The top-level module for the cores is emu. This does NOT mean emu is the project's top-level module — it's the top level from the core's perspective. The emu module is typically found in the SystemVerilog file (*.sv extension) with the same name as the project. As an example, the Arcade-Galaga project has its top-level module at Arcade-Galaga.sv.

The configuration string is stored in the CONF_STR variable of the emu module. This variable is passed to the hps_io module, which sends it to the processor to be read when needed. The lines of the configuration string are delimited with semicolons.

docs.title: Status Bit Map
docs.text:
Most cores have a Status Bit Map at the top of the CONF_STR section. Developers update it to show which status bits are occupied. Please use it when developing a core, because it is a helpful reference that aids collaboration: only one option can occupy a status bit, so this is important. Status bit [0] is reserved as a soft reset.

For example, with nothing occupied:

// Status Bit Map:
//             Upper                             Lower              
// 0         1         2         3          4         5         6   
// 01234567890123456789012345678901 23456789012345678901234567890123
// 0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUV 0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUV
//

If you add a status bit option like O89 to the core configuration string, it uses the first group of status bits on the left, since the "O" for option is capitalized (marked Upper). It then uses 8 and 9 from the bottom row (alphanumeric). Update the index after using these:

// Status Bit Map:
//             Upper                             Lower              
// 0         1         2         3          4         5         6   
// 01234567890123456789012345678901 23456789012345678901234567890123
// 0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUV 0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUV
//         XX

This tells other developers that status[9:8] are occupied and should not be used.

docs.title: Valid options for the menu
docs.text:
[] - means optional parameter

  • C[,{Text}] - Enables a cheat menu entry with the label {Text}.
  • CHEAT - like DIP, for arcades with a cheat system
  • D{Index} - Prefix which disables the option if menumask[Index] is set.
  • d{Index} - Same as 'D', but disables the option if menumask[Index] is NOT set.
  • DIP - in arcade cores, this will display the DIP menu from the MRA
  • F[S][#],{Ext}[,{Text}][,{Address}] - Load file button.
    • {Ext} - a concatenated list of 3-character file extensions. For example, BINGEN would be the BIN and GEN extensions.
    • Optional {Text} string is the text displayed before the extensions, such as "Load RAM". If {Text} is not specified, the default is "Load *".
    • Optional [S] - the core supports save files; load a file and mount a save for reading or writing
    • # is an explicit index (if not given, the index is generated from the line number).
    • Optional {Address} - load file directly into DDRAM at this address
    • ioctl_index from hps_io will be: ioctl_index[5:0] = index(explicit or auto), ioctl_index[7:6] = extension index

  • FC[#],{Ext}[,{Text}][,{Address}] - Open file and remember it; useful for remembering an alternative ROM, config, or other type of file. See F for how the options work.

  • H{Index} - Prefix which hides the option if menumask[Index] is set.

  • h{Index} - Same as H, but hides the option if menumask[Index] is NOT set.
  • O{Index1}[{Index2}],{Name},{Options...} - Option button that allows you to select between various choices.
    • {Index1} and {Index2} are values from 0-9 and A-V (like hex, but extending from A-V instead of A-F). This represents all 31 bits. The first and second index are the range of bits that will be set in the status register.
    • {Name} is what is shown to describe the option.
    • {Options...} - a list of comma separated options.
  • P{#},{Title} - Creates sub-page for options with {Title}.
  • P{#} - Prefix to place the option into specific {#} page. This is added before O# but after something like d#. (e.g. "d5P1o2,Vertical Crop,Disabled,216p(5x);", is correct and "P1d5o2,Vertical Crop,Disabled,216p(5x);", is incorrect and the menu options will not work.)
  • R{Index},{Name} - Same as T option but closes the OSD after selecting. Convenient for a reset option.
  • S{Slot},{Ext}[,{Text}] - Mount SD card button.
    • {Slot} - a value from 0-3. Up to four images can be mounted at the same time.
    • {Ext} - same as in F option.
    • (Optional) {Text} - The text that is displayed before the extensions like "Load RAM". If {Text} is not specified, then default is "Mount *".
  • T{Index},{Name} - Trigger button. This is a simple button that pulses the specified {Index} bit in the status register HIGH. A perfect example is a reset button.
    • {Name} is the text that describes the button function.
  • -[,TEXT] - empty (or with TEXT) line.
  • Lowercase options o, t, r are equal to their uppercase variants with 32 added to the status bit indexes.

docs.title: Non-OSD options
docs.text:
These must be placed at the bottom of the configuration string:

  • J[1],{Button1}[,{Button2},...] - J1 means lock keyboard to joystick emulation mode. Useful for keyboard-less systems such as consoles. {Button1},{Button2},... is a list of joystick buttons used in the core. Up to 12 buttons can be listed. Analog axes are not defined here. The user just needs to map them through the Menu core.
  • jn,{SNES Button Name1},[,{SNES Button2},...] - sets the default mapping of the buttons, e.g. jn,A maps joystick bit 4 to the A button on a SNES-style controller automatically
  • jp - same as jn but used when gamepad_defaults=1 in MiSTer.ini. Typically refers to positional mapping relative to a SNES controller
  • V,{Version String} - Version string. Takes the core name and appends a version string to the name displayed when the core is loaded. Note that the timestamp in the core browser (before the core is loaded) is not derived from Version String, but from the .rbf filename.
  • I,INFO1,INFO2,...,INFO255 - INFO1-INFO255 lines to display as OSD info (top left corner of screen).
  • DEFMRA,{mra name} - default MRA (e.g. Puckman.mra) to be used when the core is uploaded via USB Blaster (debug)

docs.title: jn vs. jp and mapping conventions
docs.text:
jn mapping is the default; jp mapping is used when the INI file has gamepad_defaults=1. The two differ only in their "philosophy", i.e. the convention used to map buttons: jn maps by button name, jp by button position.

Both refer to MiSTer's internal gamepad. In the Menu core, every controller is mapped to this internal SNES-style gamepad, whose buttons are ordered ABXYLR + Start + Select (button 1 = A, button 2 = B, and so on).

  • jn (name-based): map the core's A button to the internal "SNES A" button, B to "SNES B", and so on, so that the names (or order) match the original SNES definition (ABXYLR etc.). If the core has no button named "A", its first button takes that slot, its second button "SNES B", and so forth.
  • jp (position-based): map each button by its physical location. For a Genesis 3-button controller with buttons A, B, C, the mapping would be "SNES Y, SNES B, SNES A", because Y, B, and A are the lower 3 buttons of a SNES gamepad.

docs.title: Debugging (USB Blaster)
docs.text: While developing a core, it's convenient to upload it through the USB Blaster (JTAG) port directly from Quartus. MiSTer supports USB Blaster and automatically reloads the Linux part for the uploaded core. Since Linux requires a reboot (for better stability), you may notice a longer startup time — this is normal. It's advisable to have a console connected to the MiSTer to control the boot process. Once the core is compiled to RBF format and placed on the SD card, loading will be fast.

docs.title: Configuring USB Blaster on Linux
docs.text:
Although no drivers are needed on Linux, by default only the root user can access the cable. To use it as a regular user, add a file called /etc/udev/rules.d/92-usbblaster.rules with the following content:

# USB-Blaster 
SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTR{idVendor}=="09fb", ATTR{idProduct}=="6001", MODE="0666"
SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTR{idVendor}=="09fb", ATTR{idProduct}=="6002", MODE="0666"
SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTR{idVendor}=="09fb", ATTR{idProduct}=="6003", MODE="0666"

# USB-Blaster II
SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTR{idVendor}=="09fb", ATTR{idProduct}=="6010", MODE="0666"
SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTR{idVendor}=="09fb", ATTR{idProduct}=="6810", MODE="0666"

docs.title: overview of emu module
docs.text: On MiSTer, the top level is inside sys/sys_top.v. When writing or porting a MiSTer core, Quartus uses sys_top rather than your own top, and sys_top calls a module named emu that you must provide. This page documents the parameters your top level needs to implement. sys_top handles a lot of useful things like audio and HDMI video.

docs.title: Instantiating your core
docs.text: Your core should live inside an emu block — see the Template Top Level for an example. Some code in this article may be outdated; always reference the template linked above for the latest framework version.

docs.title: Master input clock
docs.text:
//Master input clock
    input         CLK_50M,

Most cores use the PLL instantiated from the sys folder, but the PLL must live in the rtl folder next to the top level (at the same level as sys), so that updating sys doesn't lose the PLL configuration.

NOTE: For full compatibility with the existing sys architecture, keep the PLL named pll and the instance named pll as shown below. Use the MegaWizard to edit the PLL and modify the required frequencies (including adding more outputs). If you don't have a PLL, create one or use the one from the template. sys_top.sdc requires the PLL name and instance name to be correct.

wire clk_sys;
pll pll
(
    .refclk(CLK_50M),
    .rst(0),
    .outclk_0(clk_sys)
);

docs.title: Reset
docs.text:
//Async reset from top-level module.
    //Can be used as initial reset.
    input         RESET,

Normally the RESET line is used in conjunction with the button on the I/O board, as well as a status flag. Most cores use status bit 0 (reserved for a soft reset), and a CONF_STR that includes an option like: "R0,Reset;"

wire reset = RESET | status[0] | buttons[1];

docs.title: HPS Bus
docs.text:
The HPS bus is used to communicate with the ARM processor. Pass it into the hps_io module, which does a lot of the work for the core and provides a simpler interface. Include hps_io in the emu module. See hps_io.

    //Must be passed to hps_io module
    inout  [45:0] HPS_BUS,

docs.title: Video Signals
docs.text:
The top-level module that calls emu includes the high-quality HDMI scaler, and provides a fairly simple interface to output video on MiSTer. Other helper modules can be included to provide proper video output.

At the simplest level, provide a CLK_VIDEO and/or CE_PIXEL (CE_PIXEL can be tied to 1 if your video clock is correct). The video clock needs to be above 40 MHz for all features to work.

Generally, the video signals should be at the emulated machine's native resolution; an old 8-bit computer, for example, generally outputs 15 kHz video. If the original device's native output was higher than 15 kHz, it's fine to output that natively through the VGA signals. The scaler uses VGA_DE (usually assign VGA_DE = ~(HBlank | VBlank);) to scale the image to HDMI according to the ini file settings.

For users who want VGA-compatible output on the VGA port, MiSTer has a built-in scandoubler, which you usually include through the video_mixer or arcade_video module. It is controlled by the forced_scandoubler signal from hps_io. Some users run 15 kHz cores on 15 kHz monitors, so the core itself shouldn't have its own built-in scandoubler.

docs.title: Video Mixer
docs.text: Use the Video Mixer module to add MiSTer framework standard features like gamma support, scaling, and scandoubling.

docs.title: Video Freak
docs.text: Use the Video Freak module to add cropping and scaling.

docs.title: Arcade Video
docs.text:
Use the Arcade Video module for arcade cores to support rotation, scandoubling, and most of the features in video_mixer. The file also includes screen_rotate, which adds HDMI rotation for vertical arcade games.

    //Base video clock. Usually equals to CLK_SYS.
    output        CLK_VIDEO,

    //Multiple resolutions are supported using different CE_PIXEL rates.
    //Must be based on CLK_VIDEO
    output        CE_PIXEL,

    //Video aspect ratio for HDMI. Most retro systems have ratio 4:3.
    //if VIDEO_ARX[12] or VIDEO_ARY[12] is set then [11:0] contains scaled size instead of aspect ratio.
    output [12:0] VIDEO_ARX,
    output [12:0] VIDEO_ARY,

    output  [7:0] VGA_R,
    output  [7:0] VGA_G,
    output  [7:0] VGA_B,
    output        VGA_HS,
    output        VGA_VS,
    output        VGA_DE,    // = ~(VBlank | HBlank)
    output        VGA_F1,
    output [1:0]  VGA_SL,
    output        VGA_SCALER, // Force VGA scaler

    input  [11:0] HDMI_WIDTH,
    input  [11:0] HDMI_HEIGHT,
    output        HDMI_FREEZE,

`ifdef MISTER_FB
    // Use framebuffer in DDRAM (USE_FB=1 in qsf)
    // FB_FORMAT:
    //    [2:0] : 011=8bpp(palette) 100=16bpp 101=24bpp 110=32bpp
    //    [3]   : 0=16bits 565 1=16bits 1555
    //    [4]   : 0=RGB  1=BGR (for 16/24/32 modes)
    //
    // FB_STRIDE either 0 (rounded to 256 bytes) or multiple of pixel size (in bytes)
    output        FB_EN,
    output  [4:0] FB_FORMAT,
    output [11:0] FB_WIDTH,
    output [11:0] FB_HEIGHT,
    output [31:0] FB_BASE,
    output [13:0] FB_STRIDE,
    input         FB_VBL,
    input         FB_LL,
    output        FB_FORCE_BLANK,

`ifdef MISTER_FB_PALETTE
    // Palette control for 8bit modes.
    // Ignored for other video modes.
    output        FB_PAL_CLK,
    output  [7:0] FB_PAL_ADDR,
    output [23:0] FB_PAL_DOUT,
    input  [23:0] FB_PAL_DIN,
    output        FB_PAL_WR,
`endif
`endif
