docs.title: DDR3 Memory Subsystem
docs.text:
//High latency DDR3 RAM interface
    //Use for non-critical time purposes
    output        DDRAM_CLK,          // any clock, no restrictions. Typically main core clock
    input         DDRAM_BUSY,         // every read and write request is only accepted in a cycle where busy is low
    output  [7:0] DDRAM_BURSTCNT,     // amount of words to be written/read. Maximum is 128
    output [28:0] DDRAM_ADDR,         // starting address for read/write. In case of burst, the addresses will internally count up
    input  [63:0] DDRAM_DOUT,         // data coming from (burst) read
    input         DDRAM_DOUT_READY,   // high for 1 clock cycle for every 64 bit dataword requested via (burst) read request
    output        DDRAM_RD,           // request read at DDRAM_ADDR and DDRAM_BURSTCNT length
    output [63:0] DDRAM_DIN,          // data word to be written
    output  [7:0] DDRAM_BE,           // byte enable for each of the 8 bytes in DDRAM_DIN, only used for writing. (1=write, 0=ignore)
    output        DDRAM_WE,           // request write at DDRAM_ADDR with DDRAM_DIN data and DDRAM_BE mask

docs.title: Writing to DDR3
docs.text: The internal DDR3 controller handles writes very efficiently, so burst writes are typically not required. To write, DDRAM_WE should be high for 1 clock cycle whenever DDRAM_BUSY is low. It writes the data in DDRAM_DIN to DDRAM_ADDR with respect to DDRAM_BE. For a single write, DDRAM_BURSTCNT should be 1. Multiple writes can also be issued without pausing when DDRAM_BURSTCNT = 1.

docs.title: Reading from DDR3
docs.text: To read one or more 64-bit words, hold DDRAM_RD high for 1 clock cycle while DDRAM_BUSY is low. It reads DDRAM_BURSTCNT 64-bit words starting at DDRAM_ADDR (counting up for bursts) and presents the results at DDRAM_DOUT — typically one per clock cycle — with DDRAM_DOUT_READY = 1 when the read is valid. Every read request has multi-cycle latency: around 20 cycles at 100 MHz is typical, but it can be much longer. Use higher DDRAM_BURSTCNT values to take advantage of DDR3's high bandwidth whenever possible.

docs.title: DDR3 Busy signal
docs.text: DDRAM_BUSY acts as an ignore signal for the request ports: whenever it is high, no request can be issued that cycle. However, a pending request causes no problem, so it's fine to e.g. set DDRAM_RD = 1 in a clocked process and only clear it when DDRAM_BUSY = 0. This lets the request signals be clocked rather than combinatorial, allowing higher clock speeds and fewer timing-closure problems.

docs.title: Single and Dual SDRAM interface
docs.text:
For a full understanding of the SDRAM interface, see the SDRAM chip's specifications. The hardware repository and schematic may also be useful.

Look through the 32 MB module's data sheet; the 64 MB module's data sheet isn't as detailed.

Some examples of SDRAM usage in existing cores:

  • Single-port direct usage: Gameboy
  • Multi-port request/response: Gameboy Advance
  • Complex bank machine: JT Frame
    //SDRAM interface with lower latency
    output        SDRAM_CLK,
    output        SDRAM_CKE,
    output [12:0] SDRAM_A,
    output  [1:0] SDRAM_BA,
    inout  [15:0] SDRAM_DQ,
    output        SDRAM_DQML,
    output        SDRAM_DQMH,
    output        SDRAM_nCS,
    output        SDRAM_nCAS,
    output        SDRAM_nRAS,
    output        SDRAM_nWE,

`ifdef MISTER_DUAL_SDRAM
    //Secondary SDRAM
    //Set all output SDRAM_* signals to Z ASAP if SDRAM2_EN is 0
    input         SDRAM2_EN,
    output        SDRAM2_CLK,
    output [12:0] SDRAM2_A,
    output  [1:0] SDRAM2_BA,
    inout  [15:0] SDRAM2_DQ,
    output        SDRAM2_nCS,
    output        SDRAM2_nCAS,
    output        SDRAM2_nRAS,
    output        SDRAM2_nWE,
`endif

docs.title: Serial Support
docs.text:
Serial is passed to the MiSTer's Linux ARM side, where software decides what to do with the data — e.g. send it to the shell, PPP, or MIDI.

Serial speeds and options are configured via CONF_STR.

    input         UART_CTS,
    output        UART_RTS,
    input         UART_RXD,
    output        UART_TXD,
    output        UART_DTR,
    input         UART_DSR,

docs.title: User port (extra USB 3.1 Type-A-style connector on MiSTer)
OSD Status
docs.text:
OSD_STATUS is 1 when the OSD is open. It can be used to pause the core while the OSD is open, and/or for autosave.

    input         OSD_STATUS

docs.title: Head On Sound PCB Implementation
docs.text:
Article by MiSTer core developer Jegor van Opdorp (SupraDeus/jopdorp)

This article contains a description of how we implemented the sound PCB of the game Head On from SEGA/Gremlin.

docs.title: First steps
docs.text:
We analyzed the schematics of the Head On sound PCB board, identifying the circuits for individual sounds and the repeated parts of the circuit.

We talked about what we thought each part was, and decided to start with the car sound.

docs.title: Finding real footage
docs.text:
Searching the web for videos with the sounds, we found a couple, but the quality was bad:

https://discord.com/channels/@me/950484205664612402/951108401801338890

https://discord.com/channels/@me/950484205664612402/951139287745851425

JimmyStones contacted the maker of the sound board to see if he had some tips. He seemed willing to help, but wasn't familiar enough with FPGAs to join the project. JimmyStones then found someone who owned a cabinet and obtained some good sound recordings, which gave us a way to validate our results.

docs.title: Car
docs.text:
We started by implementing the car sound in the Falstad simulator. It took some tweaking, mostly getting things like the diode type and transistor beta values right. We managed to get a result that sounded pretty much like the real deal.

This is the final circuit: car_circuit.txt can be loaded into the Falstad simulator. From there it is possible to record a .wav file, which we used to analyze the sound.

It turns out that the car sound consists of a repeating waveform that looks like this:

The frequency of this waveform is modulated. It starts inaudibly low. When the game starts, it follows an upward curve up to a limit. When the "high speed" button is pressed, the frequency momentarily drops and then follows a quick upward curve; when the button is released, it follows a downward curve, like so:

Based on this information we were able to come up with an implementation strategy:

  • Turn the waveform into an array
  • Turn the frequency response curve into three lookup tables:
    • One for the start of the game
    • One for when the "high speed" button is pressed
    • One for when the "high speed" button is not pressed
  • Follow the frequency curve as needed, according to the current state.

docs.title: Bonus
docs.text:
The bonus sound seemed simple at first, but turned out to be more complicated than we thought. When the bonus input goes high briefly and then low, the sound is quite simple:

We came up with an algorithm to describe this sound, and implemented it in a SystemVerilog module.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
Bonus is a pulse generator that goes to 100% amplitude immediately when the bonus pin goes high. The pulse is always running, just multiplied by an amplitude.

When the bonus pin goes low, the sound decreases in volume following an exponential curve. When the bonus pin is low, the pulse period is 3/4 of the length, resulting in a perfect fourth.

The amplitude halves every 28 ms so it's something like:

Amplitude = MaxAmplitude-((0.976^time_in_milliseconds)*MaxAmplitude)

MaxAmplitude should be set to the highest number that fits — e.g. 32 bits — to keep precision. Normally I use fixed-point math with 32 bits of precision for multiplications like this. Later we convert to 16 bits for the output.

When the bonus pin is high, the pulse period is 0.002746 s and the pulse is high 75% of the time — equivalent to a loop of:

{1,1,1,0}

The effective waveform looks like it has been through a very slight low-pass filter, giving a loop of:

{97{2}, 1, 33{0}, 1}

At 48 kHz this results in a period of 0.00275 s.

We implemented this in SystemVerilog like so:

module bonus(
    input clk,
    input clk_48KHz_en,
    input bonus_en,
    output reg[15:0] audio_out = 0
);

    localparam MAX_AMPLITUDE = 1 << 18 << 14;
    reg[1:0] WAVEFORM_SLOW[131:0];
    reg[1:0] WAVEFORM_FAST[98:0];
    assign WAVEFORM_SLOW[97] = 1;
    assign WAVEFORM_SLOW[131] = 1;
    assign WAVEFORM_FAST[73] = 1;
    assign WAVEFORM_FAST[98] = 1;

    genvar i;
    generate
        for (i = 0; i <= 96; i = i + 1) begin
            assign WAVEFORM_SLOW[i] = 2;
        end
        for (i = 98; i <= 130; i = i + 1) begin
            assign WAVEFORM_SLOW[i] = 0;
        end
    endgenerate

    genvar j;
    generate
        for (j = 0; j <= 72; j = j + 1) begin
            assign WAVEFORM_FAST[j] = 2;
        end
        for (j = 74; j <= 97; j = j + 1) begin
            assign WAVEFORM_FAST[j] = 0;
        end
    endgenerate


    localparam AMPLITUDE_RATIO_PER_TIMESTEP_18 = 262008; // z^(28ms*48khz) = 0.5, so z = 0.99948, 0.99948 * 2^18 = 262008

    reg[9:0] current_sample = 0;
    reg[68:0] amplitude = 0;

    reg last_bonus_en = 0;

    localparam SLOW_TO_FAST_RATIO_16 = 87381; // 4/3 * 2^16 = 87381.3333333
    reg[15:0] map_slow_to_fast = ((current_sample * SLOW_TO_FAST_RATIO_16) >> 16);

    always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
        if(clk_48KHz_en)begin
            last_bonus_en <= bonus_en;

            if(bonus_en)begin
                amplitude <= MAX_AMPLITUDE;

                if(current_sample == 131)begin
                    current_sample <= 0;
                end else begin
                    current_sample <= current_sample + 1;
                end
                audio_out <= (amplitude * WAVEFORM_SLOW[current_sample]) >> 18;
            end else begin 
                if(last_bonus_en)begin
                    current_sample <= map_slow_to_fast;
                    audio_out <= (amplitude * WAVEFORM_SLOW[current_sample]) >> 18;
                end else begin
                    if(current_sample >= 98)begin
                        current_sample <= 0;
                    end else begin
                        current_sample <= current_sample + 1;
                    end
                    audio_out <= (amplitude * WAVEFORM_FAST[current_sample]) >> 18;
                end
                amplitude <= (AMPLITUDE_RATIO_PER_TIMESTEP_18 * amplitude) >> 18;
            end

        end 
    end

endmodule

But it turned out that this was not the whole story. At the end of the game, the bonus pin goes high for a longer time, which triggers a different effect in which the frequency of the tone is modulated in a more complex way. We had to go back to simulation, where it turned out that the NOT gates at the bottom had the wrong voltage threshold assigned to them.

While this did not change the short bonus sound, which the machine makes when a jewel is picked up, it does change the sound when the bonus pin goes high for a longer period. It turned out that the Falstad simulator was not fast enough to simulate this circuit though.

We then turned to LTspice to see if that was quick enough.

docs.title: sys - hps_io
docs.text: HPS stands for Hard Processor System — the ARM part of the MiSTer FPGA. The hps_io.sv file contains the hps_io module, which talks to the MiSTer binary on the ARM side. It provides convenient signals that abstract the different types of I/O a core might need.

docs.title: Instantiating hps_io
docs.text:
The module has a few parameters that are used to set it up:

  • CONF_STR - how the HPS reads the OSD configuration string
  • PS2DIV - divides clk_sys to create a slower clock for the legacy PS/2 signals (ps2_kbd_clk_out, etc.)
  • WIDE - makes the ioctl data and sd_buff signals 8-bit (WIDE=0) or 16-bit (WIDE=1); when wide, ioctl_addr is incremented by 2
  • VDNUM - Virtual Device Number — can be 1 to 10, creating extra virtual block devices
  • BLKSZ - Block Size — sets the block size of the block device: 0 = 128, 1 = 256, 2 = 512 (default), ... 7 = 16384
  • PS2WE - PS/2 Write Enable — option to use two-way PS/2 communication. See the ao486 core.

clk_sys is the system clock — make sure to use the same clock when reading from these signals. HPS_BUS should be passed through from the top-level emu.

//
// Use buffer to access SD card. It's time-critical part.
//
// WIDE=1 for 16 bit file I/O
// VDNUM 1..10
// BLKSZ 0..7: 0 = 128, 1 = 256, 2 = 512(default), .. 7 = 16384
//
module hps_io #(parameter CONF_STR, CONF_STR_BRAM=1, PS2DIV=0, WIDE=0, VDNUM=1, BLKSZ=2, PS2WE=0)
(
    input             clk_sys,
    inout      [48:0] HPS_BUS,

docs.title: Joystick input
docs.text:
MiSTer supports up to 6 players on separate joysticks. joystick_0–joystick_5 are digital joysticks: the first 4 bits are the directions, and the rest are buttons that can be mapped with the J option in CONF_STR.

  • joystick_x[0] = right
  • joystick_x[1] = left
  • joystick_x[2] = down
  • joystick_x[3] = up

Analog joysticks are supported via joystick_l_analog_x / joystick_r_analog_x. The values are analog -127..+127, Y: [15:8], X: [7:0]. Depending on how you want to use the values, you may need to renormalize them. -128 is omitted so it's easier to invert the direction. l is the left stick and r the right stick on a PlayStation-style controller.

Paddles — paddle_x — are input devices that have a range from 0 to 255. They do not spin fully.

Spinners — spinner_x — look like paddles, but have no stop in the hardware and spin freely. They use an extra bit 8 that toggles with each update. The value is in bits 0:7, ranging -128..+127 — relative, and usually between -8 and 8.

    // buttons up to 32
    output reg [31:0] joystick_0,
    output reg [31:0] joystick_1,
    output reg [31:0] joystick_2,
    output reg [31:0] joystick_3,
    output reg [31:0] joystick_4,
    output reg [31:0] joystick_5,

    // analog -127..+127, Y: [15:8], X: [7:0]
    output reg [15:0] joystick_l_analog_0,
    output reg [15:0] joystick_l_analog_1,
    output reg [15:0] joystick_l_analog_2,
    output reg [15:0] joystick_l_analog_3,
    output reg [15:0] joystick_l_analog_4,
    output reg [15:0] joystick_l_analog_5,

    output reg [15:0] joystick_r_analog_0,
    output reg [15:0] joystick_r_analog_1,
    output reg [15:0] joystick_r_analog_2,
    output reg [15:0] joystick_r_analog_3,
    output reg [15:0] joystick_r_analog_4,
    output reg [15:0] joystick_r_analog_5,

    // paddle 0..255
    output reg  [7:0] paddle_0,
    output reg  [7:0] paddle_1,
    output reg  [7:0] paddle_2,
    output reg  [7:0] paddle_3,
    output reg  [7:0] paddle_4,
    output reg  [7:0] paddle_5,

    // spinner [7:0] -128..+127, [8] - toggle with every update
    output reg  [8:0] spinner_0,
    output reg  [8:0] spinner_1,
    output reg  [8:0] spinner_2,
    output reg  [8:0] spinner_3,
    output reg  [8:0] spinner_4,
    output reg  [8:0] spinner_5,

docs.title: Buttons
docs.text:
Buttons from the top-level emu are what the hardware sees. Buttons from hps_io can include emulated button presses from the OSD, HPS, etc.

  • buttons[1] is the user button
  • buttons[0] is the OSD button
    // I/O board button press simulation (active high)
    // b[1]: user button
    // b[0]: osd button
    output      [1:0] buttons,

docs.title: Forced Scandoubler
docs.text:
forced_scandoubler is set to 1 when the user wants the scandoubler turned on.

    output            forced_scandoubler,

docs.title: Direct Video
docs.text:
direct_video is set to 1 when the MiSTer is using HDMI as a VGA port with a proper converter.

    output            direct_video,

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
The status bits are used by the OSD to provide the core with the values the user picks in the OSD. For example, the status string:

    "O1,Colors,NTSC,PAL;",

would set status[1] to 0 for NTSC and 1 for PAL. See the CONF_STR documentation for all of the OSD options.

  • status_menumask - used to tell the OSD to turn options on and off via the H or h option. Set bit 0 to affect H0.
  • status_in, status_set - when status_set is 1, the hps_io will grab the status_in and use it to change the status bits
    output reg [63:0] status,
    input      [63:0] status_in,
    input             status_set,
    input      [15:0] status_menumask,

docs.title: Info
docs.text:
• info - info string to display from CONF_STR
  • info_req - ask HPS to display info string on OSD
    input             info_req,
    input       [7:0] info,

docs.title: Force a new Video mode
docs.text:
• new_vmode - if the core needs to force the system to change video modes, it can set this flag 
        //toggle to force notify of video mode change
    input             new_vmode,

docs.title: Virtual Hard Drives and Block Devices
docs.text:
Hard drive images are loaded with the S option in the OSD. Up to 10 images can be mounted at once if VDNUM is set to 10; 1–10 are valid values.

When an image is mounted, a bit is set in img_mounted, and img_readonly and img_size become valid for that img_mounted bit. Save these values into registers if you'll need them later.

These are block devices, so to read or write you first specify the block, then assert rd or wr — addresses start streaming through sd_buff_addr.

There is no wait line, because it's assumed you'll write one block of data into DPRAM and it writes immediately.

To read data, set the sb_lba to the block number you want to seek to. Then set the correct bit in sd_rd to 1, and the HPS will respond by raising the correct bit in sd_ack, and keeping it high for the duration of the read. The HPS will then use sd_buff_addr and sd_buff_dout and sd_buff_wr to count from 0 to BLKSZ and send a byte per clock. After reaching the last byte, it will clear the sd_ack.

To write data, set the sb_lba to the block number you want to seek to. Then set the correct bit in sd_wr to 1. Similar to a read, it will raise the sd_ack bit, and count the sd_buff_addr - the core will respond by setting each sd_buff_din to the data it wants to write. After the block is written (sd_buff_addr reaches BLKSZ) sd_ack will be cleared.

When the user unmounts the image from the OSD, img_mounted will go high, and the img_size will be set to zero. That is how the core knows to unmount the current image.

  • sd_lba[VDNUM] - logical block address - this is the block we want to start accessing
  • sd_blk_cnt - number of blocks
  • sd_rd - read number of blocks starting at address
  • sd_wr - write number of blocks starting at address

  • sd_ack - data read on the sd_buff_out is valid OR that write data must be valid on sd_buff_in[VDNUM]

  • sd_buff_addr - byte address

  • sd_buff_dout - data from disk
  • sd_buff_din[VDNUM] - data to disk
  • sd_buff_wr - Typically the read data from the blk interface is written into a FIFO or other DPRAM construct. This is a supplied control signal for the write signal to that FIFO
    // SD config
    output reg [VD:0] img_mounted,  // signaling that new image has been mounted
    output reg        img_readonly, // mounted as read only. valid only for active bit in img_mounted
    output reg [63:0] img_size,     // size of image in bytes. valid only for active bit in img_mounted


    // SD block level access
    input      [31:0] sd_lba[VDNUM],
    input       [5:0] sd_blk_cnt[VDNUM], // number of blocks-1, total size ((sd_blk_cnt+1)*(1<<(BLKSZ+7))) must be <= 16384!
    input      [VD:0] sd_rd,
    input      [VD:0] sd_wr,
    output reg [VD:0] sd_ack,

    // SD byte level access. Signals for 2-PORT altsyncram.
    output reg [AW:0] sd_buff_addr,
    output reg [DW:0] sd_buff_dout,
    input      [DW:0] sd_buff_din[VDNUM],
    output reg        sd_buff_wr,

docs.title: ROM and File loading, NVRAM saving
docs.text:
Boot ROMs are automatically loaded using the ioctl lines. You can also have ROMs loaded via the F option in the OSD, or via an MRA.

  • ioctl_download - 1 when data is being downloaded.
  • ioctl_index - [15:6] is the file type, [5:0] the file number
  • ioctl_wr - high when each byte is valid.
  • ioctl_addr - address of byte from / to file - counts by two if set to wide
  • ioctl_dout - data going to core from HPS (ROM)
  • ioctl_din - data going to HPS from core - e.g. to save NVRAM
  • ioctl_upload - indicate there is an active upload
  • ioctl_upload_req - set to 1 to ask the HPS to initiate an NVRAM save, for autosave, HPS only reads this when the OSD is open
  • ioctl_rd - data is valid to read
  • ioctl_file_ext - this is the file extension as a string
  • ioctl_wait - set this flag to 1 if the core isn't ready to process another byte from the HPS (flow control)
    // ARM -> FPGA download
    output reg        ioctl_download = 0, // signal indicating an active download
    output reg [15:0] ioctl_index,        // menu index used to upload the file
    output reg        ioctl_wr,
    output reg [26:0] ioctl_addr,         // in WIDE mode address will be incremented by 2
    output reg [DW:0] ioctl_dout,
    output reg        ioctl_upload = 0,   // signal indicating an active upload
    input             ioctl_upload_req,
    input      [DW:0] ioctl_din,
    output reg        ioctl_rd,
    output reg [31:0] ioctl_file_ext,
    input             ioctl_wait,

Note: boot.rom is sent via ioctl_index == 0, boot1.rom is sent with [5:0] set to 0 and [15:6] set to 1, boot2.rom and so on.

docs.title: SDRAM board size
docs.text:
// [15]: 0 - unset, 1 - set. [1:0]: 0 - none, 1 - 32MB, 2 - 64MB, 3 - 128MB
    // [14]: debug mode: [8]: 1 - phase up, 0 - phase down. [7:0]: amount of shift.
    output reg [15:0] sdram_sz,

docs.title: RTC
docs.text:
The RTC will pass the core the time from the HPS. If the HPS doesn't have the optional RTC board, it will pick up the time from an NTP server.

NOTE: the RTC only sends the time once, when the core starts. After that, the core is responsible for incrementing the seconds, or the seconds and the other fields of the RTC structure.

In BCD:

  • RTC[7:0] - seconds
  • RTC[15:8] - minutes
  • RTC[23:16] - hour
  • RTC[31:24] - month day
  • RTC[39:32] - month
  • RTC[47:40] - year
  • RTC[55:48] - week day
    // RTC MSM6242B layout
    output reg [64:0] RTC,

    // Seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00
    output reg [32:0] TIMESTAMP,

docs.title: UART Flags
docs.text:
// UART flags
    output reg  [7:0] uart_mode,
    output reg [31:0] uart_speed,

docs.title: Keyboard emulation
docs.text:
The hps_io module has two ways of accessing the keyboard and mouse. It provides PS/2-compatible signals, useful for porting cores that expect a PS/2 keyboard, and an easier-to-use, more reliable interface.

To use the new interface, ps2_key[10] is toggled with each keypress and ps2_key[9] indicates whether the key is pressed. The rest of the bits are standard PS/2 bits, with bit 8 being the extended bit.

docs.title: Setting PS2 Keyboard lights
docs.text:
The HPS uses numlock and scrl_lock to indicate mouse/joystick1/2 emulation. If the core wants to set any of these three LEDs, it sets the corresponding bit in ps2_kbd_led_use to enable it, then uses ps2_kbd_led_status to turn the LED on/off. The LEDs are in the order:

assign ps2_kbd_led_status = {scrl_lock,num_lock,caps_lock};

This control is quite slow, so the core shouldn't use it unless it's a pseudo-static indication.

    // ps2 keyboard emulation
    output            ps2_kbd_clk_out,
    output            ps2_kbd_data_out,
    input             ps2_kbd_clk_in,
    input             ps2_kbd_data_in,

    input       [2:0] ps2_kbd_led_status,
    input       [2:0] ps2_kbd_led_use,

    output            ps2_mouse_clk_out,
    output            ps2_mouse_data_out,
    input             ps2_mouse_clk_in,
    input             ps2_mouse_data_in,

    // ps2 alternative interface.

    // [8] - extended, [9] - pressed, [10] - toggles with every press/release
    output reg [10:0] ps2_key = 0,

    // [24] - toggles with every event
    output reg [24:0] ps2_mouse = 0,
    output reg [15:0] ps2_mouse_ext = 0, // 15:8 - reserved (additional buttons), 7:0 - wheel movements

docs.title: Gamma
docs.text: inout      [21:0] gamma_bus,

docs.title: Extension Bus
docs.text:
This should be used sparingly — it is for exceptional cases that need CD access, as in the TurboGrafx16 core. It requires code on the HPS in the MiSTer binary.

    // for core-specific extensions
    inout      [35:0] EXT_BUS

docs.title: Compiling for MiSTer
docs.text: MiSTer combines several compiled components: a customized minimal Linux kernel, a bootloader, the Main MiSTer binary written in C, and cores built on the MiSTer framework in VHDL, Verilog, and SystemVerilog. Compiling the full stack requires a variety of tools.

docs.title: To compile MiSTer FPGA cores
docs.text:
The vast majority of MiSTer FPGA cores currently use Quartus 17.0.2 for compilation. Download links for Windows and Linux:

Download URL SHA1 Checksum Linux 02aebab728d54e3ca8660d2646fdf93bc669b0ac Windows 01d1f9cea037cf4b8c666da1193f94ba626b6fb3

The Linux version is intended for Ubuntu 18.xx; you may have to download some missing dependencies if you use a newer version or another distribution.

Open the .qpf file of the MiSTer core you wish to compile in Quartus and press Compile (the play button).

docs.title: General prerequisites for ARM Cross Compiling
docs.text:
Only some of these prerequisites are strict. This guide was tested on Ubuntu 20.04.5 LTS in WSL2; other distros may work, but your results may vary. Install the prerequisites for compiling the Main MiSTer binary and Linux kernel this way:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt-get install build-essential git libncurses-dev flex bison openssl libssl-dev dkms libelf-dev libudev-dev libpci-dev libiberty-dev autoconf liblz4-tool bc curl gcc git libssl-dev libncurses5-dev lzop make u-boot-tools libgmp3-dev libmpc-dev

Download the correct cross-compiler for compiling ARM binaries on a 64-bit x86-based system:

wget -c https://developer.arm.com/-/media/Files/downloads/gnu-a/10.2-2020.11/binrel/gcc-arm-10.2-2020.11-x86_64-arm-none-linux-gnueabihf.tar.xz

Extract this archive somewhere convenient — it will be added to PATH; here it's extracted to /opt:

tar xf gcc-arm-10.2-2020.11-x86_64-arm-none-linux-gnueabihf.tar.xz -C /opt

Add this to your PATH temporarily each time you compile:

export PATH=/opt/gcc-arm-10.2-2020.11-x86_64-arm-none-linux-gnueabihf/bin:$PATH

Note: On WSL2 (the author's setup), you may have to run these export commands again after logging out — this may not be the case in your scenario. There are ways to set them permanently, or you can pass them to make as parameters (e.g. PATH=/opt/gcc-arm-10.2-2020.11-x86_64-arm-none-linux-gnueabihf/bin:$PATH make -j30).

docs.title: Main MiSTer Binary
docs.text: The Main MiSTer binary is a good place to start for this guide.

docs.title: Linux (including WSL)
docs.text:
Clone the Main_MiSTer repository:

git clone https://github.com/MiSTer-devel/Main_MiSTer.git

Then cd into the created directory and run make.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
With Apple Silicon, the commonly used toolchains do not run directly as they are built for x86_64.

You can take advantage of an IDE with devcontainers support as the Main MiSTer repo includes a devcontainer configuration.

Make sure you have enough RAM available or you will experience disconnects. For Colima, the following appears sufficient to compile MiSTer quickly: 

colima start --cpu 4 --memory 8

After the devcontainer is set up, you can proceed as before and run make.

docs.title: MiSTer Linux Kernel
docs.text:
Edit your sources file:

sudo nano /etc/apt/sources.list

Uncomment all of the lines which start with deb-src and then run the following:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get build-dep linux

To be continued — contributions welcome.

docs.title: Arcade ROMS and MRA Files
docs.text: This page explains most of the intricacies of the way MiSTer handles ROMs for Arcade systems.

docs.title: MRA Format
docs.text: Because some arcade boards can change games by just putting in new ROMs, it made sense to move the RBF files out of the menu list and browse the MRA files instead. These MRA files specify which RBF file to use and which MAME ROM zip files to merge on the fly into a ROM to pass to the arcade core — the old a.pacman.rom-style ROM, built from either merged or non-merged MAME ROMs.

docs.title: Example file layout
docs.text:
/_Arcade/<game name>.mra
/_Arcade/cores/<game rbf>.rbf
/games/mame/<mame rom>.zip
/games/hbmame/<hbmame rom>.zip
There are other locations for these files based on search paths.

docs.title: Example MRA file
docs.text:
<misterromdescription>
  <name>Donkey Kong (US set 1)</name>
  <mratimestamp>201911270000</mratimestamp>
  <mameversion>0216</mameversion>
  <setname>dkong</setname>
  <year>1981</year>
  <manufacturer>Nintendo of America</manufacturer>
  <category>Maze / Monkeys</category>
  <category>Platform</category>
  <category>Platform / Mario Bros.</category>
  <rbf>DonkeyKong</rbf>
<!-- switches element taken from "Pac-Man (Midway).mra"; for demonstration purposes only -->
  <switches default="FF,FF,C9">
    <dip bits="15"    name="Cabinet" ids="Cocktail,Upright"/>
    <dip bits="16,17" name="Coinage" ids="2c/1cr,1c/1cr,1c/2cr,Free Play" values="3,1,2,0"/>
    <dip bits="18,19" name="Lives" ids="1,2,3,5"/>
    <dip bits="20,21" name="Bonus Life After" ids="10000,15000,20000,None"/>
    <dip bits="22"    name="Difficulty" ids="Hard,Normal"/>
  </switches>
  <buttons names="Jump,Start 1P,Start 2P,Coin" default="A,Start,Select,R"/>
<!-- rom index 1 or any other index can pass additional information to a rom.
useful to say this rom is game A or game 1.  Use it in case of multiple games for
the same RBF, e.g. Dig Dug 2, Mappy -->
  <rom index="1">
    <part>0A</part>
  </rom>
<!-- romstruct element taken from "Two Tigers.mra"; for demonstration purposes only -->
  <romstruct>
ROM structure
00000 - 0BFFF  48k CPU1
0C000 - 0FFFF  16k CPU2
10000 - 13FFF  16k GFX1
14000 - 1BFFF  32k GFX2
  </romstruct>

<!-- the nvram node is used to download and upload the nvram memory. When the user hits "Save Settings" in the OSD it triggers ioctl_upload. This isn't available in Donkey Kong because it didn't originally have NVRAM -->
<nvram index="4" size="1024"/>



<!-- rom index 0 is the standard rom. The zip will be added to the name inside the part, unless the
part has its own zip. The md5 will be checked at the end. A file not found error is reported before an md5
error. -->
  <rom index="0" zip="dkong.zip" md5="05fb1dd1ce6a786c538275d5776b1db1" type="merged|nonmerged|split">
    <part crc="ba70b88b" name="c_5et_g.bin"/>
<!-- interleave element taken from "Crater Raider.mra"; for demonstration purposes only -->
    <interleave output="32">
    <part crc="579a8e36" name="crvid.a4"  map="0001"/>
    <part crc="2c2f5b29" name="crvid.a3"  map="0001"/>
    <part crc="5bf954e0" name="crvid.a6"  map="0010"/>
    <part crc="9bdec312" name="crvid.a5"  map="0010"/>
    <part crc="4b913498" name="crvid.a8"  map="0100"/>
    <part crc="9fa307d5" name="crvid.a7"  map="0100"/>
    <part crc="7a22d6bc" name="crvid.a10" map="1000"/>
        <part crc="811f152d" name="crvid.a9"  map="1000"/>
    </interleave>
<!-- begin kill screen fix -->
    <patch offset="0xf7d">
FE 04 38 02 3E 04 47 A7 17 A7 17 A7 17 80 80 C6 
28
    </patch>
<!-- end kill screen fix -->
    <part crc="d6412358" name="c-2j.bpr"/>
    <part crc="b869b8f5" zip="another.zip" name="v-5e.bpr"/>
    <part crc="b869b8f5" name="v-5e.bpr" offset="1024" length="1024"/>
    <part repeat="3328">00</part>
    <part>
80 80 80 80 80 80 7F 7F 7F 7F 7F 7F 7F 80 80 80
    </part>
  </rom>
<!-- If the first rom0 fails the md5 checksum, it will go ahead and try again if another entry is present.
Otherwise it will skip the additional entries.
-->
  <rom index="0" zip="dkong.zip" md5="05fb1dd1ce6a786c538275d5776b1db1">
  </rom>
</misterromdescription>

When creating a core, you can pass additional data in using ioctl_index > 0. 

// Retrieve Title No.
always @(posedge clk_sys) begin
   if (ioctl_wr & (ioctl_index==1)) tno <= ioctl_dout[3:0];
end

docs.title: Explanation for XML elements and attributes
docs.text:
• name: As an element this indicates what the ROM should be called. The value should be taken from MAME. As an attribute this indicates an external ROM file (or part thereof) that should be loaded by MiSTer.
  • mratimestamp: This indicates the date on which the .mra file was created (useful for users to determine if a newer version of the .mra file is available). The date format is YYYYMMDD.
  • mameversion: This indicates which version of a MAME romset the *.mra file is based on (which version was used for testing). The dot in MAME's version numbering is omitted.
  • setname: This indicates the name of the romset used as given by MAME. It is used to overwrite the core ID specified in the *.rbf file so that individual settings can be saved on a per romset basis.
  • year: This indicates the year the game was released. The format is YYYY and the value should be taken from MAME.
  • manufacturer: This indicates the manufacturer of the game. The value should be taken from MAME.
  • rbf: This indicates the filename (sans path and extension) of the core that should be used to run the game.
  • buttons: This indicates the default button mapping for the game. As the name implies, it applies to buttons only, not to directional controls. The names attribute specifies how the buttons are called in the MiSTer OSD, while the default attribute specifies how they are mapped to the virtual MiSTer gamepad. Each name corresponds to a bit in the joystick_X port output from hps_io, starting at bit 4 (bits 0-3 are the directional controls). Use '-' to pad for any unused bits. The buttons include not only player inputs but also start buttons, coins, pause, etc. How you arrange these bits is up to you: they can map directly to I/O ports in the emulated hardware, or they can be arbitrary — they are configured in the OSD in the order they appear in the attribute — and subsequently re-mapped to hardware ports in your core.
  • switches: This is to define the dip switches present on the arcade board. As this is a bit more complex, there is a specific section for it below.
  • nvram: This tells MiSTer to save the NVRAM data on Save Settings in the OSD. If an NVRAM was saved, it will be sent to the core as well.
  • romstruct: This is to give information about the rom structure, how the rom memory is mapped. Information contained herein is intended as a comment for other developers and not actually used by MiSTer.
  • remark: Free-form remarks for other developers; not used by MiSTer.
  • rom: Part, patch and interleave elements must have a rom element as a parent element. An index attribute with a value of 1 tells multigame cores which machine configuration to use. For passing actual rom data you need an index value of 0. The md5 attribute is used to specify the md5 checksum. The md5 checksum is calculated and checked by MiSTer after the whole rom is created according to the given *.mra file. You can use the Linux console to find out the checksum calculated by MiSTer when it starts the core (the command line to do so is /media/fat/MiSTer rbffilename mrafilename). ROMs whose checksum differs from the one specified in the *.mra file won't load. Specifying the md5 checksum as "none" will disable this check.
  • part: The part element is only allowed inside a rom element. It is used for specifying a part of the rom. The content of a part can either be embedded as a hex value into the .mra file itself (if copyright law allows) or there can be a reference to an external file via the name attribute. If the external file is in a different zip file than the parent rom element, the filename of the zip file must be specified via the zip* attribute.
    • The crc attribute specifies the CRC32 checksum of the respective part (format: eight hex digits). If a crc value is specified, MiSTer will try to select the appropriate file by crc, reverting to the filename in the name attribute only if the crc value does not match. This increases compatibility of the *.mra file with different MAME versions of the romset. As crc values are only relevant for external files, a crc value should only be given to a part element when there is a reference to an external file.
    • The repeat attribute only applies to embedded parts and indicates for how long (not how many times) the sequence should be repeated. By default decimal numbers are assumed. Hex numbers must be preceded with "0x".
    • Inside the rom element, the offset and length attributes only apply to external files. To use the offset attribute for internal data, the patch element must be used. Offset indicates the location inside the file from where MiSTer should start reading and length indicates the length of the sequence that MiSTer should be reading. By default decimal numbers are assumed. Hex numbers must be preceded with "0x".
    • The map attribute specifies to only read certain parts of the corresponding part element. For example a value of "0001" (binary) means to read only every fourth byte while a value of "1010" (binary) means to read only every first and third byte. To byteswap a part you need to set a map attribute value of 21 (decimal) and enclose the respective part element in an interleave tag.
  • patch: The patch element is only allowed inside a rom element. It is applied after the whole rom is created from its parts and overwrites the content of the rom with the content of the patch element, starting from the specified offset and for the length of the patch element's content.
  • interleave: The interleave element is only allowed inside a rom element and can only be used as parent element to one or more part elements. Together with the mandatory output attribute the interleave element can be used to specify that the child part elements should be read in a certain way. For example, an output value of "32" (decimal) indicates that the child part elements' ROM data should be treated as 32-bit.

docs.title: Dip Switches
docs.text:
Dip switch support in the latest version of MRA is used instead of the status bits. The DIP config string is listed in the core, and the core is responsible for reading up to 64 bits of DIP data sent via ioctl_index 254.

reg [7:0] sw[8];
always @(posedge clk_sys) if (ioctl_wr && (ioctl_index==254) && !ioctl_addr[24:3]) sw[ioctl_addr[2:0]] <= ioctl_dout;

The switches element holds the DIP switch settings, and default holds the default bytes. These let the arcade default to the proper factory settings. This is useful when the factory settings aren't all OFF/OFF/OFF. Note that in the default hexadecimal string, the leftmost byte refers to DIP bits 7:0, the next byte to 15:8 and so on. The most significant byte thus occupies the rightmost part of the string.

 <switches default="FF,FF,C9">

The value C9 will apply to DIP bits 23:16.

The dip tag lets you add a DIP switch entry. The bit number (starting at 0) is based on how the core was written — MAME source code can often help you understand the bits. The numbering depends on the ROM used, the arcade core, and how things are laid out.

  • bits: bit numbers sent to the core in ioctl_data
  • name: title for the OSD
  • ids: title for each option in the OSD
  • values: if you want the values to be different from 0,1,2,3, you can reorder them
    <dip bits="16,17" name="Coinage" ids="2c/1cr,1c/1cr,1c/2cr,Free Play" values="3,1,2,0"/>

docs.title: Porting Cores
docs.text:
MiSTer uses quite complex hardware, but thanks to open source, developers with different levels of hardware and software knowledge can develop for the platform. Many MiSTer cores share a common, nearly identical block of code, called the Framework, that simplifies access to the hardware and firmware.

This guide uses the ZX Spectrum core as an example.

docs.title: Framework
docs.text:
Most of the Framework's sources are located in the sys folder.

For a new project, you typically need to copy the following files/folders:

  • sys folder
  • jtag.cdf
  • jtag_lite.cdf
  • zxspectrum.qpf (project file — keep it read-only so switching between full and lite versions doesn't automatically change it and spam your change history)
  • zxspectrum.qsf
  • zxspectrum.srf (warning ignores)
  • zxspectrum-lite.qsf
  • zxspectrum-lite.srf (warning ignores)

Then make some changes:

  • Rename the zxspectrum.* files for your new project.
  • Inside the files, find the word "zxspectrum" and replace it with your project's name.
  • At the end of the *.qsf files you'll find the list of project files — remove files not related to your project.

The initial set of files for the new project is now ready, and you can open the project in Quartus 17.0 or higher.

Assuming you are porting an existing core to MiSTer, the top module entity should be renamed to emu. See zxspectrum.sv and its input/output signals:

module emu
(
    //Master input clock
    input         CLK_50M,

    //Async reset from top-level module.
    //Can be used as initial reset.
    input         RESET,

    //Must be passed to hps_io module
    inout  [48:0] HPS_BUS,

    //Base video clock. Usually equals to CLK_SYS.
    output        CLK_VIDEO,

    //Multiple resolutions are supported using different CE_PIXEL rates.
    //Must be based on CLK_VIDEO
    output        CE_PIXEL,

    //Video aspect ratio for HDMI. Most retro systems have ratio 4:3.
    //if VIDEO_ARX[12] or VIDEO_ARY[12] is set then [11:0] contains scaled size instead of aspect ratio.
    output [12:0] VIDEO_ARX,
    output [12:0] VIDEO_ARY,

    output  [7:0] VGA_R,
    output  [7:0] VGA_G,
    output  [7:0] VGA_B,
    output        VGA_HS,
    output        VGA_VS,
    output        VGA_DE,    // = ~(VBlank | HBlank)
    output        VGA_F1,
    output [1:0]  VGA_SL,
    output        VGA_SCALER, // Force VGA scaler

    input  [11:0] HDMI_WIDTH,
    input  [11:0] HDMI_HEIGHT,
    output        HDMI_FREEZE,

    output        LED_USER,  // 1 - ON, 0 - OFF.

    // b[1]: 0 - LED status is system status OR'd with b[0]
    //       1 - LED status is controlled solely by b[0]
    // hint: supply 2'b00 to let the system control the LED.
    output  [1:0] LED_POWER,
    output  [1:0] LED_DISK,

    // I/O board button press simulation (active high)
    // b[1]: user button
    // b[0]: osd button
    output  [1:0] BUTTONS,

    input         CLK_AUDIO, // 24.576 MHz
    output [15:0] AUDIO_L,
    output [15:0] AUDIO_R,
    output        AUDIO_S,   // 1 - signed audio samples, 0 - unsigned
    output  [1:0] AUDIO_MIX, // 0 - no mix, 1 - 25%, 2 - 50%, 3 - 100% (mono)

    //ADC
    inout   [3:0] ADC_BUS,

    //SD-SPI
    output        SD_SCK,
    output        SD_MOSI,
    input         SD_MISO,
    output        SD_CS,
    input         SD_CD,

    //High latency DDR3 RAM interface
    //Use for non-critical time purposes
    output        DDRAM_CLK,
    input         DDRAM_BUSY,
    output  [7:0] DDRAM_BURSTCNT,
    output [28:0] DDRAM_ADDR,
    input  [63:0] DDRAM_DOUT,
    input         DDRAM_DOUT_READY,
    output        DDRAM_RD,
    output [63:0] DDRAM_DIN,
    output  [7:0] DDRAM_BE,
    output        DDRAM_WE,

    //SDRAM interface with lower latency
    output        SDRAM_CLK,
    output        SDRAM_CKE,
    output [12:0] SDRAM_A,
    output  [1:0] SDRAM_BA,
    inout  [15:0] SDRAM_DQ,
    output        SDRAM_DQML,
    output        SDRAM_DQMH,
    output        SDRAM_nCS,
    output        SDRAM_nCAS,
    output        SDRAM_nRAS,
    output        SDRAM_nWE,

    // there are more needed signals - see the Template_MiSTer repository
);
These signals are the main connections to MiSTer. You need to modify your core according to these signals.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Most top-level signals should be self-explanatory and more or less familiar to core developers, so this section only covers the important parts that need attention to make your core work.

input   RESET

This signal is asserted while the ARM side is initializing. It can be used as an initial reset. It won't be asserted again during the entire runtime of the core except when the user chooses another core from the OSD. Then the ARM will assert RESET in the existing core to let it stop any activity before switching to another core (cores loaded through USB Blaster won't get this "bye-bye" RESET).

If the core uses DDR3 memory (the scaler doesn't count), the initial and bye-bye RESETs are crucial for correct operation. You will get a hard hang if DDR3 is accessed during RESET.

inout  [48:0] HPS_BUS

Pass it as-is to the hps_io module.

output        CLK_VIDEO,
output        CE_PIXEL,
output  [12:0] VIDEO_ARX,
output  [12:0] VIDEO_ARY,
output        VGA_DE,

Besides other well-known VGA_* signals, these signals are important in MiSTer to get a proper display. CLK_VIDEO and CE_PIXEL are used to sample the pixels. If the pixel rate equals CLK_VIDEO, then set CE_PIXEL=1. Many cores have a common system clock where the pixel frequency is the system clock divided by some number. In this case, set CLK_VIDEO to the system clock and assert CE_PIXEL at clock cycles where a new pixel is produced. Look in zxspectrum.sv to see how it's done.

Without CLK_VIDEO, you can still have VGA output, but the OSD won't work.

VIDEO_ARX and VIDEO_ARY define aspect ratio on HDMI output. It doesn't affect VGA output. Usually VIDEO_ARX=4, VIDEO_ARY=3 or VIDEO_ARX=16, VIDEO_ARY=9. Other values are possible, but extreme values may cause video problems.

VGA_DE is another crucial part for MiSTer. It's the inverse of the blank signals — ~(VBlank | HBlank) — with caveats: the HDMI video scaler detects the horizontal resolution from the first active video line, so make sure the first line isn't cut by misaligned VBlank and HBlank signals, or you'll get messed-up HDMI video.

VGA_HS and VGA_VS should have positive pulse polarity.

output        AUDIO_S

Make sure you set the correct signed/unsigned mode, otherwise audio will be distorted.

DDRAM_* signals belong to DDR3 memory. If the core can use this memory instead of SDRAM, it won't require an SDRAM board.

SDRAM_* signals belong to SDR SDRAM memory. The core will require an SDRAM board if it uses these signals.

docs.title: HPS_IO
docs.text:
The supplementary module hps_io.v is also required in the same entity (see zxspectrum.sv). It provides I/O control to and from the ARM side. Most signals are the same as or similar to MiST signals (the user_io+data_io or mist_io modules), so cores ported from MiST usually connect 1:1.

MiSTer has some changes/improvements over original MiST io modules:

  • Supports up to 4 images mounted at the same time (MiST has only 1). Set the module parameter VDNUM to 2..4 if more than one mounted image is required. If VDNUM=1, the related signals are the same as in MiST.
  • Because the SD card on MiSTer uses multiple partitions and holds other parts vital to MiSTer, cores cannot access the whole SD card — only image files. Cores requiring direct access to the whole SD card should be redesigned to access images only.
  • The Main MiSTer file system on the SD card is exFAT, which supports files larger than 4 GB.
  • OSD supports up to 15 lines (versus 7 in MiST), which is handy for many cores.
  • ARM↔FPGA communication runs over a parallel bus, which speeds it up. It supports 16-bit I/O.

The firmware has other under-the-hood improvements, like keyboard/mouse/joystick setup.

docs.title: Tips and Guidelines
docs.text: Tips and guidelines for contributing to the MiSTer project.

docs.title: Indent with tabs, not spaces
docs.text: Tabs over spaces may be controversial, but there's good reason here: the project lives on GitHub, which handles spaces poorly in diffs, git blame, and formatting. Tabs are more compatible and easier for everyone to work with.

docs.title: Comment your code when appropriate
docs.text:
Commenting takes extra time but saves everyone, including yourself, time in the long run. Be reasonably thorough. A good example from the Atari7800 core: TIA.sv starting at line 786:

module playfield
(
    input         clk,     // Master clock
    input         reset,   // System reset
    input logic   clkp,    // Pixel Clock
    input clock_t hclk,    // Horizontal clock phase 2
    input         reflect, // Control playfield, 1 makes right half mirror image
    input         cnt,     // center signal, high means right half
    input         rhb,     // Reset HBlank signal
    input [19:0]  pfc,     // Combined playfield registers
    output logic  pf       // Playfield graphics
);

When instantiating this module, the developer added a comment to the end of each input and output. Don't assume everyone knows that hclk is Horizontal clock phase 2, even if the name makes sense to you. Other good comment practices: separating sections of assignments or port instantiations by category, and explaining the "why" behind unintuitive code.

But code can also be commented too much — avoid that as well:

// The 16-bit Color Look Up Table
wire [7:0] color_lut[16] = '{
    8'd0,   8'd27,  8'd49,  8'd71,
    8'd87,  8'd103, 8'd119, 8'd130,
    8'd146, 8'd157, 8'd174, 8'd190,
    8'd206, 8'd228, 8'd255, 8'd255

wire TRANSP_DETECT; // Transparency Detection
};

The wire name color_lut already says it's a color look-up table, and TRANSP_DETECT obviously signals transparency detection — neither comment adds anything.

For an extreme and deliberately funny example:

//////////////////////////////////
/// ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ///
///  REGION PRIORITY HANDLING  ///
/// ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ///
//////////////////////////////////
case(status[28:27]) // Status Bits 27 through 28 
// Region priority is in CONF_STR section at line 256 of this file
// If line 256 is no longer valid then here is a reference to what it says:
// "D2ORS,Priority,US>EU>JP,EU>US>JP,US>JP>EU,JP>US>EU;",
// O = Option, R and S are the status bits.
// 2 status bits means there are 4 combinations of options
// Case statements for this begin with 0 and end in 3
// Since there were two switches and 4 options as explained above you can treat 0-3 as 1-4 if you'd like
// First Case Statement (0 is actually the first one)
    0: if(hdr_u) region_req <= 1; // NTSC-U Region
        else if(hdr_e) region_req <= 2; // PAL Region
        else if(hdr_j) region_req <= 0; // NTSC-J Region
        else region_req <= 1; // Set to NTSC-U if there is no region in the header
// Second Case Statement (1 is actually the second one)
    1: if(hdr_e) region_req <= 2; // PAL Region
        else if(hdr_u) region_req <= 1; // NTSC-U Region
        else if(hdr_j) region_req <= 0; // NTSC-J Region
        else region_req <= 2; // Set to PAL if there is no region in the header
// Third Case Statement (2 is actually the third one)
    2: if(hdr_u) region_req <= 1; // NTSC-U Region
        else if(hdr_j) region_req <= 0; // NTSC-J Region
        else if(hdr_e) region_req <= 2; // PAL Region
        else region_req <= 1; // Set to NTSC-U if there is region in the header
// Fourth Case Statement (3 is actually the fourth one)
    3: if(hdr_j) region_req <= 0; // NTSC-J Region
        else if(hdr_u) region_req <= 1; // NTSC-U Region
        else if(hdr_e) region_req <= 2; // PAL Region
        else region_req <= 0;  // Set to NTSC-U if there is region in the header
endcase // End of the case statement
// Okay I can put things that aren't in the case statement down here
//////////////////////////////////////////////
/// ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ///
/// END REGION OF REGION PRIORITY HANDLING ///
/// ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ///
//////////////////////////////////////////////

Please don't do things like this.

docs.title: Align ends, assignments, and proper indentation
docs.text:
Keep similar elements aligned for readability. For example, in EEPROM_24C0x.sv from NES_MiSTer, this:

// savestate
assign SS_MAP1_BACK[ 2: 0] = (state == STATE_STANDBY)  ? 3'd0 :
                             (state == STATE_TEST)     ? 3'd1 :
                             (state == STATE_ADDRESS)  ? 3'd2 :
                             (state == STATE_WRITE)    ? 3'd3 :
                                                         3'd4;

...is a lot easier to read than this:

assign SS_MAP1_BACK[ 2: 0] = (state == STATE_STANDBY) ? 3'd0 : (state == STATE_TEST) ? 3'd1 : (state == STATE_ADDRESS) ? 3'd2 : (state == STATE_WRITE) ? 3'd3 : 3'd4;

Both do the same thing, but the first is much easier to parse at a glance.

Another example:

always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (rst)
        q <=0;
    else
        if (d)
            q <= ~q;
        else
            q <= q;
end

is much easier to read than:

always @(posedge clk) begin
if (rst)
q <=0;
else
if (d)
q <= ~q;
else
q <= q;
end

Both compile successfully and are functionally identical, but the indented version is easier to parse at first glance. SystemVerilog won't throw compilation errors for bad indentation, but indent ends properly anyway. Aligning comments at the end of a line also helps readability, as in the playfield module example near the top of this page.

docs.title: Naming things to be easily understood
docs.text:
In EEPROM_STM95 in the Genesis core, this module's port instantiation uses _n to signify that the signal is "active low":

module STM95XXX
(
    //...
    input         hold_n,        // Hold (active low)
    input         cs_n,          // Chip Select (active low)
    input         wp_n,          // Write Protect (active low)
    //...
);

With this convention, a signal suffixed _n is understood to be active low without needing a comment every time.

docs.title: If you run out of DSP or Logic space accidentally
docs.text:
If you run out of space during compilation, your code may be inferred into DSP, which is very limited. Tell the compiler to use logic instead with the multstyle attribute:

(* multstyle = "logic" *) module myModule (
    input clk
)

This forces the module into logic space instead of DSP or block RAM. You can likewise force a module into DSP with (* multstyle = "dsp" *). The multstyle attribute works on module declarations, variable declarations, and binary expressions.

docs.title: Savestates
docs.text:
MiSTer defines a special API for fast savestate saving and loading. Enabling the savestate functionality on your core reserves a developer-specified section of DDR3 memory, which is used for fast savestate reads/writes. It does NOT provide any functionality for the actual saving/loading of all registers and memories in your project.

NOTE: MiSTer is currently limited in the firmware to precisely four savestate slots. You cannot add more slots using this API.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
As specified in the Core Configuration String, a core name definition can be followed by SS{base addr}:{savestate size}, which declares that the core uses savestates — e.g. MyCore;SS3E000000:1000;. This declares that savestates begin at 0x3E00_0000, each allocated 0x1000 bytes. The actual size on disk for the savestate does not have to match this allocated size; it just must be less than or equal to it. You probably want to choose a power of two, so that savestate slots 1–3 start at nice addresses.

NOTE: Most of the DDR controllers in various MiSTer projects hardcode the addresses to be in the 0x3000_0000 range, to give ample room to the MiSTer framework and CPU.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: The first 64-bit word of each savestate block (so 0x0, 0x1000, 0x2000, etc. from the example) contains two 32-bit values. The lowest 32 bits ([31:0]) act as a change detector. The higher 32 bits ([63:32]) store the size of the savestate.

docs.title: Change Detector
docs.text: The change detector notifies the MiSTer firmware that a savestate has been updated, and thus must be saved to disk. Saves are performed rather quickly after the write occurs, and do not require opening of the OSD, as block device saves do. While this value is persisted to disk as a part of the savestate writing process, it is not read again, and will be reset to 0xFFFF_FFFF on restarting the core or loading a new ROM.

docs.title: Savestate Size
docs.text:
The savestate size word defines the number of 32-bit words that should be read for the savestate, not including the initial 64-bit control word. For example, to fetch 64 bytes, set this value to 64 / 4 = 16. This value can vary between each of the 4 savestate slots, as it is independent per slot.

When the core launches, occupied slots have their size word set, and their memory contains the current file contents. Empty slots are initialized to 0.

docs.title: Actual Data
docs.text: After the initial 64 bits of control data, the remaining address space up to the savestate size defined in CONF_STR is yours to use: you can read and write the entire space as you like. The data is only persisted when the first word changes, according to the configured control size. This space is only initialized when there is a savestate file in that slot, and otherwise will contain random data. Remember that only the data denoted by the savestate size word will be persisted.

docs.title: Data on Disk
docs.text: The file persisted to disk will be savestate size control value + 2 in 32-bit words — that is, the size of the actual savestate contents plus an extra 64 bits for the control data at the start of the block.

docs.title: Useful Snippets
docs.text: Here are some useful HDL snippets as used throughout the MiSTer project, with sources linked for reference.

docs.title: Simple Pixel Clock Divider Using Clock Enable Generator
docs.text:
In any MiSTer core you develop you will need to attach a pixel clock to the CE_PIXEL signal. It's common to divide your video clock by 4 or 8, depending on the core. For simple division like this it is generally best practice to use a clock enable generator, as shown in the Tropical Angel core.

reg ce_pix;
always @(posedge clk_vid) begin // Divide video clock by 8
    reg [2:0] div;
    div <= div + 1'd1;
    ce_pix <= !div;
end

assign CE_PIXEL = ce_pix;

Adjust this simple clock enable generator's div register width to increase the division factor. [2:0] divides by 8 because 3 bits count from 0-7, etc.

docs.title: Fractional Clock Enable Generator
docs.text:
For clock division that doesn't divide evenly by 2, 4, 8, 16, etc., you may need a more complicated scheme. You could use a module like CEGen.vhd from the MegaDrive core and instantiate it with parameters:

wire ce_flt;
CEGen fltce
(
    .CLK(clk),
    .RST_N(~reset),

    .IN_CLK(53693175),
    .OUT_CLK(7056000),

    .CE(ce_flt)
);

This takes in a 53.693175 MHz clock and outputs a clock-enable register oscillating at approximately 7.056 MHz on average. Since 7.056 MHz doesn't divide evenly into the input clock, this requires fractional clock division, which is usually discouraged — it's not a 50% duty cycle, so only use it where that can't hurt. Here it was used for audio filtering, so it wasn't an issue.

docs.title: Reading a ROM's Data Stream
docs.text:
You can read the data stream from the ROM you load and trigger conditionals on it. This snippet from the SMS core switches behavior when a specific ROM version is detected:

reg  ysj_quirk = 0;

always @(posedge clk_sys) begin
    reg [31:0] cart_id;
    reg old_download;
    old_download <= cart_download;

    if(~old_download && cart_download) {ysj_quirk} <= 0;

    if(ioctl_wr & cart_download) begin
        if(ioctl_addr == 'h7ffc) cart_id[31:24] <= ioctl_dout[7:0];
        if(ioctl_addr == 'h7ffd) cart_id[23:16] <= ioctl_dout[7:0];
        if(ioctl_addr == 'h7ffe) cart_id[15:08] <= ioctl_dout[7:0];
        if(ioctl_addr == 'h7fff) cart_id[07:00] <= ioctl_dout[7:0];
        if(ioctl_addr == 'h8000) begin
            if(cart_id == 32'h13_70_01_4F) ysj_quirk <= 1; // Ys (Japan) Graphics Fix, forces VDP Version 1
        end
    end
end

As the ROM loads, the code watches for specific byte offsets (ioctl_addr values) and copies those bytes into cart_id one at a time. After the last offset, it compares cart_id against the hex value you're looking for. If your core needs special quirks for specific mappers and no standard detection scheme exists (like the mapper IDs in NES ROM headers), this lets you adjust behavior based on other unique identifiers in the ROM, matching how original hardware would behave.

docs.title: Analog Joystick Combinatorial Block with Deadzones
docs.text:
Analog joysticks like the Sony DualSense's are supported on MiSTer. If you have a specific control scheme you want to handle with analog joysticks, you can specify it as in the Inferno core.

hps_io #(.CONF_STR(CONF_STR)) hps_io
(
    //skip
    .joystick_l_analog_0(joystick_l_analog_0),
    .joystick_l_analog_1(joystick_l_analog_1),
    .joystick_r_analog_0(joystick_r_analog_0),
    .joystick_r_analog_1(joystick_r_analog_1)
);
//skip
logic [3:0] joyal_1, joyal_2, joyar_1, joyar_2;

always_comb begin
        joyal_1[3] = ($signed(joystick_l_analog_0[15:8]) < -20); // Up
        joyal_1[2] = ($signed(joystick_l_analog_0[15:8]) >  20); // Down
        joyal_1[1] = ($signed(joystick_l_analog_0[ 7:0]) < -20); // Left
        joyal_1[0] = ($signed(joystick_l_analog_0[ 7:0]) >  20); // Right

        joyar_1[3] = ($signed(joystick_r_analog_0[15:8]) < -20);
        joyar_1[2] = ($signed(joystick_r_analog_0[15:8]) >  20);
        joyar_1[1] = ($signed(joystick_r_analog_0[ 7:0]) < -20);
        joyar_1[0] = ($signed(joystick_r_analog_0[ 7:0]) >  20);

        joyal_2[3] = ($signed(joystick_l_analog_1[15:8]) < -20);
        joyal_2[2] = ($signed(joystick_l_analog_1[15:8]) >  20);
        joyal_2[1] = ($signed(joystick_l_analog_1[ 7:0]) < -20);
        joyal_2[0] = ($signed(joystick_l_analog_1[ 7:0]) >  20);

        joyar_2[3] = ($signed(joystick_r_analog_1[15:8]) < -20);
        joyar_2[2] = ($signed(joystick_r_analog_1[15:8]) >  20);
        joyar_2[1] = ($signed(joystick_r_analog_1[ 7:0]) < -20);
        joyar_2[0] = ($signed(joystick_r_analog_1[ 7:0]) >  20);
end

If the dead zone doesn't feel right, adjust the +/- integer threshold at the end of each line.

docs.title: sys - video_freak
docs.text:
video_freak is used to crop and scale the image.

video_freak takes the original VGA_DE_IN and outputs a new VGA_DE and VIDEO_ARX/VIDEO_ARY based on the cropping parameters.

module video_freak
(
    input             CLK_VIDEO,
    input             CE_PIXEL,
    input             VGA_VS,
    input      [11:0] HDMI_WIDTH,
    input      [11:0] HDMI_HEIGHT,
    output            VGA_DE,
    output reg [12:0] VIDEO_ARX,
    output reg [12:0] VIDEO_ARY,

    input             VGA_DE_IN,
    input      [11:0] ARX,
    input      [11:0] ARY,
    input      [11:0] CROP_SIZE,
    input       [4:0] CROP_OFF, // -16...+15
    input       [2:0] SCALE     //0 - normal, 1 - V-integer, 2 - HV-Integer-, 3 - HV-Integer+, 4 - HV-Integer
);

docs.title: sys - video_mixer
docs.text: video_mixer is a helper module that provides many of the video features the MiSTer framework supplies, including scandoubling, gamma, HQ2x scaling, and freezing.

docs.title: Instantiating video_mixer
docs.text:
Set up the module with these parameters:

  • LINE_LENGTH
  • HALF_DEPTH
  • GAMMA
module video_mixer
#(
    parameter LINE_LENGTH  = 768,
    parameter HALF_DEPTH   = 0,
    parameter GAMMA        = 0
)
(
    input            CLK_VIDEO, // should be a multiple of (ce_pix*4)
    output reg       CE_PIXEL,  // output pixel clock enable

    input            ce_pix,    // input pixel clock or clock_enable

    input            scandoubler,
    input            hq2x,      // high quality 2x scaling

    inout     [21:0] gamma_bus,

    // color
    input [DWIDTH:0] R,
    input [DWIDTH:0] G,
    input [DWIDTH:0] B,

    // Positive pulses.
    input            HSync,
    input            VSync,
    input            HBlank,
    input            VBlank,

    // Freeze engine
    // HDMI: displays last frame 
    // VGA:  black screen with HSync and VSync
    input            HDMI_FREEZE,
    output           freeze_sync,

    // video output signals
    output reg [7:0] VGA_R,
    output reg [7:0] VGA_G,
    output reg [7:0] VGA_B,
    output reg       VGA_VS,
    output reg       VGA_HS,
    output reg       VGA_DE
);

docs.title: Define Your Gamepad
docs.text: Next, define your gamepad's inputs, using a keyboard and the gamepad. Do this once for each kind of controller you have; the MiSTer stores a separate configuration for each device's unique ID.

docs.title: Defining your gamepad's buttons
docs.text:
Go to the second screen of the Menu core's On-Screen Display (where you ran the Downloader or WiFi scripts) and select "Define joystick buttons":

The MiSTer first detects your general controller type by asking you to press a few D-pad directions and possibly the analog sticks. It then asks you to assign buttons:

  • Four face buttons and two shoulder buttons
  • Start and Select
  • OSD button or 2-button combo (to use instead of F12 on the keyboard)
  • A few extra buttons for advanced functions

This picture shows what the requested buttons correspond to:

  • Skipping buttons: skip any button you don't want to assign (there may be many) with Space on the keyboard or the User button on your MiSTer. If you assign a wrong button, don't worry: just start the definition over.
  • Analog sticks: the L at the bottom left of the picture is an analog stick. Its definition step comes at the end of the list, so if your controller has analog sticks, go through the entire list. If you press Enter ("Finish") too early, you will skip this step and the stick won't work.
  • OSD button: if your controller has a "Home" button, as many modern controllers do, it's probably best to assign it to the OSD/Menu. If you assign neither an OSD button nor a combo, the only way to open the menu is F12 on a keyboard.

docs.title: Transferring Games
docs.text: To play games on the MiSTer, transfer them to your MicroSD card. Games can also be loaded in other ways, such as from a NAS or a USB drive (see the Advanced Networking page), but this guide sticks to the most basic method.

docs.title: The games folder
docs.text: ROMs are stored in the /games/ folder: NES ROMs go in /games/NES, for instance. Each core looks for its ROMs in a specific folder, so it's best to put them in the right place.

docs.title: File formats
docs.text:
• CD images must be in CUE/BIN or CHD format and can't be placed in zip archives — they are handled differently from other ROMs. Put each CD game in its own folder, and keep all discs of a multi-disc game in the same folder (e.g. Final Fantasy VII discs 1–3 in one Final Fantasy VII folder). This lets you change discs without resetting the core, and on the PSX core your save carries over from disc to disc. See CD-based games for details.
  • VHD (virtual hard drive) files must not be zipped either.
  • All other ROMs can be placed in zip archives. The core shows which file extensions it accepts. If a ROM won't load, the core's readme (on GitHub or in the /games/$CORE/ folder) should tell you which file types work with that core.

docs.title: Transfer ROMs over the network with FTP/SFTP/SCP
docs.text: The MiSTer has FTP and SSH servers enabled out of the box. See Network Access for how to connect to them.

docs.title: Transfer ROMs over the network with Samba/SMB
docs.text:
The MiSTer also comes with a Samba server. Once you activate it, the MiSTer's SD card appears on your network like any other shared folder:

  1. Go to the Scripts menu in the Menu core and run samba_on.
  2. On Windows, type \\MiSTer\sdcard\ in the File Explorer address bar and press Enter. On Linux and macOS, open the share the way you normally access network shares on your system.

In this example, ROMs are copied to the /games/NES/ folder for the NES core:

docs.title: Transfer ROMs to the MicroSD card directly
docs.text:
You can also turn off the MiSTer, remove the MicroSD card, and plug it into your computer. It has an exFAT partition named "MiSTer" that most operating systems can read and write.

Once your games are on the card, continue to the next step: Play a Game.

docs.title: Play a Game
docs.text:
Next, load the core for the system you want to play; this example uses the NES core. Select Console, then NES, and press Enter or the button you assigned as "A" on your controller. Once the core loads, you may need to press your assigned Menu button (or F12 on the keyboard) again to reopen the menu. Then select Load ROM and load your game.

If the game has saves, turn on Autosave. The MiSTer has to be told when to write a save to the card: without Autosave, each time you save your progress in-game (Final Fantasy for the NES, for example), you must open the On-Screen Display and select "Save Backup RAM". With Autosave on, opening the menu is all that's needed, so turning it on keeps you from forgetting. See Game saves for details.

Settings you change in a core's menu are only kept if you save them. To keep Autosave on, switch to the core's secondary OSD menu (press right on the controller) and select "Save Settings".

This short video shows how to load a core, load the game, and turn on autosave:

That's it — the basic setup is complete. Check the other sections of this documentation for more options and tips that will improve your experience.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: A MiSTer stack consists of the DE10-Nano board from Terasic, coupled with a number of add-on boards.

docs.title: Pre-built solutions and clones
docs.text:
Over time, two kinds of hardware solutions have appeared on the market:

  • pre-built kits (using the DE10-Nano)
  • clones of the DE10-Nano1 (and their equivalent pre-built kits)

This guide doesn't cover the options and their trade-offs. MiSTer is designed and tested with the DE10-Nano board and the stack described below.

docs.title: Build from scratch
docs.text:
You'll need the following to set up your MiSTer:

  • Terasic DE10-Nano
  • MicroSD card (minimum 4 GB) and a MicroSD card reader
  • USB OTG adapter or a MiSTer USB Hub add-on board (no USB devices will work without this)
  • USB keyboard
  • HDMI display and HDMI cable

Recommended:

  • MiSTer SDRAM add-on board (optional, but many cores require it)
  • USB gamepad
  • Cooling for the FPGA
  • Internet connection (required for the first update)

docs.title: Where to buy
docs.text:
DE10-Nano:

  • Terasic
  • Digikey
  • Mouser

SDRAM:

The MiSTer SDRAM add-on board is required by many cores, like the SNES, NES, PlayStation, and Game Boy cores. Multiple sellers carry them, and you can also assemble one yourself if you're skilled at soldering.

USB OTG Adapter/Hub:

The MiSTer USB Hub add-on board is preferred. You can assemble it yourself if you're good at soldering, or buy one from a shop that sells them.

If you want a very cheap option, the MakerSpot Micro USB OTG Hub works very well as a minimum.

Cooling:

The processor on the DE10-Nano is 21.5 mm × 21.5 mm, so a heatsink around that size is suitable. With a larger heatsink, make sure it doesn't touch components outside the processor.

There is no mounting mechanism for the heatsink — use an "adhesive thermal pad". 3M makes good ones, and heatsinks of this size usually come with them.

Do not apply a lot of pressure and do not touch the components directly with your fingers, as static shock can damage them.

  1. Clone boards can aim for compatibility with the MiSTer project, but minor hardware differences can cause occasional incompatibilities (they can be fixed, but that's outside the scope of the MiSTer project). Consult the respective sellers for compatibility and support. ↩

docs.title: Setup MicroSD Card
docs.text: First, install the software onto your MicroSD card.

docs.title: Flash Mr. Fusion to your MicroSD card
docs.text:
Mr. Fusion provides a compact image that you can download and flash onto an SD card of any size with a tool like balenaEtcher, Win32 Disk Imager, Apple Pi Baker, or even dd.

This guide uses balenaEtcher — download the latest release for your computer and install it.

Next, download the latest release of Mr. Fusion:

Insert the MicroSD card into your computer and open balenaEtcher. Select "Flash from file" and navigate to the Mr. Fusion file you just downloaded.

Then select your MicroSD card as the flash target.

And click "Flash!"

Wait for it to complete successfully.

"Flash complete!" and "1 Successful target" mean the flash worked. If it fails, try again, or try a different MicroSD card in case yours is faulty.

You can now close balenaEtcher and remove the MicroSD card.

docs.title: Boot the DE10-Nano with Mr. Fusion
docs.text:
Carefully insert the MicroSD card into the DE10-Nano (NOT the MicroSD slot on the I/O board on top!).

Now turn on your DE10-Nano.

The Mr. Fusion installer can take up to a few minutes. Be patient, or you may have to start all over again.

When the MiSTer On-Screen Display appears with fuzzy static behind it, the MiSTer software is installed on your MicroSD card.

Continue with the next tutorial in the sidebar.

docs.title: Running the Updater
docs.text:
You need to update the MiSTer after setting it up for the first time: a freshly installed card contains only the update script, no cores or arcade files, and its system files may be outdated.

The update needs an Internet connection. If your MiSTer has no wired connection, remove the MicroSD card, place the WiFi script in the scripts folder, and then follow the WiFi tutorial.

docs.title: Running the update
docs.text:
Once your MiSTer is connected to the Internet (wired or WiFi), run an update. The first update may take a while; later updates take much less time. Update regularly, because the framework, cores, and software are frequently updated with bug fixes, new features, and new cores.

To run the downloader, press F12 in the Menu core to open the OSD, go to Scripts, and select the downloader script. This video shows it running:

Continue to the next step: Define your gamepad.
